title: Top takeaways from Ravens’ Week 7 loss to Bengals
summary: The Baltimore Ravens gave up 35 unanswered points to the Cincinnati Bengals in the second half of Sunday’s game, resulting in their second AFC North loss in a row. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s takeaways from the game: Where are the Ravens’ leaders? With respect to the Ravens’ veteran players and coaches, it is clear that […]
full_text: Oct 25, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Cincinnati Bengals halfback Samaje Perine (34) holds back Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey (44) during the second half at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jamie Sabau-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens gave up 35 unanswered points to the Cincinnati Bengals in the second half of Sunday’s game, resulting in their second AFC North loss in a row. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s takeaways from the game: Where are the Ravens’ leaders? With respect to the Ravens’ veteran players and coaches, it is clear that leadership is lacking in Baltimore. For better and for worse, Lamar Jackson cures virtually all ills on the offensive side of the ball. He keeps his teammates focused and makes the impossible plays when they are necessary. But who is that on the Ravens defense? They have a laundry list of names – Kyle Hamilton, Roquan Smith, Marlon Humphrey, Calais Campbell, Nnamdi Madubuike – but they are all polished, well-spoke players, perhaps to a fault. Who is on the sidelines holding their teammates accountable – loudly, aggressively, if need be? Ray Lewis, Ed Reed, and Terrell Suggs may be nearly impossible to live up to, but they represent the standard nonetheless. Seeing some of those legends chime in during the game on social media made me cringe in embarrassment for the team. And, yes, the coaches deserve a glance here, too. Minter is occupied during the game, sure, but but keeping his players in the game should be Anthony Weaver’s bread-and-butter. – Nikhil Mehta Defensive coaching disappeared in the second half Cincy’s first half offense struggled, in no small part due Baltimore’s pass rush consistently collapsing the pocket around Joe Burrow. Even on plays that weren’t finished with sacks, he had to throw the ball away multiple times, leaving the Bengals’ two primary targets in Tee Higgins and Ja’Marr Chase quiet on the stat sheet. When the second half rolled around, the Bengals initially adjusted by getting the ball out quickly. The Ravens defense kept dropping additional guys back in coverage and rushing three or four, and giving Burrow all day to pick apart the zone defense over the middle of the field. Tee Higgins was out there bullying the secondary, and Burrow picked on Keondre Jackson as he tried to fill into a larger role. Some struggles are expected, even forgivable, against this tough offense, but Jesse Minter’s play0calling showed no aggressiveness to put second-half pressure on the Bengals when they needed to. By the time Cincy came away with their second touchdown, the DBs were looking around at each other like they did not even know the play call. Communication on the back end was a key hallmark of the failures in Zach Orr’s tenure, and today felt like it was a reoccurrence of those old issues. – Kevin McNelis Short yardage situations are (still) a massive issue . The Ravens’ offense cannot operate at its true potential when short-yardage situations feel like pushing a boulder up a mountain. Derrick Henry has been extremely ineffective on short runs this season, both due to his own lack of push and consistently being hit in the backfield. Baltimore needs to look at another back to carry the ball in such situations going forward, whether that is Justice Hill, Rasheen Ali, or Adam Randall when he returns from injured reserve. I would not be opposed to trading for a power back either at this point. – Dustin Cox
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 7: Recurring second-half issues apex in blowout loss
summary: For the second straight week, the Ravens allowed zero first-half points and built up a double-digit lead, only to get shut out in the second half and lose. This time, the end result was worse, as the Ravens were outscored 35-0 over the final two quarters. Here are report card grades for the team’s offense […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - OCTOBER 25: Ja'marr Chase #1 of the Cincinnati Bengals Runs into the endzone for a touchdown during an NFL football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Cincinnati Bengals at M&T Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Ben Hsu/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For the second straight week, the Ravens allowed zero first-half points and built up a double-digit lead, only to get shut out in the second half and lose. This time, the end result was worse, as the Ravens were outscored 35-0 over the final two quarters. Here are report card grades for the team’s offense and defense from a demoralizing Week 7 loss. Quarterback: C- Tyler Huntley’s final stat line is indicative of a solid performance, as he completed 68% percent of his 34 passes with over 300 total yards and a touchdown. However, after a few good drives in the first half, Huntley fizzled out as the game progressed. He was off-target on a fourth-down conversion throw and potential touchdown pass in the end zone. Huntley rushed only three times for 12 yards; his rushing prowess has strangely not been utilized much at all over the past few weeks. Running Back: D+ Derrick Henry had his worst rushing output in recent memory against the Bengals, gaining only 45 yards on 17 attempts. Henry continues to find little running room behind the Ravens’ offensive line and has not appeared as decisive lately hitting holes and breaking tackles. He’s averaging only 3.9 yards per carry on the year now. Justice Hill had six touches for 33 scrimmage yards and Rasheen Ali got a few carries late in the game. Wide Receiver: C+ Zay Flowers continues to excel despite the Ravens’ overall offensive struggles. He had one his best games of the season, totaling eight catches for 137 yards with a 48-yard touchdown on the first drive of the game. The rest of the wide receivers had minimal production. Rashod Bateman caught a pair of passes for 33 yards and Ja’Kobi Lane reeled in three receptions for 25 yards. Lane had a chance for a touchdown but the throw to him in the end zone was slightly too far outside. Tight End: C- For the second straight week, rookie Josh Cuevas was the leading receiver in the tight end room. He caught only two passes but gained 35 yards. Mark Andrews was targeted four times and caught three balls for 23 yards. Andrews has not exceeded 28 receiving yards in a game since Week 2 and also had another false start penalty in this game. Matthew Hibner returned from injury but was not a factor. Perhaps most concerning is the lack of notable blocking prowess the Ravens are getting from their tight ends. The offense definitely misses Pat Ricard and Charlie Kolar in the run game. Offensive Line: D+ The Ravens cannot buy any injury luck on the offensive line. As soon as Cam Jurgens made his debut with the team, Vega Ioane suffered a knee injury early and did not return. The Ravens had multiple pre-snap penalties again from different offensive linemen and surrendered four sacks along with seven quarterback hits. Even more concerning than their pass protection consistencies is the group’s struggles in run blocking. The Bengals had one of the worst run defenses in the league entering this game and yet they completely shut down the Ravens’ rushing attack. The Ravens continue to get little push up front and no runs of 10+ yards were created in this game. Defensive Line: D+ The Ravens were able to shut down a middling Bengals’ rushing attack, to the tune of just 73 yards on 20 carries (3.7 yards per carry). However, the Bengals were not looking to run the ball in the second half anyways when they trailed by 13 points. Baltimore’s defensive front did very little to impact the game in the second half from a pass rushing standpoint. Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones each finished with a pair of tackles and one quarterback hit, but Burrow had time to throw in the second half and picked the Ravens apart. Edge Rusher: C- The stage was set for Trey Hendrickson’s “revenge game” against his former team, but he had just one tackle with two quarterback hits. Hendrickson and the rest of the edge rusher group was not much of a factor versus Joe Burrow. Mike Green did have one nice sack and a tackle-for-loss, but Zion Young’s production continues to be a little underwhelming. This was the Ravens’ first game without Tavius Robinson and his absence was felt. Linebacker: D+ Impact plays from the Ravens’ linebacker group were not prevalent in this game. Roquan Smith and Trenton Simpson combined for 14 tackles, but they each recorded no tackles for loss, quarterback hits or sacks. Smith had a chance to make a pass breakup or interception on a pass attempt over the middle but was beaten for a catch instead. The linebackers evidently did a good job bottling up the run, but they were party to some of the struggles in pass coverage as well. Cornerback: D It was a difficult second-half performance for Marlon Humphrey, who missed multiple tackles that resulted in big gains. Humphrey and Nate Wiggins both struggled defending the Bengals’ star wide receivers. Tee Higgins dominated the Ravens for 148 yards on six catches with a touchdown and had a long 44-yard reception. Ja’Marr Chase only had 62 yards but scored a touchdown and ripped off a lot of yards after the catch. Safety: D+ Kyle Hamilton had one big tackle for loss on a third-and-short rushing attempt. Aside from that, there weren’t many successful plays from the safeties at all. Hamilton uncharacteristically missed multiple tackles including one at the goal line where the Bengals then scored. Malaki Starks did the same. With Jaylinn Hawkins sidelined, backups K’Von Wallace and Keondre Jackson both played expanded roles. Wallace had four tackles and a quarterback hit. Special Teams: C Tyler Loop bounced back in this game by making both of his field goal tries, albeit they were each 34 yards or shorter. Ryan Eckley was effective punting with three punts for 145 yards. LaJohntay Wester did not return any of the Bengals’ four punts The Ravens have not received many explosive plays in the return game this year.

title: Ravens Monday hangover discussion: recovering from collapse vs. Cincy
summary: We aren’t even close to the holiday season. Heck, we haven’t even made it to Halloween! And there are still almost two months until Festivus, the holiday created by Seinfeld that comes on December 23. But after Sunday’s loss to the Cincinnati Bengals, Baltimore Ravens fans deserve an early chance to air their grievances. In […]
full_text: Oct 25, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Baltimore Ravens head coach Jesse Minter reacts during the second quarter against the Cincinnati Bengals at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Tommy Gilligan-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect We aren’t even close to the holiday season. Heck, we haven’t even made it to Halloween! And there are still almost two months until Festivus, the holiday created by Seinfeld that comes on December 23. But after Sunday’s loss to the Cincinnati Bengals, Baltimore Ravens fans deserve an early chance to air their grievances. In todya Nikhil’s grievance: I’ll have to dive into the film to dissect what went wrong in coverage beyond individual mistakes, but on offense, the short-yardage issues are absolutely inexcusable. What is most frustrating is the variety of mistakes. A one-yard distance was extended to six after a false start three times. Derrick Henry was stuffed (again). After a couple of conversions, Declan Doyle got too cute with his play-calling. Tyler Huntley and Ja’Kobi Lane failed to connect on a potential touchdown that Lamar Jackson probably completes. Which brings me to the obvious: yes, the Ravens should be better in short-yardage in Jackson. And yet, it was already a problem when he was on the field. The solution comes from identifying the failures. Opponents are already stacking the box on third-and-short waiting to swallow up Henry – why run him into the pile when the pile includes Dexter Lawrence? Doyle found early success with two-RB ‘pony’ packages featuring Henry and Justice Hill, but the Bengals were ready when he went back to the well for a third time. The element of deception was lacking on Hill’s second-quarter sweep; Zay Flowers had only been eye candy, so the defense barely reacted to his jet motion. That actually would have been the time to mix in a sweep and keep the menu open for the rest of the game! As for the penalties, we’re well beyond the acceptable adjustment window for a new staff and a new scheme, even including the grace period for changes along the offensive line and at quarterback. (That last part matters less when full-year starters are committing the pre-snap fouls.) The Ravens have actually improved post-snap in the last three weeks, but after just two pre-snap penalties in Atlanta, they have 12 in their last two weeks. Like I said: well past acceptable.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: We asked, you answered: early grades for the Ravens’ new coaching staff
summary: Last week, Baltimore Beatdown asked Ravens fans to grade Jesse Minter’s new coaching staff through six weeks on the job. At the time, the team was 4-2 coming off a loss to the Browns featuring another blown double-digit lead in the second half. full_text: Last week, Baltimore Beatdown asked Ravens fans to grade Jesse Minter’s new coaching staff through six weeks on the job. At the time, the team was 4-2 coming off a loss to the Browns featuring another blown double-digit lead in the second half. In previous weeks, though, the Ravens closed out games against the Colts and the Titans and showed their mettle in tight wins over the Cowboys and the Falcons. Those results earned the coaching staff a B- overall grade from Baltimore Beatdown readers in last week’s survey: Minter and his staff came in with Super Bowl expectations, and through six games, the Ravens did not look consistently look like a true championship contender. There were two clear reasons for hope: the offense getting healthier, and positive adjustments from Minter as his first-year defense settles in. However, the team was still dealing with the second-half demons they tried to exorcise by firing John Harbaugh. It took some luck – a seven-second miracle and an overtime coin flip, to be exact – to reach four wins, and Baltimore’s record could just as easily be 2-4. So, all told, 4-2 is meeting but certainly not exceeding expectations this early in the seasons. Variance between B and C is probably based on different weights for injuries and expectations for improvements. Frequent commenter jack aka potato jones sums it up: I gotta give em a solid B. They obviously haven’t been perfect, but we’re seeing improvements with penalties and defense, and they’ve made the best of a terrible OL situation for the most part. I feel like an A would be at least a 5-1 record so B feels right. Of course, these grades would likely be drastically different after Sunday’s loss to the Bengals – firmly in the C range, likely with a sharp bump in D’s and as many F’s as A’s (if not more). The same will likely be true of fans’ overall confidence in the team’s direction, which was up at 79% after beating the Falcons before dropping to 48% following the Browns loss. After the catastrophe vs. Cincy, this number will plummet, potentially into the single-digits unless there is a positive update on Lamar Jackson by the middle of the week. But betting markets are hardly so fickle. The Ravens are still in a similar range to win the Super Bowl ( +1100, via FanDuel Sportsbook ) though their win total and playoff odds have taken a hit as they fall behind in the AFC North. Winning the division is not out of reach, but Baltimore probably has to sweep their remaining four matchups to do it.

title: Inside the awesomeness of Ravens WR Zay Flowers
summary: The Buffalo Bills will go from facing Puka Nacua to Brock Bowers to Zay Flowers in consecutive games. Such is life in today’s NFL, a league loaded with ridiculously talented receiving weapons. By the way, the Ravens receiver has made a legitimate case for himself as one of the game’s elite wideouts this season. You […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills will go from facing Puka Nacua to Brock Bowers to Zay Flowers in consecutive games. Such is life in today’s NFL, a league loaded with ridiculously talented receiving weapons. By the way, the Ravens receiver has made a legitimate case for himself as one of the game’s elite wideouts this season. You probably know Flower is a good player. This article aims to show you just how good Baltimore’s No. 1 receiver has become. Entering Week 8, Flowers, not Jaxon Smith-Njigba, is the NFL’s leader in yards per route run among receivers at a gaudy 3.73. The 5’9”, 182-pounder has three games with more than 115 receiving yards in his first seven contests of 2026, and Lamar Jackson has only played in four contests to date. Among receivers who’ve run at least 75 routes entering Week 8, Flowers is No. 1 in Fantasy Points Data “Separation Score.” That top spot needs context too. The difference in Separation Score between Flowers and the No. 2 wideout (Josh Down and Flowers’ teammate Rashod Bateman) is almost the exact same as the difference between those wideouts tied at No. 2 and the wideout at No. 30 in this metric (Malik Washington). Dude gets open. A LOT. Flowers has also gone 3-for-3 in contested-catch scenarios this season. And success in traffic this season hasn’t been fluky. His current career percentage in those situations is a very respectable 54.8%. The 26 year old is also one of the most elusive receivers in the NFL. That’s been the case since his rookie campaign, when he forced a whopping 19 missed tackles on 77 catches in the regular season. In 2024, Flowers forced 17 missed tackles. A season ago, it was 16 missed tackles forced. Through seven contests this season, he’s forced eight misses on his 40 receptions. And Flowers’ efficiency as a receiver has steadily increased in all four of his professional campaigns to date. His YPRR was 1.64 as a rookie, 2.25 in 2024, 2.53 last year, and it’s the aforementioned 3.73 now. Lightning quick with quality speed and high-end contact balance, Flowers is a nightmare of a cover in the slot, where he’s aligned on a career high 56.1% of the time this season. In his first three years in Baltimore, he’d be positioned on the outside on more than 60% of his snaps. Yes that was the case despite his smaller size. Whether it’s Dee Alford, one of their collection of young safeties, or if Christian Beford is asked to shadow Flowers, the Bills secondary will return from the bye with a daunting task of limiting one of the NFL’s most dynamic receiving weapons in Week 8 against the Ravens.

title: NFL trade deadline: Buffalo Bills trade candidate – Amani Hooker
summary: Let’s work back to safety as a potential trade target for the Buffalo Bills at the deadline. In doing so, let’s highlight Titans safety Amani Hooker, an eight-year steady veteran with over 5,000 snaps in his NFL career to date, who’s patrolling the third level of the defense on a now 1-6 Tennessee team. This […]
full_text: Let’s work back to safety as a potential trade target for the Buffalo Bills at the deadline. In doing so, let’s highlight Titans safety Amani Hooker, an eight-year steady veteran with over 5,000 snaps in his NFL career to date, who’s patrolling the third level of the defense on a now 1-6 Tennessee team. This article is the fifth in the trade-candidate series I plan to sprinkle onto the site until the actual trade deadline until November 10, which is 16 days from now, and lands after Week 9. Past installments in this series: Derwin James , Brian Thomas Jr. Jessie Bates , Tariq Woolen Age: 28 Like Micah Hyde, Hooker played his college ball at Iowa, and was, of course, a standout for the Hawkeyes. In his final two seasons in Iowa City, Hooker had six picks and a total of 121 tackles. He was selected by the fourth round by the Titans in 2019, a few months before he turned 21 years old. He rapidly moved into a full-time role in Tennessee and snagged four picks in his second season for the Titans while making 51 tackles with eight pass breakups. After playing more than 64% of the snaps in his third season, the Titans signed him to a three-year extension before the 2022 campaign began. In 2024, as a 26 year old, Hooker reeled in five interceptions with 71 tackles, the season after he set a career high in tackles with 85. He was held without an interception in 2025 but already has a pair of picks this season. 2026 snap splits Box: 55.1% Free safety: 30.1% Slot corner: 13.3% Like just about all of the Iowa safeties, Hooker is very well-versed at carrying out a variety of duties on the backend. While he’s moved into move of a box role in 2026, a season ago, his box and free safety snap counts were almost identical. When Hooker had those five picks in 2024, he was aligned at free safety at just over 51% of the time. He’s not a spectacular, truly game-changing All-Pro caliber type. He’s just rock solid across the board, and has a ridiculous amount of NFL experience relative to his age. At right around 6’0” and 210 pounds, Hooker has classic safety size, and he’s as quality athlete with 4.48 speed and an abrupt 6.81 three-cone drill on his pre-draft resume. How he’d fit with Bills If the Bills want a sure-thing at safety who can comfortably wear a variety of hats — with those roles changing potentially based on the matchup — Hooker might be ideal for the Bills. Yes, they do have Jalon Kilgore and Jordan Hancock waiting in the wings at safety, yet Hooker’s enormous amount of experience would provide a fantastic floor at this position for Buffalo. He has a career 12.6% missed tackle, which is neither amazing nor brutal, and that rate is carried by extreme consistency. After his rookie season, Hooker’s missed tackle rate has stayed between 10.1% and 14.8% every season. As many have astutely pointed out in the comments section of other trade-candidate profiles, there’d be serious value in trading for Hooker because he could play a high percentage of snaps. Financial obligation for Bills to trade for him 2026 salary: $8.4M If the Bills trade for Woolen after Week 9, they’d be on the hook for $4.2M in prorated 2026 base salary and $270k in potential per-game roster bonuses. If Hooker’s current contract remains untouched by the Bills, he’s signed through 2028, with a $9.57M base salary next season and an $11.79M base in 2028. Projected cost to acquire Using Syndicate32.com’s trade machine , and adding the “fire sale” stipulation to the assessment, the projected cost to trade for Hooker is a late late Round 3 pick in 2027. That feels slightly high for Hooker, although I do believe there could be a variety of clubs — including the Bills — that would very much value his experience, versatility, and consistency on the back end. Should the Bills trade for Amani Hooker? If the Bills aren’t happy with Gardner-Johnson’s play nor his on-field antics and are either on the verge of benching or releasing him, Hooker would be an excellent in-season acquisition for this defense. At the outset, the cost of a late Round 3 pick feels a little rich for my liking, but Buffalo shouldn’t be overly concerned with next year’s draft right now. And, it wouldn’t be unreasonable for the Titans to eat some of Hooker’s future money — by converting future base salary into a signing bonus — to facilitate a trade that features Buffalo’s 2027 third-round selection. In that case, count me in. Hooker is a still reasonably young, super-steady, do-everything safety… which is kinda-sorta what this Bills defense needs right now. Plus, the financial obligations over the next two seasons for Hooker are hardly expensive for a player of his caliber who won’t be 30 until June of 2028.

title: Buffalo Bills post-bye week reset
summary: It feels like the Buffalo Bills haven’t played in ages, doesn’t it? That’s the affect the bye week can have. Joe Brady’s team did finally get some distinct help from around the league, as the Bears beat the Patriots on Thursday Night Football to start Week 7 and the Seahawks handled the Chiefs in Seattle […]
full_text: It feels like the Buffalo Bills haven’t played in ages, doesn’t it? That’s the affect the bye week can have. Joe Brady’s team did finally get some distinct help from around the league, as the Bears beat the Patriots on Thursday Night Football to start Week 7 and the Seahawks handled the Chiefs in Seattle on Sunday Night Football . With the Bills back at this week, preparing for the Ravens at home on Sunday, here’s a quick reset to jog your memory on what very well could (or certainly will) happen for the Bills leading into and during the showdown with Baltimore in Week 8: DJ Moore returns to the field — It appeared the veteran receiver was ticked he wasn’t given the green light by coaches to play against the Rams or Raiders in Weeks 5 and 6, as he dealt with an aggravation of the AC joint sprain he injured in Week 2 against the Lions. He’s appeared in two full games and close to two other first halves to date this season. The receiver the Bills drafted a second-round pick for will be back on the field against the Rams at home on Sunday. He’ll bring a darn-good 2.47 yards-per-route-run figure into Week 8. Jordan Hancock gets activated off IR — This isn’t a lock. It’s likely. At the very least, his 21-day practice window will be opened. The second-year safety, who had a damn-good summer, was placed on injured reserve before Week 3’s contest against the Chargers. So he’s already missed the needed four contests to return to action, and he’s gotten the extra week because of the bye. The 6’0”, close to 200-pound safety with plus athleticism should give the Bills reeling secondary a lift, particularly if he immediately fills in for the suspended C.J. Gardner-Johnson. Even if he platoons with Jalon Kilgore and Damar Hamlin, Hancock is a young, springy specimen the Bills have only gotten 13 snaps from to date this season. Ed Oliver makes his return — Another possibility, and I feel less confident in Oliver’s return against the Ravens than Hancocks. Oliver, who was mostly durable from 2019 onward in Buffalo, has been stung by the injury bug the past two seasons now, and his latest knee injury came late in a play against the Patriots when his former teammate Reggie Gilliam blocked him from the side, buckling his knee. A decision is made on Zane Durant — The late fifth-round pick suffered a serious stinger late in the final preseason and we haven’t seen him since. He’s been eligible to have his practice window opened since after Week 4, but that, of course, hasn’t happened. The Bills could, in theory, keep him on IR as long as needed, but we very well could see a decision made on the rookie’s first year in the NFL this week. Or sometime in the near future. Thankfully for the Bills, DeWayne Carter has played admirably in one of the depth defensive tackle spots Durant could’ve conceivably played as a rookie. More youngsters on the field — Against the Raiders, Kilgore made his NFL debut, and Kaleb Elarms-Orr and T.J. Parker played a career high in snaps with 22 and 41 respectively. Of course, I don’t expect Elarms-Orr or Parker to suddenly faze out veterans in front of them, but maybe the Bills start to lean into their youth a little more coming out of the bye? More man coverage/blitzing — Through Sunday Night Football’s action in Week 7, the Bills are 20th in blitz rate and 24th in man coverage rate. Not exactly what any of us expected from Jim Leonhard’s defense. In Week 6’s win over the Raiders, Buffalo’s secondary showed signs of stinginess when in man. They blitzed Kirk Cousins on 40.5% of his dropbacks, a very high number. Maybe post-bye is when Leonhard’s scheme starts to look like… Leonhard’s scheme? What else are you looking for entering — and during — this Week 6 game vs. the Ravens?

title: Discussion: How hot is Ejiro Evero’s seat?
summary: The Carolina Panthers started the 2026 season with one of, if not the worst Week 1 defensive performance of all time. They gave up 59 points to the Chicago Bears while getting run all over. It looked like a college football game between an SEC school and a group of five school. There were gaping […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - SEPTEMBER 28: Carolina Panthers defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero during a game between the New England Patriots and the Carolina Panthers on September 28, 2025, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Carolina Panthers started the 2026 season with one of, if not the worst Week 1 defensive performance of all time. They gave up 59 points to the Chicago Bears while getting run all over. It looked like a college football game between an SEC school and a group of five school. There were gaping openings to run through and the Bears offensive line was living on the Panthers side of the line of scrimmage. Things started trending up after that game. The defense throttled the Falcons with backup quarterbacks in Week 2 and then more than held their own in subsequent weeks. Week 1 was starting to look like an aberration. Then yesterday happened. The Buccaneers picked up 322 yards of offense and scored 43 points while throwing the ball just 11 times. A lot of the points can be blamed on things outside of the defense’s control, but the yardage cannot. Only four of the Buccaneers’ 34 carries in the first three quarters were stopped for zero or negative yardage, and one of those was because Tre Tucker slipped in the backfield. Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell combined for 194 yards on 38 carries. The defense was simply powerless to stop the Bucs’ running game. It’s the second time this season we’ve seen the defense completely lost trying to defend and opponent’s ground attack. It’s not a dominant front seven on paper, but it’s not supposed to be this bad. Derrick Brown is here. The linebackers are good. The other players along the front are serviceable to good. It’s a group that should at least have a fighting chance against anyone, even if it’s not perfect. So with two games like this now on the season, does Ejiro Evero’s seat start to get hot? MY TAKE: I think it has to be. I’ve been somewhat resistant to the Evero hot seat talk in the past because he’s been dealt some pretty bad cards on his side of the ball since he got here. But the front office has invested a lot in getting that side of the ball up to par. That has improved overall outcomes, but there have still been a few too many meltdowns in high leverage spots. The defense is bottom ten in the league in opponent third down percentage and in penalties. It’s anecdotal, but it feels like an inordinate number of those errors are coming in situations where the defense should be counted on to get off the field. And now we have two instances in six games where Evero’s defense was thoroughly dominated top to bottom by an opposing offensive line. It does not feel like results are improving at the same rate as the roster, and that calls into question if Evero is the right fit as defensive coordinator for this team. I don’t think it’s time to fire him right now, but we’ve definitely reached a point where questions need to be asked.
author: Jonathan DeLong

title: The Optimist: I’ve got nothing
summary: There are not many good words that can be honestly ascribed to the Carolina Panthers abysmal 43-13 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. I’m not going to waste your time searching for them. The Panthers offense looked like their game plan was to see how far they could push a clown car with no wheels. […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 25: Zyon McCollum #27 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers hands a ball to a fan after an interception during the first half of a football game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are not many good words that can be honestly ascribed to the Carolina Panthers abysmal 43-13 loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. I’m not going to waste your time searching for them. The Panthers offense looked like their game plan was to see how far they could push a clown car with no wheels. The Panthers defense looked like they couldn’t figure out how to defend the most one-dimensional offense they will ever see. With any luck, they were caught peeking ahead at the Green Bay Packers. An inexcusable sin is suddenly our greatest hope. Consistency, as always, is our greatest challenge. The same team this season has given up 258+ yards twice this season (258 against the Bucs and 291 vs Chicago) and held Bijan Robinson and Jahmyr Gibbs to a combined 116 yards on 31 carries. Bryce Young was keeping statistical company with prime Peyton Manning and Drew Brees before he turned the ball over three times yesterday. Those three turnovers directly led to 11 more points than Young generated during the game. One game is not a trend and it doesn’t define a season. It can absolutely be cause for concern. All of the goodwill and optimism coming off of a two-week winning streak has now vanished. The Panthers will, once again, need to earn their fans back. The Bucs were low and provided a prime opportunity to for the Panthers to cement their intentions for a winning season. Baker Mayfield could hardly complete a pass downfield and that was what stood between them and their first three game winning streak since the 2021-Sam Darnold season. A win yesterday would have put the team in a strong position atop the NFC South and put them more than one game above .500 for the first time since that 2021 season as well. Instead, they proved that every game this season is likely to be a struggle. Poor protection—whose future looks worse with Taylor Moton’s fractured fibula —complemented poor run defense and whatever exactly that effort from the Carolina special teams unit was. None of these are flaws that are we can expect the team to snap back from with any immediacy. They will show up in every game to varying extents. The best news of the weekend is that the NFC South remains so hilariously bad that the Panthers are still in sole possession of first place in the division. At 3-3, all the Panthers have to do for now is beat the Green Bay Packers on Thursday Night Football. The 3-4 Atlanta Falcons have the opportunity to take the lead with a win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Tampa and a Panthers loss while the 2-5 New Orleans Saints are on a bye as they come home from Paris. This division is chaotic, but that also means it is forgiving. Yesterday was a terrible, demoralizing loss that imperiled our hopes for an NFC South repeat, but it didn’t sink them entirely. There is a lot of season left to play, so let’s all wash the taste of this game out and see what Thursday brings. Deep breaths, everybody. Let’s not burn everything down until it is cold enough outside to be worth it.

summary: Just yesterday, reports surfaced that the Chicago Bears would be aggressive at the NFL’s November 10 trade deadline and that they had already spoken with the Los Angeles Chargers about Khalil Mack. The Chargers insist they aren’t ready to trade anyone, but a loss on Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams would drop them to […]
full_text: Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles speaks at a news conference at Halas Hall on April 21, 2026, in Lake Forest, Illinois. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Just yesterday, reports surfaced that the Chicago Bears would be aggressive at the NFL’s November 10 trade deadline and that they had already spoken with the Los Angeles Chargers about Khalil Mack. The Chargers insist they aren’t ready to trade anyone, but a loss on Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams would drop them to 0-7, and that might get them to listen. Especially if other teams are willing to move their defensive linemen before the deadline and there are multiple suitors. Earlier today, NFL Insider Jordan Schultz shared a clip from his segment on Ryan Clark’s The Pivot about the two teams he expects to be most aggressive in the next two weeks. “I think we’re heading into a very active NFL trade deadline,” Schultz said. “We could see anywhere from 12 to, call it, 20 trades, and two teams I’m watching closely: the 49ers and Bears. I’ve heard both teams connected to several defensive players, including rushers Josh Sweat, Khalil Mack also DeForest Buckner. Along with some names who aren’t necessarily on the trade block. I think both Chicago and San Francisco want to be aggressive, and I’ll be shocked if they don’t make a move before the deadline.” The Bears are 5-2, second in the NFC North, and are currently the 5th seed in the NFC, and history suggests general manager Ryan Poles is willing to make an in-season trade.

title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Won vs. the Patriots
summary: The Chicago Bears hosted the defending AFC Champion New England Patriots on Thursday Night Football this past week. Here are my top three reasons Chicago won the game. Let’s get to it! 1. Belief It’s hard to summarize what we all witnessed Thursday night. Not only did Chicago host one of the best teams in […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - OCTOBER 22: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears runs the ball during an NFL football game against the New England Patriots at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears hosted the defending AFC Champion New England Patriots on Thursday Night Football this past week. Here are my top three reasons Chicago won the game. Let’s get to it! 1. Belief It’s hard to summarize what we all witnessed Thursday night. Not only did Chicago host one of the best teams in the league, but they also didn’t play their best ball in the process – which usually equates to a loss for The Beloved. But not these Bears. Not only do they believe they can beat anyone, they believe in each other. Whether it is Caleb Williams believing in Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland after they drop an easy pass early in the game, only to come up clutch when it matters most. Or the Head Coach believing in his kicker to nail a career-long kick despite already missing a shorter kick earlier in the game. We also saw the belief of the coaching staff (and GM Ryan Poles) in the players who have been brought along over the course of time to play a prominent role in the victory. Guys like D’Marco Jackson, who had never started a game before becoming a Bear, or Daniel Hardy, who had been sequestered to special teams before being called upon to play more on defense than he ever has as a Bear, only to show some serious juice off the edge rushing the passer and an ability to disrupt the passing game. We could also talk about various rookies stepping into large roles or the return of Kyler Gordon – a player many openly wondered if he had played his last snap in Chicago – but the theme is hard to miss. There is a palpable level of belief with this team. So much so that I am skeptical that the Bears win that game without it. 2. D’Andre Swift Everyone has been talking about Caleb Williams since the game ended on Thursday, and rightfully so. The Iceman was once again played like a top QB in the league and was pivotal in the win. What I don’t hear, however, is how integral D’Andre Swift was against New England. Though the stat line was nothing noteworthy to look at – 22 carries for 78 yards with a TD and a long rush of 10 yards – Swift was consistent throughout. If you have known me for a while, you have long known I have been a believer in Swift’s game, before, during, and after his first season in Chicago, when he posted some career lows across the board as a rusher. But the way his game has evolved the more time he has spent in this offense has been so fun to watch. Rightfully known as a big-play-back, it was the methodical 2-4 yard runs that wore down the Patriots’ defenders all night, where he continually ran with aggression and forward lean. Of course, you also saw a few explosive runs where he made the first guy miss in the hole and maneuvered his way through multiple other defenders when there appeared to be nowhere to run – but Swift was huge against New England, and his 26 total touches were a season high for the former Georgia Bulldog. And he said it best when he pointed out how much he needed this “mini-bye” that comes with playing on Thursday one week and Monday night the following. When he returns to action, I am sure nobody will appreciate Kyle Monangai’s return more than he will. 3. The Problem Child Tied with the aforementioned running back for third on the team in catches (4) and targets (4) against the Patriots, Luther Burden III, AKA “The Problem Child” (courtesy of Caleb Williams), made the most of each one – leading both teams in yards from scrimmage with 130 and added a single rush for 7 yards to boot. Burden was a beast on Thursday, consistently getting open for Caleb Williams and making defenders miss after the catch for extra yards. Like Swift, Burden is a big play waiting to happen each time he touches the ball, and it seems past due for him to be leading the team in targets moving forward instead of being third, which he has been in three of the last four contests. Unlike Swift, Burden picked up chunk gain after chunk gain Thursday night, where he averaged more than 30 yards per catch (!), and unlike Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland (or even Kalif Raymond), Burden caught everything thrown his way. If LB3 can continue to play the way he has and provide that spark to this offense, Chicago will be hard to stop. What about you? Who or what stood out most when you watched Chicago beat the Patriots in Primetime?

title: The First All Pro Tight End: Correcting Mike Ditka’s Place in NFL History
summary: When Mike Ditka died and the tributes poured in, we heard, as we often do, that Ditka was “the NFL’s first tight end.” That’s not quite right. In a sense, he wasn’t even the first Bears tight end. Ditka is credited as the first tight end in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. That is […]
full_text: When Mike Ditka died and the tributes poured in, we heard, as we often do, that Ditka was “the NFL’s first tight end.” That’s not quite right. In a sense, he wasn’t even the first Bears tight end. Ditka is credited as the first tight end in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. That is true. He is also the first tight end with a 1,000-yard season. But to understand why Ditka was the first tight end in Canton, you should understand the most notable “NFL first” for Iron Mike: he was the tight end who played the position so well that All Pro voting bodies added a slot just for tight end. Yesterday was the ninth annual National Tight Ends Day, founded in 2018 by two childhood Bears fans : George Kittle and Jimmy Garoppolo. It makes sense that a pair of Bears fans saw the power of tight end. Here is the story of how Mike Ditka changed NFL history and made “tight end” its own position. From “end” to end lined up tight to “tight end” — introducing Bears’ end Willard Dewveall If you search Pro Football Reference to determine the first Bears tight end, Mike Ditka’s name comes up second. Willard Dewveall comes up first. The Bears drafted Dewveall (rhymes with “ball”) in 1958, and he joined the team in ‘59 after one year in the CFL. He was an “offensive end”; the 1959 media guide listed him as an “end,” along with all other players who today we would consider either a tight end or a wide receiver. In the two-way era, before 1950, football had three buckets of positions: line, back, end. The names of the positions were generally the same on offense and defense: the starting lineups would simply list the line (same positions as today) the backs (a mix of quarterback, halfback — sometimes LHB/RHB for “left” and “right” — and fullback) and the ends: right end and left end, or RE and LE. As the passing game developed, teams began changing the formations of their backs and ends. The great NFL historian Timothy Brown outlines several key years in the evolution of the end position : Late 1920s: Teams start splitting an end one or two yards wider than usual 1938: The famed Amos Alonzo Stagg, then head coach at University of the Pacific, starts specifically using the term “split end” 1940s: The proliferation of Clark Shaughnessy’s modern T-formation leads to more teams in both college and the pros sending one end wide to spread the defense 1956: NFL teams start placing a halfback between the split end and offensive tackle to create the slotback 1957: Texas Tech officially names the end tied to the line as the “tight end” to distinguish it from the split end “The distinction caught on,” Brown writes. “By 1959, numerous NFL and college teams made the same distinction.” Nineteen fifty-nine, you will recall, was the year the Bears signed Dewveall. Teams might have ends more focused on blocking and others more focused on receiving, and the terms “tight end” vs. “split end” grew more common. But the position was still “end.” “Tight” and “split” were really just adjectives, not official position designations. Remember in Seinfeld when Jerry and Kramer accidentally toss a Junior Mint into the body of a patient during surgery, and Jerry recounts the story to George, and George is stunned that doctors didn’t notice the mint? “How could they not notice it?” George shouts. “Because it’s a little mint!” Jerry explains. And then he adds : “It’s a junior mint.” When I hear him say that, I don’t hear someone saying a brand name. I hear someone literally saying “junior” mint. That was the tight end position before Mike Ditka. Willard Dewveall didn’t play Tight End™. He played “tight” end. One newspaper in the 1959 preseason described Dewveall as playing “a tight end,” in the same way we might today call someone “a slot corner.” If Jerry and George were around in 1959, that’s how Jerry would have explained Willard Dewveall: “He’s a tight end.” “Football changes are not like an on-and-off light switch,” John Turney, another premier NFL historian, wrote upon Ditka’s death . “Changes in schemes or personnel are more like a dimmer switch, going from off gradually to on.” In January of 1961, Dewveall made a bit of fairly niche pro football history himself: he became the first player to jump leagues from the NFL to the new AFL, which had just finished its first season. Dewveall, George Halas said, “would not be missed too much.” Two weeks earlier, they had drafted his replacement. Mike Ditka: the first All Pro tight end With the #5 pick in the 1961 NFL draft, the Bears chose offensive end Mike Ditka from Pittsburgh. Just as with Dewveall, the Bears media guide listed Ditka’s position as “end.” But in George Halas’s explanation of Ditka’s value, we can once again see how the term “tight end” prior to Ditka was really just an adjective and a noun. “(Ditka) will play the closed end,” Halas said upon signing Ditka. “We’re counting on his rugged blocking to give our running a big lift.” Bears publicity man Dan Desmond echoed the term during the preseason. “We got a big guy at our closed end position, Mike Ditka,” Desmond said. “For his size, Mike’s speed amazes everybody.” This is where the All Pro definitions come in. The Newspaper Enterprise Association, or NEA, was one of many outlets that selected an All Pro team, though the NEA was different than the AP or UPI or others, because the NEA’s team was voted on by players. In 1960, the AP and NEA had the same first-team All Pro skill position designations on offense: two halfbacks, one fullback, two ends. The All Pro ends were players who today we would consider wide receivers: Raymond Berry (6’2, 187 pounds) for both outlets, with Sonny Randle (6’2, 189 pounds) for the AP and Tommy McDonald (5’9, 178 pounds) for the NEA. Then came the rookie Ditka. In his first game, the Bears listed him in the starting lineup at right end, while Johnny Morris, who we commonly think of as a wide receiver, was listed at “RH” or right halfback. The “LH” — left halfback — was Willie Galimore. Rick Casares was the fullback and Angela Coia was the left end. The Bears were already stretching the possibilities of the tight end position: through 1960, at least using Stathead’s positional designations, only one tight end had ever had a 100-yard game, and that was Dewveall, who had two such games, both in 1960. The great Packers tight end Ron Kramer (6’3, 234 pounds), known more for his blocking — and also listed as an “end” in the Packers media guide — never even had 90 yards receiving. In Ditka’s second game, he led the Bears with 130 receiving yards and a touchdown. He would have four more 100-yard games, including a then-NFL TE record 190 yards, with three TDs, against the Packers. Ditka ended the year as the team’s leading receiver and finished in the top 5 in the NFL in receptions, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns, easily the best season ever to that point for a tight end. When the 1961 All Pro teams arrived, the AP stuck with the same positions: one fullback, two halfbacks and two WR-style ends: Del Shofner (6’3, 186 pounds) and Red Phillips (6’1, 197 pounds). But the player-led NEA and sportswriter and cartoonist Murray Olderman saw that football was changing. They had three backs, with Jim Taylor, Lenny Moore as “flanker back” and Jim Brown at fullback, and two ends: Shofner at “split end” and the 6’3, 230-pound Ditka at “tight end.” “Mike is the tight end of the Chicago Bears and signifies an up-dating in the voting method,” Olderman explained. “For the first time, ends were designated as ‘tight’ and ‘split.’” This made Mike Ditka the first All Pro tight end. “Mike Ditka and a few like him introduced a new element into the concept of an all-pro team,” Olderman wrote in December of 1962 to explain Ditka’s impact. Ditka, along with Green Bay’s Kramer, “represent a unique species gaining accreditation in pro football — the tight end.” Olderman noted that Ditka and Kramer had the size to block Big Daddy Lipscomb, while Ditka also had the receiving ability that…

title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: A Tale of Two Halves
summary: “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times……” Actually, no. Reverse that. “It was the worst of times, then it was the best of times.” I have zero understanding of how the Cincinnati Bengals went into the locker room down 13-0 to the Ravens in Baltimore, looking about as bad as […]
full_text: “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times……” Actually, no. Reverse that. “It was the worst of times, then it was the best of times.” I have zero understanding of how the Cincinnati Bengals went into the locker room down 13-0 to the Ravens in Baltimore, looking about as bad as I’ve ever seen them, and definitely worse than they’ve ever looked in the Joe-Burrow era, only to turn around and outscore the Ravens 35-0 in the second half. They looked like pod people in the first half—like they were all still on their bye week and sleepwalking through the game. The offense gained a pitiful 59 yards in the first half. They only had three first downs. Then, in the second half, they gained 298 yards, picked up 19 first downs, and scored five touchdowns on five possessions. I know the Ravens have struggled in the second half of games, but this was so far beyond that. They made me think of the movie Seabiscuit . To make a long story short, it’s a true story about a racehorse that could only win once it got behind and made eye contact with another, less-talented horse (it came out in 2003, and I saw it only once, so forgive me if I’m leaving a lot out). Basically, Seabiscuit had to have his back against the wall to tap into some deep reserve of potential. It’s a neat little story about the competitive spirit and how it can transcend species. It’s NOT a neat story for my football team! Could the Bengals have pulled off a 35-0 run in the second half if Lamar Jackson had been in the game? Can they afford to play only one half of football against the Steelers or Browns (I can’t believe I’m writing this)? They have a winning record, but teams can’t play only two quarters of winning football and expect to win very often. Here are some random thoughts on Sunday’s game: The Bengals, once again, really tried to force the under-center offense in the first half. They really, really want to get that run game established. They just couldn’t do it. They have the third-fewest rushing yards in the NFL so far this season (487) and are on pace for just over 80 rushing yards per game. It’s not easy to win in the postseason when you can’t run the ball. Having said that, the offense flowing through Joe Burrow to his star wide receivers is a sight to behold. When the engine is running clean, it’s a beautiful thing. When it’s not, though, it’s incredibly frustrating. Ja’Marr Chase reportedly gave a fiery halftime speech that got everyone pumped up for the second half. They shouldn’t need a Tony D’Amato speech at halftime to get ready to play. They’re way too talented for that. Once again, Dexter Lawrence has been worth every single bit of the No. 10 overall pick. He has completely reshaped the defensive front. Al Golden’s defense is not perfect—not even close—but Lawrence makes up for so much. Tee Higgins is proving, once again, that he’s a WR1 who just happens to play on the same team as the best wide receiver in the NFL. Double Chase and leave Higgins in single coverage at your own peril. Mike Gesicki is the Bengals’ WR3. He’s a tight end in name only. It was hard seeing Erick All leave the field looking as upset as he was. He’s had a long history of injuries to his right knee dating back to college, and it’s the same knee he injured in November of the 2024 season, which kept him out for the entirety of the 2025 season. Drew Sample is the next man up. While he’s not capable of stretching the field the way All can when he’s healthy, he’s a capable blocker, and I love seeing a Sample touchdown because it’s as close as we’re going to get to a big-man TD, which is one of the greatest moments the sport has to offer fans—like the NFL’s version of a no-hitter. Shemar Stewart was a healthy scratch, and if that’s not a damning indictment of the Bengals’ scouting department, I don’t know what is. The No. 17 overall selection in the 2025 draft is fully healthy, and the Bengals decided they had a better chance to win with him not on the field. He’s been passed on the depth chart by rookie second-round pick Cashius Howell (who recorded his first sack on Sunday) and 2024 sixth-round pick Cedric Johnson. Teams are reportedly interested in a potential trade for Stewart in hopes they can develop him in a way the Bengals haven’t or can’t. I doubt he goes anywhere other than the bench, though. The Bengals return home in Week 8 to host the 1-6 Tennessee Titans, who are dealing with a ton of issues. The best way to beat them is for the Bengals to play a complete four quarters of football the way they played in the second half in Baltimore. More specifically, if they can get out to an early lead, force the ball into Cam Ward’s hands, and make the Titans one-dimensional, they will win. They’re the much better team—on paper and on the field—but they have to play like it. The best thing that could come out of Week 8 (I hate that we’re already at Week 8) is a blowout win over an outmatched and struggling team. Would I be surprised if they won 35-0? No. Would I be surprised if they won 17-14? Also no, but I’ll be mad. Who Dey! Relative Song Lyrics: An angels smile is what you sell You promised me heaven, then put me through hell Chains of love got a hold on me When passion’s a prison, you can’t break free

title: CBS reported that Ravens were surprised Lamar Jackson did not play vs. Bengals
summary: Late last week, there appeared to be some optimism that the Baltimore Ravens quarterback would suit up against the Cincinnati Bengals. Jackson hasn’t played since October 4th, and as he eased back into practice before Week 7, the Ravens changed his “week-to-week” status to “day-to-day.” Jackson spoke to the media on Friday, and while he […]
full_text: Late last week, there appeared to be some optimism that the Baltimore Ravens quarterback would suit up against the Cincinnati Bengals. Jackson hasn’t played since October 4th, and as he eased back into practice before Week 7, the Ravens changed his “week-to-week” status to “day-to-day.” Jackson spoke to the media on Friday, and while he said the injury was still painful, he did not rule out taking the field while the internet speculated on his status. The speculation didn’t last too long, as the Ravens would rule Jackson out for the game on Saturday afternoon. During Sunday’s game, the CBS broadcast crew mentioned that Baltimore was surprised that Jackson didn’t play, so Jackson may have informed the staff on Saturday that he wouldn’t be able to play, leading to even more speculation about the disconnect between Jackson and the team. When asked if he was surprised, first-year head coach Jesse Minter said it was a mischaracterization. Jesse Minter on Lamar Jackson: "Lamar is working his butt off to be back and be out there. … I think he'll be in a decent spot, but we'll know more Wednesday." He was asked about CBS broadcast reporting about his ankle having swelling after practicing, but Jesse said he… pic.twitter.com/Ev8PSrN3u4 — Sarah Ellison (@sgellison) October 26, 2026 Minter was pretty quiet on the subject after saying that “shocked” wasn’t the right word. In the end, Tyler Huntley got the start, and the Bengals left with a 35-13 victory, but it sounds like there may be more questions than answers in Baltimore when it comes to their starting player. The Bengals and Ravens will meet again on Thursday Night Football in Cincinnati on New Year’s Eve.

title: Zero to 35: The Bengals’ second half vs. Baltimore Ravens belongs in the history books
summary: It was an extremely frustrating first half of football for the Cincinnati Bengals in Baltimore on Sunday, with questions looming about their 2026 playoff viability. Heading into the locker room at the halfway mark with a 13-0 deficit, very little was working on both sides of the ball. Whatever the message and adjustments were during […]
full_text: It was an extremely frustrating first half of football for the Cincinnati Bengals in Baltimore on Sunday, with questions looming about their 2026 playoff viability. Heading into the locker room at the halfway mark with a 13-0 deficit, very little was working on both sides of the ball. Whatever the message and adjustments were during halftime worked beautifully (Joe Burrow said in a CBS postgame interview that Ja’Marr Chase was the most vocal), as the Bengals came out determined to change the course of the game. They did so with immense gusto, throttling the Ravens with 35 unanswered points in the final two quarters, while disallowing Baltimore to score again. How rare was that? The Bengals are only the 10th team in NFL history to be shut out in the first half and still score 35+ points in the second half. Their 35 second-half points are the most by a team shut out in the first half since the Minnesota Vikings scored 39 points in Week 15 of 2022 to complete the largest comeback in NFL history (trailed 33-0) against the Indianapolis Colts. Cincinnati’s Demolition Began on Offense The Bengals received the third-quarter kickoff and promptly moved down the field. Joe Burrow started to gain momentum, hitting Mike Gesicki for a touchdown to start the avalanche. Burrow started the game just 6-of-12 passing for 43 yards through the first two quarters. As the Bengals shifted to working less under center in the second half, Cincinnati’s star quarterback went 16-of-18 for 249 yards and four passing touchdowns. Ja’Marr Chase caught fire late with an electric 33-yard gain off of a short pass, and a touchdown grab a few plays later. Tee Higgins was incredible in this contest, grabbing six catches for 148 yards and a touchdown—all in the final two quarters. Cincinnati also found some semblance of the run game on Sunday, getting 55 yards and a touchdown on 15 combined carries from Samaje Perine and Chase Brown. While it’s not eye-popping, there were a couple of crucial runs that converted first downs to continue the Bengals’ barrage of Baltimore. Don’t Forget About the Defense The defense had some issues in the first half, namely on two huge conversions on third-and-long (one for a 48-yard touchdown reception by Zay Flowers) in the first two quarters. However, they did hold Baltimore to two field goal attempts when it looked like more points would have been scored. But the Bengals’ defense ended up swarming the Ravens’ offense, netting four sacks, an interception, and a stop on downs deep in their own territory in the second half. Dexter Lawrence and Co. also clamped down on Derrick Henry all day, limiting him to just 2.6 yards per carry on 17 attempts. Cincinnati’s defensive smothering of Baltimore led to this second-half sequence of Ravens’ offensive possessions: Punt (following a Bengals touchdown) Turnover on Downs Punt Interception Turnover on Downs Special Teams Continues to show up Evan McPherson didn’t have a field goal attempt opportunity, but he was 5-of-5 on extra point attempts (all in the second half). Through six games, he remains perfect on all field goal and extra point attempts. Ryan Rehkow was a bit of an anomaly with his performance, as he punted well in the first half. Baltimore had three first-half drives start at their own 3-yard line, their own 6-yard line, and their own 12-yard line. He didn’t get an opportunity to punt in the second half, with the Bengals charging for five touchdowns. While he had a bad drop early on, Dohnte Meyers atoned for the mistake with a big 31-yard punt return when the Bengals were down 13-7 in the third quarter. A Complete Team Comeback While the deplorable first half was a team effort, it was a rally by the whole team to flip this game on its head. Kudos to the Bengals coaches and players for lighting a fire under everyone at halftime, and perfect execution in all phases for the final two quarters of the game. Some cynics may point to Lamar Jackson’s absence and/or the Ravens’ penchant for having second-half troubles this season, but there are no easy wins in the NFL—much less in the AFC North.

full_text: (Photo by: Paul Tepley Collection/Diamond Images/Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns enjoyed a much-deserved day off on Monday after their latest last-minute win of the season. It also allowed the team to start mentally preparing for this week’s trip to Pittsburgh to take on the Steelers. Of all the bizarre stats that have enveloped the franchise since 1999, the fact that the Browns have not won a regular-season game in Pittsburgh since 2003 has to rank high on the list. It won’t be easy – it rarely has been for the Browns in Pittsburgh going all the way back to 1970 – but with the way the season has gone so far, this could be the team to finally come back home with a win. To do that, the Browns are going to have to keep playing defense at a high level, and have the offense finally put together a full game. They certainly trended in the right direction against Tennessee with 26 first downs and 491 yards of offense, but the offense is still ranked just 26th in EPA per play after seven weeks. That is an improvement over last season, when the Browns finished No. 32, but also an indication that the offense is still leaving some meat on the bone. title: Browns make expected QB move, waive recent draft pick; one injury decision looms
summary: The quarterback conversation dominated most of the Cleveland Browns offseason, with most of the energy focused on the battle between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders for the starting job. For a moment, Dillon Gabriel seemed to have a chance to squeeze into the competition, but Watson won the job and has now won five of […]
full_text: The quarterback conversation dominated most of the Cleveland Browns offseason, with most of the energy focused on the battle between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders for the starting job. For a moment, Dillon Gabriel seemed to have a chance to squeeze into the competition , but Watson won the job and has now won five of seven games as the starter. Gabriel’s preseason back injury landed him on IR, with his return option opened three weeks ago . According to a report this weekend, Cleveland planned to roll with four quarterbacks on their roster this season, an almost unheard-of number for long periods of time in the NFL. As expected, the Browns activated Gabriel from injured reserve on Monday, at the start of Week 8, 20 days after he returned to practice. Instead of risking losing Taylen Green to waivers, GM Andrew Berry waived TE Carsen Ryan to make room for Gabriel on the roster. Ryan, the team’s seventh-round pick in 2026, played in six games for Cleveland with 73 snaps on special teams and just two with the offense. The Browns still have to make a decision on DT Kalia Davis , who returned to practice the same day Gabriel did, but has not been able to practice much since that time. After the 21-day practice window passes, Davis would revert to injured reserve for the rest of the season if Cleveland does not activate him. Gabriel is expected to slot in as the team’s emergency third quarterback on game days.

title: Browns Week 7 win over Titans revealed 3 things about the team
summary: The Cleveland Browns recorded another win this season, much like many of their previous wins. It came down to a fourth-quarter drive that ended in a field goal, giving the Browns the win. This 27-24 win brings Cleveland to 5-2. They now have as many wins as they had throughout the entire 2025 season. This win was important to keep them at the top of the AFC North, but it also revealed interesting […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns recorded another win this season, much like many of their previous wins. It came down to a fourth-quarter drive that ended in a field goal, giving the Browns the win. This 27-24 win brings Cleveland to 5-2. They now have as many wins as they had throughout the entire 2025 season. This win was important to keep them at the top of the AFC North, but it also revealed interesting things about this team. One of the biggest takeaways from this game is that the Browns’ ability to drive down the field and secure a fourth-quarter win is no fluke. It is a pattern. This is the fifth time this season that Cleveland has had this type of result. Andre Szmyt has been a huge part of the Browns’ success in these game-winning drives with his ability to make a kick in a crucial moment. The running game has started to find its rhythm in recent weeks and had a solid showing against the Tennessee Titans. Quinshon Judkins rushed for 96 yards, his best performance of the season thus far. When the team establishes the running game, it helps open up the rest of the offense. The rookies are continuing to shine. Against the Titans, KC Concepcion had his breakout game. He recorded eight receptions for 129 yards and added three rushes for 23 yards. His versatility is exciting to watch, and it is clear that when the offense puts the ball in his hands, he can make exciting things happen. Let me know what you think in the comments – What did the Browns win over the Titans reveal about this team?

title: Cowboys news: Javonte Williams runs team back into NFC East race
summary: The Dallas Cowboys beat the Philadelphia Eagles 38-21 on Monday night, which is always a welcome rivalry win. The schedule for the Cowboys is favorable all the way until they see these Eagles again on Thanksgiving, putting a huge dent in Philly’s chances of repeating as division champions while keeping their own alive with a […]
full_text: Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys beat the Philadelphia Eagles 38-21 on Monday night, which is always a welcome rivalry win. The schedule for the Cowboys is favorable all the way until they see these Eagles again on Thanksgiving, putting a huge dent in Philly’s chances of repeating as division champions while keeping their own alive with a primetime win. More importantly than all of this perhaps, the Cowboys saw Javonte Williams be the back they need him to be with a huge game on the ground, leading to a balanced approach that helped Dallas get out with a big win. Javonte Williams on career day that helped power the Cowboys over the Eagles: ‘It felt good’ – DallasCowboys.com Javonte Williams picked a great time to have his best game of the season. All told, not including the scrambles from Dak Prescott, the Cowboys ran the ball a total of 36 times, setting up the most efficient passing game of the season, one that featured three passing touchdowns from Prescott, two to CeeDee Lamb and one to George Pickens, and the two-dimensional attack both wore down the Vic Fangio’s’ defense and simultaneously kept them guessing. “It was huge,” Williams added. “We were just trying to get back to a balanced offense, and I feel like we did a great job tonight. … We’ve got a high-powered offense, and when you’ve got G.P., CeeDee, Jake Ferguson, those guys on the outside, I mean, it’s going to open up the running.” 5 Winners and 4 Losers from Cowboys Win in Philly: Dak Prescott’s three touchdown outing overshadowed by teammate – Mauricio Rodriguez, A to Z Sports A strong running game is a QB’s best friend, too. Winner: QB Dak Prescott It wasn’t always pretty as Dak finished with a 56% completion rate, but it was a three passing touchdown showing for the Cowboys quarterback, who also ran into the endzone for a two-point conversion. Prescott did a good job of getting both CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens involved, as both combined for three touchdowns and each got at least 70 receiving yards. 3 things we learned about the Cowboys from the Eagles game – Dyllan Rivers, Blogging The Boys The Cowboys may have even found glimpses of a RB tandem in this game with Tyler Goodson running well behind Williams. The hammer and speed approach worked well against the Eagles all night long. This offensive line bullied defenders in the trenches, Williams made tacklers pay, and Goodson offered a bit of speed and agility, cranking out some nifty runs throughout the night. This is a pairing that Dallas should continue to utilize at a high rate for the remainder of the season. Cowboys flummox Fangio, steamroll Eagles 38-21 in primetime win – K.D. Drummond, The Cowboys Wire Dak Prescott continues to be great against the NFC East, but more specifically, the Vic Fangio defense. The last time QB Dak Prescott faced off against Fangio, he passed for 354 yards and two scores in a 24-21 win. This time, Prescott only had to complete 15 passes for 212 yards. He tossed three touchdowns to go along with RB Javonte Williams’ career high of 155 yards on the ground. Monday Night Football: Cowboys run past Eagles 38-21 – Charean Williams, Pro Football Talk The Cowboys did a great job staying ahead of the chains to keep the full playbook open all night. Brian Schottenheimer, whose play calling was criticized after he abandoned the run in the second half last week, called for more runs than passes. The Cowboys ran it 38 times for 204 yards and threw it 27 times for 212 yards. The Eagles had zero tackles for loss. Javonte Williams set a career-high with 155 yards and scored a touchdown on 25 carries. He is the Cowboys’ first 150-yard rusher since Ezekiel Elliott in 2018. Cowboys-Eagles on ‘Monday Night Football’: What We Learned from Dallas’ 38-21 win – Bobby Kownack, NFL.com The NFC East is still up for grabs, and the Cowboys made the claim they had to about being in the mix on Monday night. NFC East watch. Both teams came into Monday night desperate for a win, especially after the division-leading Giants moved to 4-2-1 on Sunday. By emerging victorious, the Cowboys can breathe a momentary sigh of relief. Their 3-4 record is far from ideal, but they remain in shouting distance of New York and proved plenty capable of lighting up the scoreboard after two worrying weeks.
