title: 3 things we learned about the Cowboys from the Eagles game
summary: The Dallas Cowboys secured the win versus the now 2-5 Eagles on Monday Night Football, advancing to 3-4 on the season. Here is what we learned. Dak Prescott is at his best with a balanced attack This is shocking to all football-knowers out there, I’m sure. But if you give any quarterback in the NFL […]
full_text: Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys secured the win versus the now 2-5 Eagles on Monday Night Football , advancing to 3-4 on the season. Here is what we learned. Dak Prescott is at his best with a balanced attack This is shocking to all football-knowers out there, I’m sure. But if you give any quarterback in the NFL an adequate rushing attack, you instantly elevate both them and the receivers on offense. This is basic football knowledge yet coach Brian Schottenheimer has gotten away from it situationally throughout the year and outright altogether last week. After an absurd 54 pass attempt game from Dak Prescott, balance was the word of the week. Schottenheimer delivered on the night, calling 37 designed rushes on what was ultimately the most balanced they’ve looked all season. There is a reason this offense made moving the ball look effortless for most of the night; much of that comes from the balanced attack we saw from start to finish. Javonte Williams and Tyler Goodson pair well together Javonte Williams ran for 155 yards on the night – the first time a Cowboys running back crossed the 150 mark since Ezekiel Elliot in 2018. This offense also featured a steady dose of Tyler Goodson, racking up 38 yards on 10 carries. The one-two rushing punch helped the Cowboys offense put up the most points they’ve scored this season. The hammer and speed approach worked well against the Eagles all night long. This offensive line bullied defenders in the trenches, Williams made tacklers pay, and Goodson offered a bit of speed and agility, cranking out some nifty runs throughout the night. This is a pairing that Dallas should continue to utilize at a high rate for the remainder of the season. The defense played well enough; concerns still exist The first two drives of the night for the Eagles were laughable for the Cowboys defense. This looked like it was going to be a long night against a backup quarterback, backup wide receivers, a banged up offensive line, and a mash unit at running back led by an obviously hurting Saquon Barkley. But after the first two nightmarish drives, the defense buckled down and let up just seven points for the rest of the night. The run defense was the most problematic piece of the night. This is supposed to be a strength of the Cowboys defense yet on the opening drive they were absolutely gashed by an ailing Saquon Barkley behind a suspect offensive line. They struggled to stop the run throughout the night allowing nearly five yards per rush to the Eagles backfield. Against backup quarterback Tanner McKee, the Dallas defense fared a bit better but still was not as good as you’d hope considering who they were matched up against. Quinnen Williams and Donovan Ezeiruaku were able to each sack the quarterback, both coming late, and DeMarvion Overshown snagged himself an interception on his first night back into the lineup. As a whole, the defense played well enough to win, especially after the first two drives. They really shined once Dallas went up two scores and forced McKee to catch up with under nine minutes left. But they lacked a consistent pass rush and they allowed far too many easy catches on the night, constantly sticking too tight to their zones and abandoning receivers just to cover grass across the middle. Christian Parker needs to tighten up the zone-match concepts with his players or we’ll continue seeing receivers run wide open in the flats as we did tonight and have throughout the season. Still, this was the third straight game the defense allowed 24 points or less, and for that, we celebrate.
author: Dyllan Rivers

title: Cowboys vs. Eagles: 5 winners and 3 losers from the game
summary: The Dallas Cowboys needed a response after consecutive losses, and they produced one on the road against their biggest rival, defeating the Philadelphia Eagles 38-21.  Dallas was the much sharper team offensively, with Dak Prescott getting his best players involved and the running game finally providing balance. There were still some frustrating defensive moments and […]
full_text: Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys needed a response after consecutive losses, and they produced one on the road against their biggest rival, defeating the Philadelphia Eagles 38-21. Dallas was the much sharper team offensively, with Dak Prescott getting his best players involved and the running game finally providing balance. There were still some frustrating defensive moments and far too many penalties, but the Cowboys took control in Philadelphia and came out with a bounce-back win the fans wanted. Winner: Dak Prescott This was the response Dallas needed from Dak Prescott. He had a day throwing three touchdowns without an interception, finding CeeDee Lamb twice and George Pickens once. More importantly, he looked considerably calmer than he did during the losses to Tampa Bay and Green Bay. When Philadelphia went ahead 21-20 in the third quarter, Prescott immediately answered. He led Dallas back down the field, found Lamb for the touchdown and then ran in the two-point conversion himself. That’s what Dallas needed from its quarterback who finished with a 118.1 passer rating on the night. Winner: CeeDee Lamb When Dallas needs its best offensive player, CeeDee Lamb continues to deliver. Lamb has five catches for 74 yards and two touchdowns, with both scores coming at important moments. His first put Dallas ahead in the opening quarter, while his second immediately answered Philadelphia taking the lead in the third. Philadelphia knew where Prescott wanted to go with the football and still couldn’t prevent Lamb from finding the end zone twice. Winner: Javonte Williams This is the Javonte Williams performance Dallas has been waiting for. Williams registered 155 rushing yards on 25 carries, averaging more than six yards per attempt. He consistently found space between the tackles and then punished Philadelphia once reaching the second level. Dallas entered the night needing to recommit to a running game that had largely disappeared over the previous two weeks. Williams has made sure that decision paid off tonight. Winner: Cowboys offensive line Maybe the biggest winner of the night is the entire Cowboys offensive line. Prescott was given enough time to work through his reads and attack Philadelphia downfield, while the run blocking produced Dallas’ best rushing performance of the season. Williams rushed for 155 yards and Dallas went over 200 rushing yards as a team, with the unit totaling 65 plays and allowing zero tackles for loss with very little pressure in the passing game. Against an Eagles defensive front capable of causing problems, the Cowboys consistently created movement and gave Williams and Tyler Goodson lanes to exploit. This looked much more like the offensive line Dallas expected entering the season. Winner: DeMarvion Overshown Welcome back, DeMarvion Overshown. Playing for the first time since injuring his hamstring in Week 1, Overshown produced one of the biggest defensive plays of the night exactly when Dallas needed it. Philadelphia was trailing in the fourth quarter but had started moving the football. With seven minutes remaining, Tanner McKee tried to complete a short pass to his right in Dallas territory, but Overshown read it perfectly. It was a huge moment. Philadelphia still had enough time to make things uncomfortable with a touchdown, but Overshown ended the drive and handed possession back to an offense that began bleeding the clock. Loser: Cowboys run defense Dallas’ offense has been excellent on the ground. Unfortunately, Philadelphia also found success there too. Saquon Barkley produced 62 yards on only seven carries, including a 29-yard run and an eight-yard touchdown. Dameon Pierce added another 47 yards and a score. Dallas knew that with Tanner McKee starting instead of Jalen Hurts, stopping Philadelphia’s running backs had to be priority number one, the Cowboys haven’t consistently done that. Loser: Cowboys third-down defense The same issue that hurt Dallas against Green Bay followed them into Philadelphia. The clearest example was the Eagles’ third-quarter touchdown possession. Philadelphia put together a 17-play drive lasting more than nine minutes, repeatedly converting opportunities when Dallas had chances to get off the field. Dallas has shown improvement defensively tonight, and Overshown’s interception finally produced the big fourth-quarter stop it needed. But getting opponents into third down means little if they repeatedly convert it. This remains an area Christian Parker’s defense has to fix urgently. Loser: Cowboys penalties Dallas has made tonight considerably harder than it needed to be. The Cowboys accumulated eight penalties for 47-yards. The yardage itself wasn’t disastrous, but the timing of those penalties was. The biggest came on special teams. Tyler Goodson appeared to break a kickoff return for a touchdown, only for a holding penalty on Justin Barron to wipe the score completely off the board. Barron had already been called for another hold earlier in the game. Those are potentially game-changing mistakes. Dallas was the better team for significant stretches, but penalties have repeatedly damaged field position, stalled momentum and even removed points from the scoreboard. Against Philadelphia, you don’t need to make the game harder. The Cowboys have done exactly that to themselves.
author: Mike Poland

title: Cowboys beat Eagles to stay alive in NFC East race
summary: The Dallas Cowboys have officially responded. America’s Team marched into the City of Brotherly Love on Monday night and the Dallas Cowboys emerged victorious over the Philadelphia Eagles. Obviously the state of the Eagles team is one very far removed from what they hoped it to look like this season, but a win is a […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 26: Dallas Cowboys wide receiver Ceedee Lamb #88 catches a touchdown during the game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Dallas Cowboys on October 26th, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys have officially responded. America’s Team marched into the City of Brotherly Love on Monday night and the Dallas Cowboys emerged victorious over the Philadelphia Eagles. Obviously the state of the Eagles team is one very far removed from what they hoped it to look like this season, but a win is a win and the Cowboys were in sore need of one. To be clear Monday night’s victory was not without areas to address. The defense still looked suspect and the game was only as close as it was because they allowed Tanner McKee and co. to thrive a bit. Still, they stood tall when it absolutely mattered the most. Sunday saw the New York Giants beat the Houston Texans so pressure was really mounting on the Cowboys to get this done. Now that they have the NFC East appears like it is going to be a race between Dallas and New York, and given that the two are set to meet in Week 18 at AT&T Stadium that is a bit of fun. We needn’t look that far down the road, though. For now the Cowboys are winners and up next is an old school NFC East rival in the Arizona Cardinals… and we all know how those games have gone as of late. Again… tonight we breathe. The Dallas Cowboys (3-4) are winners and they can say with fullness that they earned the right to be called that on Monday night. Below you will find our recap of the game as it unfolded. First Quarter The Eagles won the toss and deferred. GOTI was up first. Dallas started by running the ball with Javonte Williams and rode him a bit. Unfortunately Dak Prescott was a bit off when he took to the air and missed CeeDee Lamb for what would have been a huge gain. The Cowboys wound up settling for a Brandon Aubrey 55-yard field goal on 4th and 8. Philly was called for an illegal formation as the ball went through the uprights so Brian Schottenheimer could have taken it and considered going for it on 4th and 3, but he kept the points to take the early lead 3-0. Whatever good vibes were in existence after that did not last long. The Eagles went 70 yards in 4 plays thanks to Saquon Barkley, and he capped it off for the lead-taking touchdown to make it 7-3. First opening drive TD of the season for Philly 🦅 DALvsPHI on ESPN⁰Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/UEJ7eK5Mn4 — NFL (@NFL) October 27, 2026 This next drive had the chance to say a lot about the Cowboys in terms of responding. They handled it well! Javonte Williams and Tyler Goodson helped things move on the ground, but it was Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb who cashed in to re-take the lead at 10-7. DAK. CEEDEE. TD. pic.twitter.com/5r8Gu8PKEM — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) October 27, 2026 The Eagles tried a tush push on their next drive on their side of midfield, and for a moment it appeared that the Cowboys stopped them. Unfortunately Quinnen Williams was found to have committed a neutral zone infraction, his second frustrating penalty of the night to that point. The quarter came to a close with Philly coming close once more. Second Quarter As the second quarter began it appeared as if the Eagles were going to wind up scoring another touchdown. Dallas did stop them on third down near the goal line, but LT Overton was called for roughing the passer and the drive had new life. Shortly after… the Eagles were back in the endzone. This time it was Dameon Pierce and Philly lead once again, 14-10. Dameon Pierce and the Eagles answer right back! DALvsPHI on ESPN⁰Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/C9ZCp7Cmue — NFL (@NFL) October 27, 2026 The Cowboys offense returned, both literally and figuratively. Coming off of having scored in both possessions and a touchdown on their most recent… they kept their foot on the gas. Javonte Williams was heavily involved, but more than anything Dallas handled Philadelphia’s blitzing in a way that seemed impossible over the previous two weeks. The team even converted a fourth and short to keep things alive, and they turned it all into points with an incredible touchdown from Dak Prescott to George Pickens. GP3!!!! pic.twitter.com/tAeyeO93CO — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) October 27, 2026 It was then that a miracle happened… the Dallas Cowboys defense forced a punt. To be clear it happened after they committed a penalty when a punt would have happened sooner, but it was a punt nonetheless. Baby steps. Unfortunately Philly was able to down the ball at Dallas’ 2-yard line which made things tough to start. The Cowboys were barely able to move it at all and punted to Philly. A penalty on their return put the ball on their 39-yard line with 1:39 remaining and two timeouts in their pocket. This felt particularly treacherous with them set to receive the second half kickoff. Thankfully the Eagles had to punt themselves. Dallas took over at their own 13 with 1:14 left and a pair of timeouts to work with. Ultimately the Cowboys did come away with points, but only a field goal. It looked like they were going to score a touchdown, but unfortunately time got the best of them which is why they had to settle. They took a 20-14 lead into halftime. Third Quarter What happened next was very impressive if we are being fully honest. It did happen against the Cowboys defense so perhaps that warps your perception, but the Eagles absolutely out-classed them to start the second half. Philadelphia came out of the gate and put together a 17-play drive that absorbed 9:16 of game clock. It was as perfect of a drive as they could have had in the game given all circumstances, and they obviously capped it off with a touchdown. It was Tanner McKee finding Makai Lemon to give the home team the lead once more, 21-20. The Cowboys deserve credit for responding in this game becuase they really and truly did. With the prospect of the game slipping away from them… the offense locked in. Everybody was involved as the Cowboys matriculated down the field (who doesn’t love saying that?), but it was Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb who capped it off with another beautiful touchdown. DAK TO CEEDEE AGAIN pic.twitter.com/1cfuIpREp0 — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) October 27, 2026 Given that the touchdown made things 26-21 the Cowboys chose to go for two. Brian Schottenheimer dialed up an excellent play call. Credit where it is due. ✌️ pic.twitter.com/2si3JBw670 — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) October 27, 2026 The Cowboys kicked off with a full touchdown lead (28-21) and just a bit left in the third quarter. Philly ran a couple of plays and took it to the fourth. Fourth Quarter Right after the fourth quarter began the Eagles punted the ball away. Dallas had possession and a touchdown lead. Things were looking promising. The offense did move right along, partly due to Javonte Williams. They were unable to cash all the way in, but they did come away with 3 points to make it 31-21 with just over 9 minutes to go. Things felt good. Things soon felt very good. It was a tall order for Philly at that point in time, but they were driving a bit. And then DeMarvion Overshown really put things on ice. OVERSHOWN!!! pic.twitter.com/EQSWCh7d0Y — Blogging The Boys (@BloggingTheBoys) October 27, 2026 Right as the Cowboys began their next possession Javonte Williams set a new career high for rushing yards in a game. His previous was 135. Javonte wound up punching in the last touchdown to really put this one on ice. It was a proper end to things for that reason. Javonte Williams puts the Cowboys up three scores 🤠 DALvsPHI on ESPN⁰Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/imLAU5GWEh — NFL (@NFL) October 27, 2026 Cowboys win! 38-21!

title: Keys before kickoff: Cowboys at Eagles Week 7
summary: The 2-4 Dallas Cowboys travel to Lincoln Financial to face the 2-4 Philadelphia Eagles this week on Monday Night Football. Here are three keys to the game. Run. The. Ball. We sound like a broken record at this point. If the run game is working, coach Brian Schottenheimer needs to keep the ball on the […]
full_text: Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images | Getty Images The 2-4 Dallas Cowboys travel to Lincoln Financial to face the 2-4 Philadelphia Eagles this week on Monday Night Football . Here are three keys to the game. Run. The. Ball. We sound like a broken record at this point. If the run game is working, coach Brian Schottenheimer needs to keep the ball on the ground. If the run game is not working, the offense still needs to remain balanced. They cannot once again afford for Dak Prescott to throw the ball over 50 times this week. According to SumerSports, the Eagles are one of the league’s worst run defenses, ranking 28th with a 44.2% rush success rating allowed. The Cowboys should be able to attack this defense on the ground should they choose to do so. We saw a similar situation in last week’s keys before kickoff article , with Green Bay ranking as one of the league’s least competent run defenses. It was imperative that Dallas attacked them on the ground. When they did, it worked well. But the play-caller got away from the run too early, leading to a completely unbalanced offense. This week, Dallas simply cannot afford to do the same. The Eagles are terribly beat up, on the brink of implosion (if they haven’t imploded already). Running the ball at will and controlling the flow of the game will suck the remaining soul out of Philadelphia quickly. It’ll be up to coach Schottenheimer to decide if he wants to stick with the run game this week or if he wants to attack the Vic Fangio defense primarily through the air. Exploit Tanner McKee The Eagles are without their star quarterback Jalen Hurts for the remainder of the season. While Tanner McKee is a capable backup, he’s limited in what he brings to the field. The 2023 sixth-round pick is a classic pocket passer that lacks the mobility of modern NFL quarterbacks. He also struggles under pressure, as displayed last week versus the Panthers. He has slow feet and a long release, meaning sacks and turnovers are on the table for Dallas this week. McKee also struggles in tight window throws . Last week, he completed just 3-of-15 throws in tight coverage and was inaccurate on 8-of-9 throws further than ten yards downfield and outside the numbers. With DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks out this week, the Cowboys corners must show up on the outside. They simply cannot allows the Eagles’ backup receivers to get open on a consistent basis. If they are able to tighten up, this will be a long day for the Philadelphia offense. Limit the remaining Eagles weapons After a slew of injuries, the Eagles have essentially two weapons remaining on their offense. Saquon Barkley is expected to return this week to play on Monday night. The dynamic back has averaged 5.1 yards per carry this season, totaling 182 yards on 36 carries. Interestingly, 59 of those yards came on just two carries. Without those two big gains, the yardage shrinks to 3.6 per carry. Barkley could be in for a boom or bust game, and Dallas cannot allow him to boom. To stop Barkley, the Cowboys must take advantage of this Eagles offensive line that’s seen Lane Johnson retire and Cam Jurgens traded mid-season. They’ve also dealt with shifting assignments due to injuries. They are a patch-job at the moment, struggling to both run and pass block. This is a game for Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark, and Otito Ogbonnia to show up. The other weapon, Dallas Goedert, is always a point of focus for opposing defenses. With Smith and Wicks out, the Eagles tight end should be the primary receiving option for McKee on Monday night. The Cowboys will need to disrupt him at the line of scrimmage and force the backup quarterback to look elsewhere, outside of his comfort blanket. We could see plenty of DeMarvion Overshown and Caleb Downs matched up against Goedert this week. The rest of the Eagles weapons are more situationally dangerous than consistent threats. But you can’t put it past this Cowboys defense to break a coverage or to slip, allowing a player like Hollywood Brown to blow by for a deep touchdown. While that’s never great, this is certainly a week where this Eagles offense can be contained by simply playing mistake free football.

title: Cowboys key matchup: Brian Schottenheimer vs Vic Fangio
summary: For the first time this season, we will be focusing more on the coaches on the sideline than the players on the field. With the Philadelphia Eagles extremely banged up on offense, and Brian Schottenheimer scooting closer-and-closer to the hot seat, this may be the biggest game of Schottenheimer’s coaching career. The Cowboys head into […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images For the first time this season, we will be focusing more on the coaches on the sideline than the players on the field. With the Philadelphia Eagles extremely banged up on offense, and Brian Schottenheimer scooting closer-and-closer to the hot seat, this may be the biggest game of Schottenheimer’s coaching career. The Cowboys head into this week seven matchup fully healthy on offense with the Eagles near full health on defense, minus Nolan Smith out due to a concussion. We have yet to really see it so far this season, but the Cowboys need Schottenheimer to be the “elite play caller” he referred to himself as late last week. Unlike the last two weeks, the Cowboys should expect a pretty clear picture of Vic Fangio’s plan. Like we have learned with Christian Parker, Fangio is not a heavy blitzer and relies on his coverage scheme to keep opposing offenses under control. While we should expect Fangio to ramp up his pressure a bit more due to the Cowboys struggles to handle it the last few weeks, Dak Prescott should not be dealing with as many exotic blitz looks pre-and-post snap like he did against Tampa Bay and Green Bay. The Philadelphia Eagles defense currently looks like a shell of itself from recent years. Through six weeks, the Eagles defense ranks 25th in EPA/play, 23rd in drop back EPA/play, and 31st in rush EPA/play. Given the struggles of the Cowboys running game this season, this is a matchup they can get back on track with. Jalen Carter has turned it on over the last few weeks, after playing with an injured wrist early in the season. Zack Baun is still one of the better linebackers in the NFL, but the depth behind him can be targeted in the running game. With Nolan Smith out tonight, expect the Cowboys to run it early towards AJ Epenesa and/or Arnold Ebikete. With the names like Quinyon Mitchell, Cooper DeJean, Riq Woolen, and Andrew Mukuba in the secondary, you would think the running game would be the only path to success for the Cowboys offense, but their secondary outside of Mitchell has struggled this year in coverage. Similar to Javonte Williams, this is a solid matchup for the Cowboys wide receivers to get back on track both as pass catchers and run blockers. At the end of the day, this all comes down to Schottenheimer’s ability to prove himself as a play-caller and game-planner. We have not seen much consistency from the Cowboys offensive coaching staff so far this season, but it’s a great week, in a must-win game, to get back on track.

title: 3 under-the-radar players for Cowboys at Eagles
summary: Last week against the Green Bay Packers, wide receiver Ryan Flournoy was named as a player to watch, given the attention on CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. He caught seven passes for 40 yards and a touchdown on 11 targets, his first of the season. Dallas is traveling to Philadelphia to face an Eagles team […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images | Getty Images Last week against the Green Bay Packers, wide receiver Ryan Flournoy was named as a player to watch, given the attention on CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. He caught seven passes for 40 yards and a touchdown on 11 targets, his first of the season. Dallas is traveling to Philadelphia to face an Eagles team in a similar situation. Both teams have been ravaged by injuries and are in must-win territory, considering the New York Giants continue to stack wins. The city of brotherly love hasn’t been kind to the Cowboys recently, winning just two games there since 2018. It’s the kind of game where players who aren’t expected to shine need to stand out, and the team needs to play as one. Here are three under-the-radar players who could be big contributors Monday night. Brandon Aubrey The Cowboys kicker signed a well-deserved contract extension this offseason after performing like the best kicker in the NFL for the last three seasons. However, the start to the 2026 season hasn’t been his best from long distance. On 50-plus-yard kicks, Aubrey is just 2-for-5. Dallas’ offense has struggled to find its identity over the last two weeks, so scoring will be at a premium against the Eagles. Not to mention it’s an outdoor stadium, which can give the three-time Pro Bowl kicker some trouble. The Cowboys will have to rely on their kicker in a game that could end 15-10. He’ll also need to be better on kickoffs and keep the ball in bounds to give the Philadelphia offense good starting field position. We saw in the Baltimore Ravens game how that could really hurt the Cowboys’ defense. Cooper Beebe Dallas has invested first-round picks at both guard spots and left tackle. While much of the spotlight is on Terence Steele for his struggles, Cooper Beebe is the often-forgotten man along the offensive line. This week, Beebe might have his toughest matchup of the season. He’ll face three premier defensive tackles: Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo. When facing that group of players one-on-one, he has allowed five pressures across 31 pass blocks (16.1%), per NFL Pro. In most cases, Beebe has had double-team help when facing the group. Tyler Smith’s recent return to the lineup should help Beebe, but he’ll still have to win his one-on-one matchups. Dak Prescott got hit against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Green Bay Packers. Keeping the pocket clean will be paramount, especially if the offense wants to get CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens back on track. Jonathan Mingo With KaVontae Turpin out with a rib injury, Tyler Goodson and Jonathan Mingo will be relied on in the return game. Goodson won’t get many opportunities if Dallas’ defense limits Philly’s scoring. That means all eyes will be on Mingo as the team’s primary punt returner. Mingo showed a bit of something against the Packers, returning one punt for 16 yards. Mingo’s not on the same level as Turpin as a return specialist, but his biggest test will be avoiding turnovers. We’ve seen players make mistakes, especially in situations they aren’t too familiar with. It would be a win if Mingo spent the entire game waving his hand for a fair catch on every punt. As long as he doesn’t cough it up and give the Eagles offense momentum to score in what could be a tightly contested game. Just give Dallas’ offense the ball back and let them go to work.

title: 4 Cowboys players or things to  buy or sell vs the Eagles
summary: The Dallas Cowboys head to Philadelphia for a Monday night divisional matchup that could have major implications for the NFC East. Dallas has lost two straight games, and while there are still plenty of playmakers on offense, the team has struggled to put everything together. The Eagles are dealing with their own offensive problems after […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys head to Philadelphia for a Monday night divisional matchup that could have major implications for the NFC East. Dallas has lost two straight games, and while there are still plenty of playmakers on offense, the team has struggled to put everything together. The Eagles are dealing with their own offensive problems after losing Jalen Hurts for the season, and are hoping their defense steps up. Buy: Javonte Williams If the Cowboys want to make life easier for Dak Prescott, the best place to start is with Javonte Williams. Dallas has leaned heavily on its passing game this season, but the offense has become increasingly predictable as the running game has struggled to find consistency. Williams deserves more opportunities to change that. Through six games, Williams has carried the ball 85 times for 317 yards and seven rushing touchdowns, averaging 3.7 yards per attempt. He has also contributed 19 receptions for 103 yards and a receiving touchdown. Though his rushing average isn’t particularly impressive, his touchdown production shows Dallas has found a player it can trust when it gets close to the goal line. There has been some discussion about Philadelphia’s susceptibility to I-formation, suggesting balance is the best way to attack this defense, but really Dallas needs to improve its rushing production, and Williams has already shown he can finish drives. The Cowboys’ offensive line has struggled to create consistent running lanes, so this is not simply a matter of handing Williams the ball and expecting a breakout. Still, more carries would give Dallas a better chance to establish rhythm, keep the Eagles’ pass rush honest and avoid putting the entire offense on Prescott’s shoulders. Williams is not guaranteed to have a huge game against a talented middle, but the Cowboys need to find out what their running game can do when they commit to it. Seven rushing touchdowns through six games is a good reason to keep feeding him. Sell: The Cowboys’ passing game against Philadelphia’s defense The Cowboys’ passing attack has plenty of talent, but this is a difficult week to expect a quick turnaround. Philadelphia has the personnel to make Prescott uncomfortable, especially if Dallas cannot establish the run or improve its protection. Prescott has thrown four interceptions over the past two games, tied for the most in the NFL over that span. Against the blitz during those two games, he has completed just 52.6% of his passes without a touchdown, posting a 67.2 passer rating. Those numbers are a scary heading into a matchup against a defense that can challenge receivers on the outside and create problems in the middle of the field. Quinyon Mitchell and Cooper DeJean are important pieces of that secondary, and Jalen Carter can disrupt an offense from the interior. Philadelphia also has a deep group of defensive contributors, including linebacker Zack Baun and run-stopper Jordan Davis, but edge rusher Nolan Smith will miss the game. The Eagles have not been overwhelming in every pass-rush metric, so Dallas should have opportunities if the offensive line holds up. But the Cowboys have not earned the benefit of the doubt after two consecutive losses in which the offense struggled to sustain its production. Prescott’s recent turnovers are especially glaring because Dallas cannot afford to give Philadelphia extra possessions in a divisional game. Until the Cowboys show they can handle pressure and take care of the football, the passing game is a sell against this Eagles defense. Buy: Joey Porter Jr. While the Cowboys’ defense has struggled to create turnovers, Joey Porter Jr. has given the secondary a reason for optimism. His physical style of coverage and ability to stay tight to receivers make him an important piece of a defense that needs more consistent playmaking. Porter is particularly valuable heading into Monday night’s matchup because Philadelphia’s passing game is adjusting to life without Jalen Hurts. With Tanner McKee taking over at quarterback, the Cowboys need their cornerbacks to challenge receivers at the line of scrimmage, contest throws and make the Eagles work for every completion. Porter has the size and physicality to make those matchups uncomfortable. Of course, good coverage only goes so far if the pass rush cannot pressure the quarterback. The Dallas pass rush has left the defensive backs to cover for extended stretches. That has contributed to the unit’s inability to consistently finish plays, even when the coverage is competitive. Porter is a buy because he gives Dallas a potential building block in the secondary, not because one cornerback can fix the defense by himself. If the Cowboys can pair his coverage with more pressure up front, they have a better chance of forcing McKee into mistakes and creating the takeaways that have been missing. Sell: The pass protection The Cowboys’ offensive line has to give Dak Prescott more time to operate, because the pressure he has faced over the last two games has helped derail an offense that was previously one of the team’s biggest strengths. Dallas has scored just 29 points combined in its last two games, and Prescott’s protection has been a significant concern as opposing defenses have disrupted the passing game. The Cowboys have allowed six sacks through six games, but the bigger issue has been the pressure and hurried decisions that prevent Prescott from getting through his progressions and finding CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens downfield. The matchup against Philadelphia offers a potential reprieve, but it is hardly a reason to relax. The Eagles have recorded eight sacks this season, and Jalen Carter remains a disruptive presence on the interior. Philadelphia hasn’t consistently generated pressure with its standard four-man rush, but Dallas still needs to communicate well up front and keep Carter from collapsing the pocket. If the Eagles bring extra rushers, Prescott must have enough time and reliable outlets to punish them. Dallas’ tackles, Tyler Guyton and Terence Steele, need to hold up on the edges, while the interior must keep Carter from disrupting the play’s timing. Until the Cowboys show they can consistently keep Prescott comfortable in the pocket, the offensive line remains a concern heading into Monday night.

full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 04: Marvin Mims Jr. #19 of the Denver Broncos warms up prior to the start of the game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s another season and another slow start for Marvin Mims Jr. in the Denver Broncos offense. The strange usage early on in seasons seems to be a recurring theme and something head coach Sean Payton mentions about this time every year of getting more touches to Mims. He did so again on Monday. “We’re trying to get him touches,” Payton said of adding Mims to kickoff duties. “He’s one of our explosive playmakers. Quite honestly, we need to get him more touches on offense, and we’ll do that. A lot of it had to do with the way they were kicking off. We kind of, you noticed, went more to a single returner and certainly that first one (return) that puts us at midfield was a big one for us.” Before Sunday, Mims had a grand total of 29 yards receiving and 24 yards in kickoff yardage. Against the Arizona Cardinals he had 53 yards receiving and 103 yards in kickoff return yardage. However Payton needs to do it, I would agree that getting Mims more involved in everywhere they can is a smart plan. Hopefully we see his involvement increase through the next two games as Denver winning both would have them sitting quite pretty atop the AFC West. title: Buildings blocks for offensive success established in Broncos’ win over Cardinals
summary: With their 30-16 rout of the Arizona Cardinals, the Denver Broncos finally played their first complete game of the season. In all three phases, the Broncos won their battles and were triumphant securing their fifth victory of their 2026 gridiron campaign. At 5-2, Denver remains in a great spot in a super competitive AFC playoff […]
full_text: Oct 25, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton talks with quarterback Bo Nix (10) before the game against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect With their 30-16 rout of the Arizona Cardinals, the Denver Broncos finally played their first complete game of the season. In all three phases, the Broncos won their battles and were triumphant securing their fifth victory of their 2026 gridiron campaign. At 5-2, Denver remains in a great spot in a super competitive AFC playoff race. While there is still plenty of room for improvement, the building blocks for success on offense were effectively laid against the Cardinals. One aspect where the Broncos came up big was establishing the run. The commitment to the ground game wasn’t there early on, but it was a huge emphasis for the team in the second half. By the end of the game, the Broncos had rushed for 159 yards—their highest total of the season and just their third outing this season eclipsing the 100-yard mark. After the game, Head Coach Sean Payton discussed what he felt worked well for their rushing attack. “I thought we had a good plan relative to some of the gap schemes. It’s a pretty tough unit. We wanted to be in a little bit more base personnel. Someone asked last week about Adam Prentice and it’s kind of like ‘ah.’ We’re leading into this game where we were going to be in a little bit more 21 personnel to keep them out of some of their nickel looks so that was good,” stated Payton. Quarterback Bo Nix’s 62-yard touchdown scamper late in the first half was a huge spark for the offense. That led to an off-kilter performance by the Cardinals’ defense, who gave up a handful of splash plays the remainder of the game. In the second half, Payton switched up his playcalling and was more dedicated to dictating the pace of the game by running the ball with authority. Rookie running back Jonah Coleman looked fantastic. In his first performance since the Jacksonville Jaguars game, Coleman impressed. He notched 54 yards on 9 carries and sported a six yard per carry average. The fourth-round pick led all backs with 30 snaps—half of Denver’s offensive snap counts—followed by RJ Harvey with 16, and J.K. Dobbins at 14. Moving forward, it’s quite clear Coleman should be the lead back in the Broncos’ backfield. His decisiveness at the line of scrimmage and ability to break tackles made a huge difference in yesterday’s game. Payton told reporters after the win that he certainly needs to find a way to get him more touches . With Denver’s run game kicking into high gear, we saw a rebound performance from Nix. While his overall completion percentage wasn’t great, the third-year quarterback played his most aggressive game of the season. On numerous occasions, Nix stepped up in the pocket and dialed up great throws down the middle of the field. He also took a few deep shots which were absent from his performances earlier in the year. Nix told reporters after the game he was pleased with the offense’s production against the Cardinals. However, he noted there are a lot of things they can clean up. Their Week 8 opponent is the Kansas City Chiefs, who lost against the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday Night Football . That means next Sunday’s game will be for division lead. “I hope we are coached tough. I hope they make it really important this week to find those details. There’s several things in the game that we can grow from. It’s an important week and we know that and we have to be really sharp and disciplined so we can carry the coaching from this game on into this week,” stated Nix. Last night, we saw the Seahawks stay dedicated to the run to topple the Chiefs. Hopefully, the Broncos take notice and attempt to establish that in front of a hometown crowd on November 1st. Good things happen when you run the ball effectively. It keeps defenses honest and opens up big play opportunities for the quarterback. If Denver can accomplish that, they’ll have a great shot at reclaiming their spot atop the AFC West.

title: Broncos Stock Up, Stock Down: Week 7 vs. Cardinals
summary: The Broncos, and specifically quarterback Bo Nix, needed a game like this. After a week and a half of dealing with the fallout from Ryan Fitzpatrick’s rant, the media piling on, Sean Payton being asked if Nix should be benched, and so on, Nix and the Broncos responded in a big way. Nix led the […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 25: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos runs for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. The Broncos defeated the Cardinals 30-16. (Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Broncos, and specifically quarterback Bo Nix, needed a game like this. After a week and a half of dealing with the fallout from Ryan Fitzpatrick’s rant, the media piling on, Sean Payton being asked if Nix should be benched, and so on, Nix and the Broncos responded in a big way. Nix led the offense to 30 points on the road vs. the Cardinals and had multiple big plays, including a 62-yard run where he silenced any and all questions about his ankle. He reached nearly 20 miles per hour on the run and instantly snapped himself and the Broncos’ offense out of the funk they have been in. This was a rare two-score win by the Broncos, who didn’t need to have a fourth-quarter comeback or really had any drama in the later stages of the game. Stock up and stock down is a weekly series where I go through the Denver Broncos’ 53-man roster and tell you which Broncos players’ stock is going up, down, or remains unchanged. After a big win with lots of positivity on Sunday, we are looking at a lot of stocks trending in the right direction, with just a few trending down. Quarterback Bo Nix – Stock up: Man, he NEEDED a game like this. Yes, he struggled against the Seahawks, but so did Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs, and they lost 20-3. Nix was able to lead two touchdown drives against that talented defense and still had his performance called “disrespectful”. Anyways, he looked more confident on Sunday and started the game off by throwing the ball down the field and hitting Courtland Sutton for a 20-yard strike. He kept this up throughout the game and had multiple long touchdown plays. The 60+ yard rushing touchdown and the 50+ yard screen pass to RJ Harvery. He led the offense to 30 points and silenced most of the haters for at least one week. Jarrett Stidham – Unchanged: Remains the Broncos’ veteran backup Sam Ehlinger – Unchanged : Emergency third-string quarterback Running Back Jonah Coleman – Stock WAY up: We are starting off with Jonah Coleman because he was the Broncos’ lead running back on Sunday. He led the team in snaps, carries, and total yards on Sunday, and Sean Payton told reporters after the game that he needs to give him more touches moving forward. Coleman played 49% of the snaps on Sunday, had 69 total yards, averaged 6.0 yards per carry, and looked like a damn good running back. He displayed elite vision, good short-area burst, ran with power, and was a threat in the passing game. He is a true three-down back and should see his role grow even more moving forward. RJ Harvey – Stock up: Harvey has been the Broncos’ best and most explosive playmaker this season and had yet another impact play on Sunday. The Broncos called a timely screen play to Harvey, who took it untouched 50+ yards for a touchdown and showcased his elite speed. His role in this offense remains unchanged as the pass-catching threat out of the backfield who has the speed to take it all the way whenever he touches the ball. His production as a ball-carrier is not what you want, but overall, he has been a consistent weapon for the Broncos. JK Dobbins – Stock down: With Jonah Coleman seeing an elevated role in the offense and Harvey’s role unchanged, Dobbins was the odd man out on Sunday. He played just 14 snaps(23%), and his production was once again not great. He had 6 carries for 23 yards, but did score a touchdown for a third straight game. We will have to see how his role evolves in the coming days/weeks. Adam Prentice – Stock up: Played 10 offensive snaps and had a blocked punt on Sunday. He does the dirty work as a lead blocker while also playing a key role on special teams. Wide Receiver Jaylen Waddle – Unchanged: Waddle had a good game and showed off his big-play potential in this one, but left the game late with a chest injury. Payton called himself out after the game for the dumb play call that led to Waddle’s injury, and as of this writing, do not have an update on the severity of his injury. Courtland Sutton – Unchanged: Played 70% of the snaps and had 3 catches for 45 yards. If Waddle is sidelined at all moving forward, the veteran will need to step up and be WR1 once again for the Broncos. Troy Franklin – Stock up: His production and stat line are not great, but with Waddle leaving the game and Bryant on IR, Franklin could see himself as a starter next week in a key game vs. the Chiefs. He had 2 targets for 0 catches on Sunday, which included a drop on a deep ball before halftime. Marvin Mims Jr. – Stock up: Big play Mims is back! He had a couple of nice kick returns and had 2 catches for 53 yards, including a 47-yard catch that got the Broncos inside the 5-yard line. If Waddle is indeed sidelined, Mims would see an elevated role moving forward, Lil’Jordan Humphrey – Unchanged: He played 25% of the snaps and has his role in this offense. Tight End Evan Engram – Stock down: Ever since Sean Payton took over play-calling, Engram’s role has taken a hit. He went from leading the tight ends in snaps to being tied with Nate Adkins for the second-most snaps. He also had just 2 targets for 1 catch for 2 yards. Adam Trautman – Unchanged: Played 61% of the snaps and will continue to see these snaps with Sean Payton running this team and offense. Nate Adkins – Stock up: Another Payton favorite saw 39% of the snaps, tied with Engram, and is a key run blocker for the Broncos. He has been the Broncos’ most productive pass-catching tight end this season, even though it is a very limited stat line. Dallen Bentley – Unchanged: Continued to be inactive. Offensive Line Garett Bolles – Stock up: Remains one of the better left tackles in all of football and continues to be the blindside blocker for Bo Nix. Ben Powers – Stock down: Powers has had an up-and-down season for the Broncos, and that continued on Sunday. We’ll see if the Broncos make any additions to their offensive line moving forward. Luke Wattenberg – Unchanged: I did not notice Wattenberg stand out, good or bad, in this one (again, not an offensive line expert). Quinn Meinerz – Stock up: Stud. Mike McGlinchey – Unchanged: I believe he played solid on Sunday, but again, not an offensive line expert. Alex Palczewski – Stock up: Played 23% of the snaps on Sunday, all as an extra blocker, and could see that role continuing moving forward. Matt Peart – Unchanged: Played on special teams. Alex Forsyth – Unchanged: Played on special teams. Kage Casey – Unchanged: Continued to be inactive. Defensive Line Zach Allen – Stock up: Allen was his dominant self once again on Sunday. He is arguably the Broncos’ best player and continues to be a disruptive presence in the middle of their defense. DJ Jones – Unchanged: I did not notice Jones as much in this game, but their run defense was solid for the most part. Malcolm Roach – Stock up: Every game, he’s out there making at least one or two impact plays a game. On Sunday, he had a sack and yet another pass deflection. He’s one of the more underrated players on this Broncos defense. Eyioma Uwazurike – Stock up: The big man made multiple stops in the run game and led all Broncos DL in snaps on Sunday with 51 (63%). Sai’vion Jones – Stock up: Jones had a big hit on Sam Darnold last week and, this week, had a sack and a TFL vs. the Cardinals. He has quietly been playing well in a reserve role and appears to be coming into his own in year two. He played 28 snaps (35%) on Sunday. Jordan Jackson – Unchanged: Was inactive. Tyler Onyedim – Unchanged: Continued to be inactive. Edge Rushers Nik Bonitto – Stock up: Bonitto was a pass-rushing menace on Sunday, and it’s a shame he did not come away with a sack. Cardinals QB Jacoby Brissett was annoyingly good at getting rid of the ball, but Bonitto…

There were ample options for game balls in this game and since we’ve all been starved for a breakout offensive performance that is where most of ours went, but I feel like we left a few out there for the outstanding defensive effort. Mention those in the comments, especially the egregious omission of Nik Bonitto here. There are only so many of us on staff to hand these out, sadly. The most important test of the Broncos 2026 season will be how they respond against those Chiefs after what happened to this team in Arrowhead in Week 1. Hoping to see a playoff-caliber effort then. Here’s who we’re giving our game balls to from the Broncos win over the Cardinals: Bo Nix Bo Nix gets my game ball. He is the 4th QB in modern NFL history to throw for and run for a 50 yard TD in the same game. The other three were Cam Newton in 2012, and Lamar Jackson and Justin Fields who both did it in 2022. Bo finished the game with 295 yards of total offense (222 passing and 73 running). He also hit 19.9 mph on his 62 yard TD run, which is flying. It’s not fast enough to make the Top 20 on NFL NExtgen stats , but it is close and there are currently no QBs in the top 20. Bo’s 62 yard TD carry is the longest run by a QB this season. title: Plenty to be proud of in Broncos win over Arizona
summary: As the losses mounted during the dark, pre-Bo Nix era, it was common for Broncos fans to lower their expectations from week-to-week. Broncos games were watched, not for the promise of a win, but in the hopes that there would be a glimmer of hope from players’ growth and development. This season Broncos fans are […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - OCTOBER 25: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos scores a touchdown after being hit by Kei'trel Clark #13 during the second quarter of the game at State Farm Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. The Broncos defeated the Cardinals 30-16. (Photo by Chris Coduto/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the losses mounted during the dark, pre-Bo Nix era, it was common for Broncos fans to lower their expectations from week-to-week. Broncos games were watched, not for the promise of a win, but in the hopes that there would be a glimmer of hope from players’ growth and development. This season Broncos fans are getting both. The much maligned Bo Nix spread the ball around to 9 different receivers, going 15 of 29 for 222-yards, averaging 7.7 yards per pass, spreading the ball around to 9 different receivers. While the the much improved passing stats are a welcome relief to those losing sleep over Bo Nix’s performance in recent weeks, Sunday’s game against the Cardinals was won on the ground. Bo Nix did it all Sunday💪 With a 62-yard TD run and 52-yard TD pass, he's just the 5th player in NFL history with a 50 yard rush TD and pass TD in the same game! He's the first to do it on the road since Ace Parker of the 1938 Brooklyn Dodgers vs the Pittsburgh Pirates🤯 pic.twitter.com/HFSxiYORI3 — ESPN Insights (@ESPNInsights) October 26, 2026 The Broncos 159-yards on the ground was headlined by two different notable ball carriers on Sunday. First of all, we need to welcome back the ‘tuck-and-run’ version of Bo Nix. There isn’t a defense around that saw his 62-yard run that won’t have to linger over the gameplan when considering his explosive scrambling ability going forward. Then there’s rookie Jonah Coleman who dazzled in his return from IR going for 54-yards on 9 carries. Sean Payton and all of Broncos Country was impressed with his team-leading (if you take out Nix’s run) 6.0 yards-per-carry. “He looked really good. Have to get him more touches definitely.” RJ Harvey’s 52-yard house call and Dobbins’ goal line touchdown should also be highlighted as part of this very good night in Broncos Country. Heck, even Will Lutz crushed all three of his field goal attempts continuing to make the naysayers from earlier this season (me) choke on their words. It turns out, that in the end, all Bo Nix needed to stifle concerns over offensive production was to play a team outside the top-10 and outside the division. The crisis of confidence crowd can release their stranglehold on their pearls, take a breath, and enjoy this dominant win over the Arizona Cardinals. At 5-2, the Broncos are poised to meet, if not exceed, expectations for this season. Enjoy the ride, Broncos Country!

title: Lions injury news: Good news for Amon-Ra St. Brown, Ennis Rakestraw
summary: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell gave a couple of injury updates in his Monday afternoon press conference, and it’s mostly good news. Let’s start with Amon-Ra St. Brown. I’m guessing many weren’t aware St. Brown was even dealing with an injury, as he never exited the game and wasn’t given a specific injury designation on […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-OCTOBER 25: Detroit Lions wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown (14) carries the ball under the pressure of Green Bay Packers safety Xavier McKinney (29) during an NFL football game between the New York Jets and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, September 27, 2026. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell gave a couple of injury updates in his Monday afternoon press conference, and it’s mostly good news. Let’s start with Amon-Ra St. Brown. I’m guessing many weren’t aware St. Brown was even dealing with an injury, as he never exited the game and wasn’t given a specific injury designation on Sunday. However, Detroit Football Network’s Justin Rogers noted that the Lions did not make him available in the locker room because he was getting treatment for a swollen ankle . Campbell said they expect to sit St. Brown for Wednesday’s practice, but they’re optimistic he’ll be okay and are hoping he’ll be ready to go for Thursday. “He and Ennis (Rakestraw), I think those guys will probably sit Wednesday, but the plan is to get them going Thursday, and I think that they’ll be fine. They should be good,” Campbell said, before adding. “Now, we’ll see when we get there, but—yep.” St. Brown is coming off his best game of the season, hauling in nine catches for a season-high 153 yards. That’s the fifth-most yards he’s had in a single game for his career. Obviously, missing him would be a big deal, but Campbell doesn’t sound too concerned at the moment. The Lions are expecting the same trajectory for cornerback Ennis Rakestraw, who did leave the game early with an ankle injury. “It’s not major, he’s got a little ankle here,” Campbell said. “We feel like, as of right now, he’ll be at practice on Thursday. That’s kinda what we’re looking at. But we don’t feel like it’s major as of today.” Rakestraw was part of a pretty massive cornerback rotation against the Packers. Rakestraw (21 snaps) shared playing time with D.J. Reed (61), Roger McCreary (67), Rock Ya-Sin (14), and Khalil Dorsey (14). It was a game plan inspired by the Dallas Cowboys’ attack against the Packers to keep the players fresh. Campbell said it’s an approach they will continue to consider moving forward. “I think there was also merit for a number of those guys plays,” Campbell said. “Letting them all kinda play, getting some reps and using them in different situations, different packages.”

title: Detroit Lions Week 7 snap counts: Secondary rotation leads to success vs. Packers
summary: The Detroit Lions moved to 4-2 on the season and 1-0 in the NFC North after taking down their division rival, the Green Bay Packers, 20-17 in Week 7. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Brian Branch #32 of the Detroit Lions intercepts a pass intended for Christian Watson #9 of the Green Bay Packers during fourth quarter of a game at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions moved to 4-2 on the season and 1-0 in the NFC North after taking down their division rival, the Green Bay Packers, 20-17 in Week 7. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. Quarterback Jared Goff: 68 (100%) Josh Dobbs: DNP Goff continues to play well, producing another 300-yard passing game, while also adding two touchdowns and no interceptions. He did take responsibility for the fumble on the snap exchange, but it’s hard to tell whether he was actually at fault or simply being a good leader. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs: 61 (90%) Sione Vaki: 9 (13%) — 12 special teams snaps (57%) Jacob Saylors: 0 (0%) — 12 (57%) After a couple of weeks of the Lions scaling back Gibbs’ usage to preserve him for a long season, Sunday’s game was too important and too close for them not to want him on the field as much as possible. His 34 total touches are more than the Lions would prefer in any given week, but sometimes that’s the necessary path to take. Vaki saw one carry early in the game, taking it a strong five yards, and probably would’ve seen more action had the Lions pulled away in this one. Wide receiver Jameson Williams: 57 (84%) Amon-Ra St. Brown: 53 (78%) Isaac TeSlaa: 33 (49%) Tay Martin: 1 (1%) — 12 (57%) DeAndre Carter: 0 (0%) — 6 (29%) After opening things up with their wide receivers in the first half, the Lions wanted to assert their will more in the second and deployed “bigger” sets, which led to a slightly lower snap count for this unit. Still, St. Brown and Williams were terrific and huge contributors to the win. Tight end Sam LaPorta: 66 (97%) Brock Wright: 38 (56%) — 4 (19%) Tyler Conklin: 8 (12%) Jackson Meeks: DNP ( INACTIVE ) While the Lions tight ends caught only two passes for 22 yards, they were on the field a lot in blocking situations. Both LaPorta and Wright were sharp as pass protectors, and while LaPorta’s only catch came in the fourth quarter, it helped set things up for the Lions to get into game-winning field goal range. Offensive line LG Christian Mahogany: 68 (100%) — 4 (100%) RT Blake Miller: 68 (100%) — 4 (100%) RG Tate Ratledge: 68 (100%) — 4 (100%) LT Penei Sewell: 68 (100%) C Cade Mays: 68 (100%) LT/6th OL: Larry Borom: 12 (18%) — 4 (19%) C Juice Scruggs: 0 (0%) — 4 (19%) RG Miles Frazier: 0 (0%) — 4 (19%) C Seth McLaughlin: DNP ( INACTIVE ) Mays had some ups and downs in his Lions debut, struggling at times as a blocker—he was credited with giving up the Lions’ only sack allowed on the day—and was involved in both the Lions’ fumbles, but you could see the potential as a people-mover in the run game. He should keep ascending as he acclimates. Borom saw the field 12 times in this game, with 10 snaps coming as a sixth offensive lineman, and two snaps at left tackle, allowing Sewell to shift into the sixth OL role. Borom wasn’t credited with giving up a pressure, but he was beaten on the play where Sewell ran a short crosser, which drew the eyes of the defense and opened the window for Goff to find Williams for the touchdown. If the Lions want to get Sewell back into a pass-catching role again, they’ll need Borom to be ready. Interior defensive lin e 3T Alim McNeill: 52 (78%) — 5 (24%) DT Tyleik Williams: 34 (51%) — 5 (24%) 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 31 (46%) — 5 (24%) — 2 offensive plays (3%) DL Levi Onwuzurike: 14 (21%) 3T Mekhi Wingo: DNP ( INACTIVE ) The Lions have found an IDL rotation they like, which essentially consists of McNeill pairing with Williams or Gill-Howard in specific situations, with Onwuzurike filling in as needed, mainly to give McNeill a breather. PFF credited McNeill with six pressures, while Williams accounted for two and a run stop. EDGE EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 58 (87%) Rush End DJ Wonnum: 48 (72%) — 5 (24%) Big End Tyler Lacy: 21 (31%) — 4 (19%) Rush End Derrick Moore: 20 (30%) — 5 (24%) Rush End Eric O’Neill: 0 (0%) — 13 (62%) Big End Ahmed Hassanein: DNP ( INACTIVE ) Not much has changed in the Lions’ edge-rusher snap distribution following the bye; Hutchinson registers near 90% weekly, with Wonnum and Lacy splitting reps based on the opponent’s approach to offense. This week, with the Packers wanting to throw the ball, Wonnum saw his opportunities increase. Moore is still getting a lower percentage of snaps, but that number is steadily increasing as the coaches begin to trust him in more situational roles. Linebacker MIKE Jack Campbell: 67 (100%) — 5 (24%) SAM Derrick Barnes: 67 (100%) — 5 (24%) SAM Trevor Nowaske: 14 (21%) — 17 (81%) WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 0 (0%) — 12 (57%) WILL Amen Ogbongbemiga: 0 (0%) — 12 (57%) MIKE Jimmy Rolder: 0 (0%) — 12 (57%) The Lions made some tweaks to their linebacker usage this week, opting to deploy Campbell and Barnes on every defensive snap (typically Barnes is closer to 80-85%), and electing to only use Nowaske at WILL. The remainder of the reserves only saw the field on special teams. While the entire linebacking corps was solid against the run, Nowaske was the only linebacker who didn’t struggle in coverage. Cornerback CB/NB Roger McCreary: 67 (100%) — 5 (24%) CB D.J. Reed: 61 (91%) CB Ennis Rakestraw: 21 (31%) — 2 (10%) — Injured CB Khalil Dorsey: 14 (21%) — 13 (62%) CB Rock Ya-Sin: 14 (21%) — 4 (19%) After watching the Dallas Cowboys rotate their secondary to stay fresh while defending the Packers’ deep ball, the Lions instituted a rotation of their own, and it proved effective, as the corners were credited with giving up only 75 yards through the air. McCreary continued shifting between outside and in the slot; Reed said he felt fresher after taking a few snaps off; Rakestraw was the first off the bench as CB3 (until he was injured); Ya-Sin returned from injury and contributed on the outside, while Dorsey, who is arguably the fastest corner on the roster, was tasked with covering the Packers’ deep shots. While Dorsey was tasked with taking away the Packers’ most effective offensive play and sprinting downfield on most snaps, he was targeted just four times and allowed only 5 receiving yards. Pretty spectacular day. Safet y S Chuck Clark: 55 (82%) — 5 (24%) S Brian Branch: 45 (67%) DB Keith Abney: 34 (51%) DB Christian Izien: 0 (0%) — 10 (48%) S Bishop Fitzgerald: DNP ( INACTIVE ) Welcome back, Brian Branch. With Branch back in the mix, the Lions secondary played with more confidence, and the Pro Bowl safety’s impact was felt throughout the game. Branch not only delivered big hits, but he also intercepted Jordan Love on a bomb downfield, energizing the entire defense. Branch was on a snap count in Week 7, and the Lions leaned on Clark and Abney to work opposite him, while also overlapping their responsibilities. Clark continues to look steady but is physically limited, while Abney is physically gifted but still learning the position. With Branch unlikely to be on a snap count moving forward, the Lions will likely scale back Clark and Abney’s snaps, while their situational roles will remain. Specialist s K Jake Bates: 8 (38%) P Jack Fox: 6 (29%) LS Hogan Hatten: 6 (29%) With the game on the line, Bates delivered again.

title: The Green Bay Packers were lucky to keep it close vs. the Detroit Lions
summary: If you hang around Green Bay Packers fans on Monday morning, you’re likely to see a lot of bellyaching about officiating. And to their point, I do think the Packers were victims of a few questionable calls. The roughing the passer on the Lions’ game-winning drive was terrible. The unnecessary roughness on Devonte Wyatt was […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-OCTOBER 25: Defensive tackle Tyleik Williams #91 of the Detroit Lions reacts after a play during the first half of an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, October 25, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images If you hang around Green Bay Packers fans on Monday morning, you’re likely to see a lot of bellyaching about officiating. And to their point, I do think the Packers were victims of a few questionable calls. The roughing the passer on the Lions’ game-winning drive was terrible. The unnecessary roughness on Devonte Wyatt was ridiculous, when it was Amon-Ra St. Brown who got up from the ground and tried to gain extra yardage. But if we’re being real, the Packers were the luckier team on Sunday night, because the Lions were wiping the floor with them most of the game and made just enough self-inflicted errors to make officiating factor in this game. Nowhere is this better highlighted than looking at the success rate for each team. It’s not the end-all, be-all statistic, but it tends to really highlight which team was better on a down-to-down basis. Before we take a peek at the numbers, a quick explanation of what success rate is. It marks every single offensive play as a binary: either a success or failure. A play is considered a success if it increases the team’s likelihood to score points on that drive. And while each success rate model varies differently, the general outline deems a play successful if: On first down: It gains at least 40% of the yards required for a new set of downs (ie: 4 yards on a first-and-10) On second down: It gains at least 60% of the yards required for a new set of downs (ie: 6 yards on second-and-10) On third or fourth down: It results in a first down or touchdown For Sunday’s game, the Lions offense produced a successful play on 53.7% of their plays rbsdm.com , good for the fifth-best output of any team in Week 7. The Packers, meanwhile, produced just a 34.3% success rate, the second-worst output of the week. That is a massive difference. In fact, it was the second-highest difference of any matchup in Week 7. Did we really get beat that bad? Comparing offensive success rates for NFL games in Week 7: pic.twitter.com/pqarLvhGCZ — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 26, 2026 So how were the Packers able to keep it close? Luck. They were lucky Cade Mays accidentally jarred the ball loose from teammate Jahmyr Gibbs while the Lions were threatening to move it to a two-score game at halftime. They were lucky Jared Goff missed a snap exchange from Mays on the next drive to give Green Bay stellar field position, leading to a touchdown. That alone is a potential 14-point swing in Green Bay’s favor. That isn’t to say the Lions didn’t benefit from some luck, too. A missed field goal is lucky—the other one blocked by DJ Wonnum was forced. A Packers’ drop or two is lucky. And certainly some officiating luck is lucky—ignoring the fact that the Lions were on the end of some poor calls/non-calls. But when it comes to a play-by-play basis, there really is no question who was better. And you can look beyond success rate, too. Detroit averaged 6.3 yards per play, while the Packers were at 5.0. The only statistic the Packers had the clear edge in was turnovers, and both of Detroit’s giveaways were unforced errors. To be fair, Green Bay did make key plays in key moments, holding the Lions to 0-for-2 on fourth down and just 2-for-5 in the red zone. But the Lions were just as good, or better, in those moments too. Though Green Bay was 3-for-4 on fourth down, they were just 1-of-4 in the red zone, and posted a much worse third-down conversion rate (33% vs. 50%). The Lions were the better team on Sunday, and the better team won.

title: Detroit Lions grades: Secondary shines in breakout win vs. Packers
summary: The Detroit Lions eeked out a win over the Green Bay Packers, but generally looked like the better team for most of the game. How does that translate to a weekly report card? Let’s take a look at my instant grades before a rewatch. Quarterback: A- Jared Goff was red-hot in the first half, dicing […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Khalil Dorsey #30 of the Detroit Lions breaks up a pass intended for Bo Melton #16 of the Green Bay Packers during fourth quarter of a game at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions eeked out a win over the Green Bay Packers, but generally looked like the better team for most of the game. How does that translate to a weekly report card? Let’s take a look at my instant grades before a rewatch. Quarterback: A- Jared Goff was red-hot in the first half, dicing up what was one of the best pass defenses in the league coming into the game. He went 13-of-17 for 207 yards, a touchdown, and a 136.2 passer rating. He was accurate; he was reading defenses well, and he managed the pocket well. However, he did take a pretty significant step back in the second half. He put a couple of balls in danger’s way, struggled to find open receivers, and finished the final two quarters by completing just 9-of-15 passes for 96 yards and a score (101.0 passer rating). The statline would’ve looked worse if a couple of his interceptable passes had been actually picked off. Still, considering this was one of the best pass defenses in the league, he deserves a ton of credit for moving the ball pretty consistently through the air. Running back: C It doesn’t matter if it was Cade Mays who jarred the ball loose; Jahmyr Gibbs CANNOT fumble in the red zone. That was a huge play that was just one of many opportunities for the Lions to pull away in that game. The rest of his game was really odd. Of Gibbs’ 29 carries, 12 went for at least 7 yards, but eight went for 0 yards or less. There was a little too much dancing from Gibbs, but at the same time, how many running backs are turning this play into a significant gain? A tackle for loss against most backs, not against Jahmyr Gibbs pic.twitter.com/19IxKIoAaB — Steve Palazzolo (@StevePalazzolo_) October 25, 2026 Tight ends: C I’m sure conspiracy theorists will be loud about Sam LaPorta only getting two targets all game, and I will admit it was particularly hard to explain why he wasn’t more involved, but I suppose with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams tearing apart a good Packers secondary, you can’t complain. Upon live viewing, I don’t really have any positives or negatives to say about the tight end group, but LaPorta’s catch on the final drive of the game was huge. Wide receivers: A- As just alluded to, St. Brown and Williams seemed near unstoppable for the majority of this game. St. Brown, in particular, was dominant in a matchup against one of the better nickel corners in the league (Javon Bullard). He pulled in nine catches for 153 yards on 11 targets. Meanwhile, Williams came down with 91 yards and two touchdowns (and nearly a third) on nine targets. Both players deserve a ton of credit for finding spots in the Packers’ zone coverage and taking advantage of all the opportunities they had. Offensive line: B- Early on, the offensive line looked absolutely dominant against the Packers. Goff had plenty of time, particularly on play-action passes, which allowed him to hit several explosive passing plays. In fact, Goff only saw pressure on 21.2% of his dropbacks, the third-lowest figure of Week 7. However, many of the aforementioned inconsistencies in the run game were due to lapses in run blocking. Too often, Gibbs was hit in the backfield. In fact, the Lions averaged -0.80 yards before contact, which was easily the worst performance of Week 7. I’m eager to see what went wrong there, because the Packers do not have that good of a front seven, particularly with all of their injuries. Defensive line: B Aidan Hutchinson was dominant again, tallying a sack, forcing a holding penalty, and earning nine pressures on the day, per PFF. And Detroit’s run defense was absolutely smothering until late in the game. But in the fourth quarter, this unit seemed to run out of gas a little. And there weren’t really any other standout performances along the defensive line (except for DJ Wonnum’s special teams play, but that’s later). Against an absolutely injury-devastated offensive line, I was hoping for a little more. Still, hard to be disappointed on a day in which the Lions produced pressure at an average of 2.39 seconds (sixth-best of the week). Linebackers: D It was a pretty brutal day for the Lions’ linebackers on live viewing. Most of the Packers’ damage was done over the middle of the field, be it Tucker Kraft (four catches, 48 yards, 1 TD) or Josh Jacobs (five catches, 55 yards, 1 TD). The Lions’ linebackers weren’t particularly strong in man or zone coverage. But I can’t in good faith give them a failing grade, because their play was also critical in holding the Packers to just 60 rushing yards and 3.2 yards per carry. Secondary: A- Shout out to one of the biggest winners of the week: Pride of Detroit’s own Anthony Balaj. He endured a week of hate from Packers fans for this article: Film study: Packers’ deep passing attack is a paper tiger https://t.co/TXC1qoxMo7 — Pride of Detroit (@PrideOfDetroit) October 20, 2026 The Lions held up their end of the bargain. Here was Jordan Love’s statline on passes with at least 20 air yards: 1-for-6 for 14 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT, and a 39.6 passer rating … and that one completion was a broken play in which Jack Campbell fell down in coverage. The Lions secondary was phenomenal in defending the deep pass, and really strong in most situations despite facing one of the hottest two-headed attacks in Matthew Golden (six catches on 12 targets, 39 yards) and Christian Watson (five catches on eight targets, 57 yards). And I just can’t handle the beauty of Brian Branch’s interception. It is quite literally a picture-perfect defense of that pass. Sure, it may not have actually meant much in the game—the Packers were about to punt and Detroit was likely to get the ball there anyways—but, man, that got the juices flowing on the sidelines and in the stands of Ford Field. Let’s watch it again: Branch back y'all pic.twitter.com/vjACYfESmQ — Detroit Lions (@Lions) October 25, 2026 Special teams: B+ DJ Wonnum’s tipped field goal turned out to be one of the biggest plays of the game, so that tips the scales pretty heavily on what I would consider a pretty average-to-below-average day from the special teamers. I thought DeAndre Carter looked promising in the return game, nearly breaking two big returns on the day. However, he did commit a costly penalty on a kick return in the fourth quarter—Detroit’s second penalty on kick return of the day. And while Jake Bates was perfect on his field goals and extra points, he did put two kickoffs in the end zone, giving the Packers strong field position. Coaching: B Let’s start with the fourth down hysteria. Admittedly, I wasn’t a fan in the moment, but I’ve come closer to Dan Campbell’s side after hearing his argument and seeing some of the analytical data . I no longer have a strong feeling on it, but I will say this: the Lions’ short-yardage running game has not been good this year, and that should factor into the decision. Going into this game, the Lions’ success rate in short-yardage situations (FTN Fantasy’ “power rate” statistic) ranked 20th in the NFL. And given it was closer to fourth-and-2 than fourth-and-1, it made that call a toss-up, in my opinion. You can really have the same discussion about Detroit’s decision to go for it and pass on a field goal earlier in the fourth quarter. I think there’s enough nuance to those discussions to call them 50/50 toss-ups, and I’ll always feel better about erring on the side of aggression, particularly with an offense that currently ranks top-five in most categories. And, ultimately, Campbell’s strategy worked on the last decision. It was largely made knowing that the Lions offense would have the ball last, and that’s an advantageous place to be. If Green Bay had even made the field goal, Detroit was still in a stellar…
