full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 2: Detroit Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs #0 runs the ball against Minnesota Vikings cornerback Isaiah Rodgers #2 during the second half of an NFL football game between the Minnesota Vikings and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, November 2, 2025 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Detroit Lions (4-2) will host their division rival, the Minnesota Vikings (6-0), in Week 8. Despite the Vikings being the last undefeated team standing, the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook believe the 1972 Dolphins will be sipping champagne next Sunday and have set the opening betting line at Lions -3 points . The Vikings’ biggest offseason moves included signing starting quarterback Kyler Murray and WR3 Jauan Jennings, as well as trading away EDGE Jonathan Greenard to the Eagles. While the offense gained and the defense lost talent, the results on the field in 2026 couldn’t be more opposite. The Vikings defense has been dominant and the primary reason Minnesota is undefeated. They are the top defense in DVOA, but not just overall; they also rank No. 1 in defending the pass and No. 3 in defending the run. They allow teams to score only 12.3 points, on average, and are holding teams to 253 yards of total offense. They’re playing at an incredibly high level. On offense, we see the other end of the spectrum. The Vikings offense ranks 27th in DVOA, 27th in the passing game, and 22nd in rushing. They average 20.8 points per game, but much of that is because their defense sets them up in many favorable situations. The Lions are still working out some of the kinks in their roster, but there have been noticeable signs of improvement, and it doesn’t take much for the offense to catch fire quickly. This will be a true good-vs.-good matchup on Sunday afternoon at Ford Field, as the Lions’ explosive offense will do their best to find cracks in a defense that doesn’t have many flaws. title: NFC Playoff Picture: Lions are in the thick of the Wild Card standings
summary: All of the NFC North teams are in the playoff picture. It’s that kind of year again. The Detroit Lions vaulted the Green Bay Packers by beating them in Week 7. The Minnesota Vikings are the only undefeated team in the NFL. The Chicago Bears pushed their record to 5-2 on Thursday night. The Lions […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-OCTOBER 25: Wide receiver Jameson Williams #1 of the Detroit Lions scores a touchdown during the second half of an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, October 25, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images All of the NFC North teams are in the playoff picture. It’s that kind of year again. The Detroit Lions vaulted the Green Bay Packers by beating them in Week 7. The Minnesota Vikings are the only undefeated team in the NFL. The Chicago Bears pushed their record to 5-2 on Thursday night. The Lions are 4-2, and the Packers are 4-3. Currently, all the Wild Card teams are from the NFC North, with the Seattle Seahawks just outside. Minnesota Vikings (6-0) 2. Chicago Bears (5-2) 3. Detroit Lions (4-2) 4. title: Discussion: Is Dan Campbell taking too many risks?
summary: Whether you trust the odds or trust your gut, there is no denying that critical decisions at pivotal moments can win or lose you a football game. Football is a game of risk, but some coaches try to minimize it while others try to capitalize on it. Dan Campbell and the Detroit Lions have been […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions looks on against the Green Bay Packers during the first quarter at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Whether you trust the odds or trust your gut, there is no denying that critical decisions at pivotal moments can win or lose you a football game. Football is a game of risk, but some coaches try to minimize it while others try to capitalize on it. Dan Campbell and the Detroit Lions have been classified as high rollers since he was hired as head coach—is it time to change? The Lions defeated the Green Bay Packers in their Week 7 tilt, but things could have turned out far different if not for a few key moments. If the Packers had converted one or both of their failed field goals, the Lions would have needed a touchdown, not a field goal, on their final drive. If the Packers had converted on a few of their deep shots, the Packers likely put up more than 17 points. If the officiating had been less strict with roughing the passer or more strict with pass interference, perhaps some drives would have flipped from success to failure or vice versa. In such a close matchup, one decision can alter the outcome of the game. We nearly saw that happen on Sunday when the Lions boldly attempted a fourth-and-1 at their own 24-yard line . With around five minutes left in the game, the win probability would have swung wildly based on the play’s outcome. Had Detroit converted, they would have had a fresh set of downs with a chance to drain the clock and march downfield for a game-winning field goal. With a failed conversion, Green Bay would have been set up deep in Lions territory with a great chance to take the lead via field goal or touchdown. It was only natural that both outcomes happened. The Packers stopped Jahmyr Gibbs for a loss on the play, yet their subsequent four-play drive ended with a missed field goal, aided by a tip from DJ Wonnum. Detroit promptly marched down the field and drained the remaining three minutes to set up a Jake Bates game-winner. In a way, the Lions were both punished and rewarded for their risk taking. Had the Lions punted outright, Green Bay likely would have drained more of the clock on their next drive, potentially keeping the ball out of Detroit’s hands. Campbell said as much in his post-game press conference: Dan Campbell on why he went for it so deep in his own zone at the end of the game. 2 reasons: "I thought we would get it." "I knew we would get the ball back if it didn't work out." — Jeremy Reisman (@DetroitOnLion) October 25, 2026 However, now that the Lions have a playoff-caliber roster, wouldn’t it make sense to tone down the risky plays and let the roster’s talent speak for itself? For a team that had already shot themselves in the foot twice with fumbles, committing two turnovers on downs only added to the circus that was this game. Wouldn’t it make more sense to trot out the kicker for easier points, or the punter booting one to flip the field? Taking too many risks can backfire and cost you a game. Today’s Question of the Day is: Is Dan Campbell taking too many risks? My answer: I do not think so. In the early years of Campbell’s head coaching tenure, many people saw the risk-taking mindset as a byproduct of a bad roster. If the Lions wanted to win games, they needed to roll the dice. They nearly did so against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 7 of the 2021 season, a game in which the Lions ran two fake punts and a surprise onside kick . For one, after having watched Campbell since 2021, it seems clear that the risk taking in 2021 was just as much about his identity as it was about the roster. This isn’t to say that Campbell is keen to take a risk whenever he can. For a guy that still gets the label of “meathead” after a half decade, Campbell’s risk senses are genuinely elite. He’s not a guy that crunches the numbers on every given play, but his gut instinct is often in-line with what analytics say. This comes from being immersed in football for years as a player and as a coach. Simply put, he has the knack for knowing when to make a calculated risk, even if he is not actually doing that calculation. There have been moments where Campbell has taken risks and it has backfired, without doubt. However, I think you need to live with those mistakes because the reward is worth it. Campbell trusts his players and trusts their talent. If you need to get two yards, how many of us wouldn’t want to run Jahmyr Gibbs behind the likes of Penei Sewell? The execution can be flawed even when the logic was sound. Sometimes an opponent throws rock when you throw scissors—that is how football goes. I really believe that the Lions are a better team because Campbell trusts his instincts so often. This will lead to frustrating moments that can alter the outcome of a game, but I think this is a necessary consequence of a winning mindset. When a gamble fails, it is easy to have a knee-jerk negative reaction. However, often upon reflection, the gamble was actually revealed to have been a savvy move. Personally, I do not want Campbell to change his ways. Do you agree or disagree with my stance? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Packers Injury Report: 7 to start the list on Monday
summary: The Green Bay Packers did not have a practice on Monday, but the team did release a practice estimation due to their quick turnaround to prepare for their Thursday Night Football game against the Carolina Panthers. As of now, the Packers’ injury list has seven players, but remember this could be a very aggressive list, […]
full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers did not have a practice on Monday, but the team did release a practice estimation due to their quick turnaround to prepare for their Thursday Night Football game against the Carolina Panthers. As of now, the Packers’ injury list has seven players, but remember this could be a very aggressive list, as Green Bay’s players had a game just one day ago. The estimated non-participants on Monday were: WR Matthew Golden (shoulder/foot) C Sean Rhyan (ankle) RG Travis Glover (knee) DL Devonte Wyatt (ankle) DL Anthony Campbell (ankle) LB Zaire Franklin (shin) Golden, Glover, Wyatt and Campbell were all able to finish Sunday’s game against the Detroit Lions, though Wyatt did drop out of action for a period. Mike linebacker Zaire Franklin missed the game with a reported fracture of his shin, which is expected to keep him out this week against the Panthers. Rhyan, like Jacob Monk, went down in-game and did not return, forcing John Williams into the center position. Earlier today, Monk was placed on the injured reserve . The only estimated limited participant today was guard Aaron Banks, who is still dealing with both knee tendinitis and a toe injury. Cornerback Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring), the only player scratched in Sunday’s game due to injury, was an estimated full participant. The Packers’ roster is pretty straightforward right now, as the team needs to get a full 53-man roster to a 48-man game-day roster by Thursday. Assuming that Franklin and Rhyan are out, Green Bay’s other three scratches will likely be two offensive linemen (the team rarely keeps more than eight on the game-day roster) and running back Kaleb Johnson, who was also a healthy scratch against the Panthers. The only real monkey wrenches here are if the defensive linemen (Wyatt and Campbell) can’t get back up for Thursday’s action or if Golden can’t suit up. Keep an eye on those situations throughout the week. The Panthers didn’t have a full practice on Monday, but they did hold a walkthrough. The non-participants for their walkthrough were: G Damien Lewis (starter) OL Torricelli Simpkins DL Bobby Brown III ED Jaelen Phillips (starter) CB Akayleb Evans The biggest news out of Carolina, though, is that right tackle Taylor Moton, one of the better offensive linemen at his position in the league, fractured his fibula yesterday against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and has been placed on the injured reserve.

title: Packers Film Room: Long snapping on kicks in Week 7
summary: In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got 6 we’re looking at this week. There were only 5 attempted kicks, but the initial field goal attempt went through the entire operation before getting waved off (the delay of game flag was thrown just after the snap […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got 6 we’re looking at this week. There were only 5 attempted kicks, but the initial field goal attempt went through the entire operation before getting waved off (the delay of game flag was thrown just after the snap and everyone on the field plays it out), so I decided to include it as Kick 0. I decided to bring in an assistant (my 8 year old son) to help me with the charting & stick figure this week. Kick 0: Field Goal 21 yards Made (No Play) Snap is a tick high, but not overly so. Charted this one as to the body. Rotation is good, allowing Whelan to catch the ball by the laces and get the ball down with a nice hold-and-spin. Ball is leaning slightly forward and away from Smack, which is exactly what you want in perfect conditions. Smack doesn’t tend to have a lot of movement on his kicks: they go in a straight line more often than not. This one starts off hugging the upright and goes through hugging the upright. Kick 1: Field Goal 26 yards Miss This was Orzech’s worst snap of the day. It’s high and at Whelan’s head. Whelan has to rise up to catch the ball, but he’s able to catch it by the laces and get it down. The whole operation took ~1.34 seconds, which is right in the range of what you want (typically looking between 1.3-1.4 seconds). Laces are out, aligned to the middle of the uprights. Good hold from Whelan. Ball is down at the same spot as the previous kick (right on the inside edge of the hash), so it’s not a different aiming point for Smack. Good snap. Good hold. I’m not an expert in kicking mechanics so I don’t really know what happens from here, but it looks like this is on Smack. The ball starts straight, but ends up drifting outside while in the air. It looks like he gets the same spot of the ball, but I would guess he strikes more of the inside part of the ball on this kick, which causes that outside draw. Kick 2: Extra Point Made Good snap (up and to the body), good hold, good kick. Kick 3: Extra Point Made Great snap (over the place where the ball is placed on the hold), good hold, good kick. Worth noting the outside draw on this kick as well. It starts directly to the middle of the uprights so that draw to the outside is fine, but if the kick starts more at the outside upright it would be a problem. Again, not an issue on this kick given the starting point of the kick but just something to keep in mind, given the missed kick earlier. Kick 4: Field Goal 43 yards Made A tick low, but over the point of the hold. Good snap, good hold, good kick. A couple things on the protection here. With the ball on the left hash, the Lions are loading up over the right side of the line. Since the ball has to travel back to the right to get to the uprights, it makes sense to overload that side to try to get a push for a block. Watch Travis Glover [79] on this play. He starts low, but the man across from him is lower and the initial contact gets Glover raised up and off-balance. As more rushers push, Glover is completely raised up; one foot completely up in the air, entire body getting shoved back. This one very easily could have been blocked. Kick 5: Field Goal 35 yards Miss (Blocked) – BODY Good snap from Orzech. Up and to the body, with the rotation allowing Whelan to catch it on the laces and get down a nice snap. Good hold, place and spin. The entire snap-to-kick operation takes ~1.29 seconds. No issues there. The issue is what we looked at in the last play. Once again we’re on the left hash, so the Lions are loaded up on the right. Glover starts out slightly better than last time, but is still easily out-leveraged and shoved back. This time the hand gets through and gets a hand on the ball as it crosses the line. It could just be me, but this doesn’t look like an issue with operation or with kick height. Snap, hold & timing were all fine. More than anything, the issue seems to be with Glover getting outleveraged. Albums listened to: beabadoobee – Pylon

title: The Lions had a good game plan to limit Lukas Van Ness
summary: The Green Bay Packers are dealing with several injuries in their front seven right now. The team is currently out its star edge rusher, Micah Parsons, and three interior defensive linemen are on the injured reserve (with Devonte Wyatt being limited due to injury). On top of that, both of the team’s starting linebackers, Zaire Franklin […]
full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are dealing with several injuries in their front seven right now. The team is currently out its star edge rusher, Micah Parsons, and three interior defensive linemen are on the injured reserve (with Devonte Wyatt being limited due to injury) . On top of that, both of the team’s starting linebackers, Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper, weren’t able to play on Sunday, too. With all the uncertainty in the box, I’m sure a lot of Packers fans were hoping that edge defender Lukas Van Ness would step up and win some one-on-one reps against the Detroit Lions…but that never came. So what happened? Did Van Ness lose a bunch of snaps on the edge? Well, not really. When watching the film, the first thing that became immediately apparent was that the Lions had a pretty good game plan to limit Van Ness’ impact in the game and force the other defenders to “win” to get to quarterback Jared Goff. LVN's first pass rush rep on the edge came with 10:14 in the 2nd Q (the Goff sack-fumble) — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) October 26, 2026 In total, Van Ness got to line up on the tackle and rush the tackle just five times on Sunday. For perspective, Goff threw the ball 32 times (and was sacked once, a play where Van Ness lined up on and rushed the tackle – funny enough). If you want to count it, there was a sixth rep where Van Ness played a screen over the tackle and rushed. He tipped the ball from Goff on that play. There were times when Van Ness lined up inside, only to get double-teamed, or dropped into coverage, to allow for a blitzing linebacker or safety without the defense being down an extra man in zone coverage. That can be controlled by the Packers, and maybe they want to stop playing fewer games with how Van Ness is deployed until their hand isn’t so short on cards. Still, it sure seemed like Detroit was much more willing to pass the ball when Van Ness was off the field than when he was on it. In the run game, Detroit mostly ran away from Van Ness’ side of the field or gave Van Ness a long surface (like multiple tight ends) to try to limit his impact. Even on “outside runs” at the NFL level, the ball is expected to usually hit off-tackle, so having Van Ness line up outside of a tight end or two, when the Lions actually did run toward him, meant that the edge defender was going to have little impact, anyway. To put it simply: The Lions were going to make the Packers’ backups make plays by accounting for Van Ness on nearly every down. Worth mentioning: Several of the five snaps that Van Ness got to rush the passer on the edge one-on-one were in Detroit’s two-minute drill, where they really had no other option but to let him get after Goff. Here were the Packers’ top box defenders, in terms of their snap counts, outside of Van Ness on Sunday: LB Isaiah McDuffie: 66 LB Ty’Ron Hopper: 62 DL Karl Brooks: 46 DL Chris McClellan: 38 ED Dani Dennis-Sutton: 33 ED Barryn Sorrell: 32 DL Jordan Riley: 29 ED Brenton Cox Jr.: 28 DL Anthony Campbell: 26 DL Devonte Wyatt: 23 (banged up during the game) LB Nick Niemann: 1 That lineup looks more like the group that played Green Bay’s third quarters in the preseason this year than the projected starters, due to the injuries they’ve already faced in 2026. Detroit has a good offensive line, but clearly, they went out of their way to limit Van Ness and take their one-on-one chances elsewhere on the roster. And it worked. Look for other teams to replicate the Lions’ game plan moving forward, at least until the Packers get some pieces back in the box that can tilt things back in their favor. If opposing offenses are going to “overcommit” to making Van Ness’ life hard on a down-to-down basis, the group of misfit toys are going to have to be the ones who have to step up to the plate.

title: Packers kicker Trey Smack adds two more misses to uninspiring start
summary: Among many other reasons, the Packers lost to the Detroit Lions on Sunday because they couldn’t put two short field goals through the uprights. 2026 draft pick Trey Smack missed outright from 26 yards, then had a 35-yard attempt blocked on the Packers’ final drive. In a game the Packers lost 20-17, you don’t have […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 25: Trey Smack #28 of the Green Bay Packers lines up a field goal during the fourth quarter of a game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on October 25, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Among many other reasons, the Packers lost to the Detroit Lions on Sunday because they couldn’t put two short field goals through the uprights. 2026 draft pick Trey Smack missed outright from 26 yards, then had a 35-yard attempt blocked on the Packers’ final drive. In a game the Packers lost 20-17, you don’t have to be a math major to see how things could have played out differently. The Packers spent three (admittedly very late) draft picks to get Smack, trading their final two picks in this spring’s draft to move up to select him with the 216th pick. He was the only kicker drafted this spring and, so far, he’s been one of the worst kickers in the NFL. In an era where kickers are making more of their attempts than ever, Smack lags far behind the field. The league average field goal percentage this season is 84.2%, but Smack has made just 68.8% (11 out of 16) of his attempts. Not all of those misses are his fault; two of his field goal attempts this year have been blocked, and those still count against his overall percentage. But even if Smack had converted those two blocks, he’d still be below the league average this year. Worse, it’s where he’s missing that’s concerning. Smack can’t seem to make field goals from an area of the field that are all but a sure thing for most kickers. All five of Smack’s misses have come from 49 yards or less; he’s nine of 14 (64.3%) from that distance this season. Among the five total kickers this season who have made less than 70% of their field goals this year, only Smack and Harrison Mevis have multiple misses from under 49 yards. Mevis, you’ll note, is currently out of a job. His two misses against the Buffalo Bills in Week 5 were enough to cost the Rams the game and earn him his walking papers. And it’s worth noting that Mevis made all 14 of his PATs while with the Rams this year. Smack is 13 of 15 in that department, and his miss against the Vikings in Week 1 played a big role in how that game played out down the stretch. Smack is off to an even worse start than the last kicker the Packers drafted. Anders Carlson’s misses from 43 and 45 yards cost the Packers dearly in losses to the Raiders (19-17) and Giants (24-22) in the 2023 regular season, and his late miss against the 49ers in the playoffs (from 41 yards) changed San Francisco’s final drive from a game-tying effort to a game-winning one. But on the whole, Carlson’s stats look downright desirable. He finished his rookie year converting 29 of 36 field goals (80.1%) counting the playoffs and hit 83.9% of his kicks from 49 yards and in. If Smack hits at that clip, the Packers’ season might look a whole lot different. Smack still has a job for now, and 16 field goal attempts is hardly a big enough sample size to judge a rookie kicker. Things could still improve. But it’s hardly an inspiring start, and it leaves the kicking game as just one more thing the Packers need to improve as they try to keep their season on track.

title: Packers vs. Panthers odds: Opening lines for Week 8 matchup
summary: In Week 7, the Green Bay Packers and Carolina Panthers both had disappointing losses, but they came in very different ways. The Packers fell on a last-second field goal on Sunday, losing 20-17 to the Detroit Lions in a game where everyone — but particularly the refs and the Packers themselves — deserve blame. Even […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - NOVEMBER 02: Carolina Panthers linebacker Trevin Wallace (32) hits Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) during a game between the Green Bay Packers and the Carolina Panthers at Lambeau Field on November 2, 2025 in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In Week 7, the Green Bay Packers and Carolina Panthers both had disappointing losses, but they came in very different ways. The Packers fell on a last-second field goal on Sunday, losing 20-17 to the Detroit Lions in a game where everyone — but particularly the refs and the Packers themselves — deserve blame. Even so, the Panthers’ day was much worse. Carolina lost at home 43-13 to a Tampa Bay Buccaneers team that came into the day 1-5, and they somehow managed to allow those 43 points with the Bucs gaining only 64 passing yards. Tampa Bay racked up a whopping 258 rushing yards on Sunday and they got points from both their defense (a fumble return for a score) and special teams (a two-point conversion after a blocked PAT). To make matters worse, Carolina also lost Taylor Moton, their longtime right tackle, to an injury. On Thursday, the Packers will host the Panthers on a short week, with both teams coming off these disappointing results. But between the short week, Carolina having to travel, and the relative results of the two Week 7 games, it should come as no surprise that the Packers are favored for the Thursday Night Football matchup. According to FanDuel sportsbook, the line is open at Packers -4.5 for Thursday’s game. If it holds up, that would tie for the biggest amount that the Packers have been favored by in any game this season; unfortunately, the last time that they were giving 4.5 points was in the team’s previous TNF game earlier this season, which saw Bijan Robinson run over, around, and through the Green Bay defense. Overall, the Packers are sitting 3-2-2 against the spread in their seven games so far, covering in each of the past three. They did manage to cover as 3.5-point underdogs in Detroit after clearing the bar in wins over the Bears and Cowboys the two weeks prior. This week’s game has a more typical number of points expected, however. While the game in Detroit had lines of well over 50 points as the over/under, Thursday’s contest is at a more typical 47.5. Five of seven Packers games have gone under the projected total so far this season, including each of the last four. The Packers and Panthers met in Week 8 of the 2025 season as well. That game, which had the Packers as whopping 13-point favorites, ended in a 16-13 Panthers win.

title: Packers Injury Updates: Sean Rhyan, Zaire Franklin likely to miss time
summary: The Green Bay Packers got some unpleasant news on the injury front on Monday morning following the team’s 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 7. Two starters, one in the middle of each of the offense and defense, are likely to miss more time with injuries, though neither one is expected to be […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Sean Rhyan #75 of the Green Bay Packers stands on the sideline during the national anthem prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers got some unpleasant news on the injury front on Monday morning following the team’s 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions in Week 7. Two starters, one in the middle of each of the offense and defense, are likely to miss more time with injuries, though neither one is expected to be season-ending. First up is linebacker Zaire Franklin, who was ruled out for Sunday’s game after suffering a leg injury in practice during the week. Ian Rapoport of NFL Network reports that Franklin has a hairline fracture in his leg, which explains why he was unable to play in Week 7. That injury will likely keep him out for the Packers’ Week 8 game against the Panthers on Thursday Night Football, but the team is not expected to put him on injured reserve. On the other side of the football, it appears likely that starting center Sean Rhyan will head to IR. Rapoport is on the Rhyan injury as well , and it is believed to be a high ankle sprain. Rhyan is fortunate to have avoided any fractures, but he still could be looking at a month-plus for recovery time, which could line up with a stint on injured reserve. Green Bay also lost backup center Jacob Monk to an injury just a few plays after Rhyan left the game, meaning John Williams had to enter the game as an emergency option. He performed admirably for the most part, and could be in line to start on Thursday against Carolina if Monk is also unavailable on a short week. The decision not to shut Franklin down suggests that the Packers expect him to return to the field before the end of November. Had they put him on IR, he would need to sit for the next four games before being eligible to return to the active roster. Should either of these injured players actually go on injured reserve, they would be ineligible to return until the game against the New Orleans Saints in Week 13, due to the Packers’ bye coming in Week 11.

The offense continued to suffer from another case of the dropsies, Jordan Love lost two more offensive linemen, and the refs…the refs! Let’s dive into this weekend’s winners and losers. Winner: Jordan Love QB Jordan Love […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - OCTOBER 25: Green Bay Packers place kicker Trey Smack (28) misses a short field goal during the Detroit Lions versus Green Bay Packers game on Sunday October 25, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers are officially 4-3 after a frustrating last-second 20-17 loss to the division rival Detroit Lions. The offense continued to suffer from another case of the dropsies, Jordan Love lost two more offensive linemen, and the refs…the refs! Let’s dive into this weekend’s winners and losers. Winner: Jordan Love QB Jordan Love is once again making do while the world falls apart around him. After starting C Sean Rhyan went down with an injury in the first quarter, Jacob Monk subbed in and…also left the game with an injury. Like, almost immediately after. Did you guys know John Williams played center? Does John Williams know he plays center? Love was running for his life on Sunday, and still able to make some incredible plays in the process, like his gorgeous TD pass to TE Tucker Kraft in the first quarter. Absolute rocket from Jordan Love on the run pic.twitter.com/f4FGrObEBj — Poor Man’s Packers Podcast (@PMPPod) October 25, 2026 With almost no time to throw, he was somehow able to get this one to WR Savion Williams on 4th and 5. Later in the game, he had another gorgeous throw to WR Christian Watson on 4th and 3. 4th and 5 and Jordan Love and the @Packers get more than enough GBvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/wcRJ5jXbcP — NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026 Along with the pocket collapsing around him, Love had to deal with the drops. THE DROPS. This time it was Bo Melton and Josh Jacobs getting into the act. Jacobs’ drop, in particular, cost the team a go-ahead touchdown. Love finished the game 27 for 45 (60%) for 274 yards, 2 TD, 1 INT, and 0 roughing the passer calls. Winner: Javon Bullard The Packers safety continues to impress this season. He had some great coverage on WR Amon-Ra St. Brown to force an incompletion on 3rd and 17, and the Lions punted as a result. Later in the game, he tackled St. Brown for a big loss on a jet sweep, a play which otherwise might’ve done some damage to the Packers in years past. Bullard is playing like a stud in 2026. He finished the game with 2 total tackles and 1 PD. Winner: Evan Williams Lions QB Jared Goff has yet to throw a pick this season, and S Evan Williams came close to changing that, twice. The drops from the offense unfortunately carried over to the defense, because Williams dropped both of his near-picks. That’ll be the big story about Williams’ play from Sunday, but he was disruptive all over the field, as he has been all year. Williams finished the day with 9 total tackles and 1 PD. All-Pro season: still on. Loser: Matthew Golden WR Matthew Golden has blossomed into one of Jordan Love’s favorite targets, and for good reason. Golden is a playmaker, and he’s hard to beat without getting called for PI. Love targeted Golden a game-high 12 times on Sunday but he caught just 6 of 12 targets for 39 yards. He had some really great plays, like his first quarter catch below, but the drops continue to stain the Packers offense in 2026, and they need to be fixed, fast. Catch was good as Golden 👀 GBvsDET on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/pwD104kt3K — NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026 Loser: Josh Jacobs The RB finished the day with 11 carries for 36 yards, 5 catches for 55 yards, and 1 TD. He also pled no contest to battery in September after a May 2026 incident involving his former girlfriend and dropped a go-ahead touchdown. Yikes. Loser: Trey Smack Brandon McManus, I order you to stop haunting my rookie kicker’s body immediately. Smack was absolutely atrocious on Sunday, ruining what was otherwise a pretty nice opening drive for the Packers offense when he missed a 26 yard FG. Later in the game (and exactly one play after Jacobs’ drop), he missed a 35 yarder after it looked like a Lions player got a hand on it. 6 points left on the field by the kicker. The Packers lost by 3 points. Math is fun (derogatory.) The Packers have a short week as they head back home to face off against the 3-3 Carolina Panthers, who just got blown out by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this weekend. The Panthers have given the Packers a bit of trouble in recent years: they beat them 16-13 in 2025, and nearly beat them on Christmas Eve during their 2023 meeting (with a 2-12 record!) Can the Packers right the ship with just a couple days off? Find out on Thursday Night Football .

title: Green Bay Packers News: Plenty of blame to go around for loss to Lions
summary: Blame the referees. Blame the kicker. Blame the drops. The Green Bay Packers can find a way to put blame on every single person who went out between the lines at Ford Field for their 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions on Sunday. That includes both teams and the cohort of referees, all of whom […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-OCTOBER 25: Head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers talks to referee Alex Moore #49 during the second half of an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, October 25, 2026 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Blame the referees. Blame the kicker. Blame the drops. The Green Bay Packers can find a way to put blame on every single person who went out between the lines at Ford Field for their 20-17 loss to the Detroit Lions on Sunday. That includes both teams and the cohort of referees, all of whom contributed to yet another excruciating, frustrating loss. The refs put the Packers in terrible positions time and time again with bad, inconsistent officiating, and yet the team still had plenty of opportunities to win the game. They let those chances slip through their fingers — literally, in many cases — and now they sit at 4-3, in fourth place in the NFC North division, and on the cusp of undoing all of the good that had come from their recent three-game winning streak. Going 5-for-15 on third downs isn’t good enough. Jordan Love can’t will this team to a 50 percent conversion rate every game, particularly not when the team can’t get out of its own way on first and second down and when his receivers can’t hold on to the football. Going 1-for-4 in the red zone, thanks in large part to a pair of missed chip shot field goals (one of which was blocked), isn’t good enough. And so, here we are, seven weeks into the season and still holding more questions than answers about this team. Rapid reaction: Red zone, not yellow flags, lost game for Packers | Packers.com It’s always interesting to see which facets of the game certain reporters focus on. This is not intended as criticism, but it’s notable that Mike Spofford takes the team to task rather than the officials. Packers rip officiating after roughing penalties prove costly in loss | ESPN The players, meanwhile — especially on defense — weren’t pulling any punches in the locker room, however. Xavier McKinney was the most outspoken, and he’ll surely get fined for his comments, but at this point someone has to call out the league’s embarrassing officating. Matt LaFleur Nailed It, But Will Anything Change for Packers After Loss to Lions? | SI.com The comment referred to in the headline here is LaFleur saying “We’ve got to grow up fast.” It’s tough to argue that the Packers were truly that immature in this game, though, when you have two roughing the passer calls that are questionable at best and another personal foul for tackling a player despite the whistle never blowing. Josh Jacobs apologizes to team after crucial drop in loss to Lions | Packers Wire Jacobs’ drop led directly to a field goal attempt that got blocked (but might have been missed anyway). Green Bay Packers rookie kicker Trey Smack takes blame for missed field goals | Packersnews.com ($) Somehow, Smack doesn’t have the most EPA lost on field goal attempts this year, probably because he has hit some really long ones. That not-so-honorable lead goes to Harrison Butker, who is no stranger to going wide right. LISTEN: The Repack – The NFL doesn’t care about its officiating problem | Frozen Tundra Frequencies When will the NFL actually do something about their refs? Probably never, as long as fans keep watching and the money keeps coming in. This is a thing that can happen? Where’s the replay assist on some of the calls against the Packers? Brewers erase four-run deficit, take 2-0 World Series lead | Brew Crew Ball In much better news, Milwaukee won the first two games of the World Series at home, and both came in thrilling fashion. Game 3 is tonight, starting at 8 PM ET at Tropicana Field. Go Pack Go—wherever you go! title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: This one hurt in particular because the commentator was in attendance. I have lived in Houston for most of my life and it is the first NFL game I have attended since the Houston Oilers roamed the plains. More than anything, this felt like a season where the momentum was finally running in the right […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 25: Cam Skattebo #44 of the New York Giants runs the ball against the Houston Texans in overtime at NRG Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images This one hurt in particular because the commentator was in attendance. I have lived in Houston for most of my life and it is the first NFL game I have attended since the Houston Oilers roamed the plains. More than anything, this felt like a season where the momentum was finally running in the right direction. That came to a crashing halt on Sunday as the Texans perished 27-21 in a disappointing overtime loss. There is a lot to comment on in this one and being in attendance definitely has a different feel than watching on television. You can feel the emotion of the moment and that is one of the things that becomes more acute as we look back on this game. The team is now 0-4 at home this season. You aren’t going to go very far in the playoffs when you can’t win at home. The Numbers Total Yards: Texans 54/237, Giants 65/420 Rushing Yards: Texans 25/84, Giants 34/188 Passing Yards: Texans 29/153, Giants 31/232 Third Downs: Texans 3/12, Giants 5/13 Fourth Downs: Texans 1/1, Giants 2/2 Sacks: Texans 3, Giants 1 Turnovers: Texans 0, Giants 0 Penalties: Texans 10/80, Giants 4/50 Time of Possession: Texans 26:45, Giants 35:50 Obviously, some of these numbers are skewed as the Giants went 81 yards on three plays in overtme. Take those yards and points away and the defensive effort looks different. That’s obviousl rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic, but context matters when we are looking at numbers and it will matter when we take a look at the good, bad, and ugly. The Good There wasn’t a whole lot to write home about, but one feel good story came to fruition on Sunday. Tank Dell made his return after nearly two calendar years on the shelf. Officially, the stat line shows he had only one catch and one carry. He also had a promising punt return as well. He made it through the game healthy and contributed to the cause. If they can count on him for one game changing play a game that will be a win for the remainder of the season. Welcome back Tank and we are hoping to see a lot more from you this season. TheBad As we were walking out of the game I asked my wife which of these she would put first. We ended up agreeing. I mentioned the numbers above because I am giving the defense the relative pass by considering them as just bad and not ugly. Yes, the Giants seemed to run it at will at certain times during the game, but you left regulation giving up only 21 points and it had to be deflating to see your offense go three and out to start the overtime period. It was a proverbial double whammy for this defense. You were asked to play an extra quarter and that was after being on the field for the majority of regulation. The Texans offense had more three and outs in today’s game since they have had in the Indianapolis game. Yiu cannot leave any defense on the field for that long and expect things to come out roses. Sure, there were opportunities for them to get off the field and they couldn’t do it. The Giants had too many key third and fourth down conversions to be considered a good defense. Plus, it’s another game where you were not able to generate any turnovers. This is officially not last season’s defnese. It doesn’t matter who is calling the plays. These guys are just not doing the job. The Ugly You could credibly claim the defense was worse than the offense and I wouldn’t disagree that strongly. This is more of a disappointment. I thought we had figured out that we aren’t a running football team. I really thought Nick Caley had finally reached that determination. It turns out we were all wrong on that front. In the 1990s there was a Pep Boys commercial featuring two mechanics trying to fit in a battery that obviously didn’t fit. You flashed back to them trying to knock a square peg into a round hole. That is the Texans running attack over any of the last ten seasons. You could feel the deflation every time the Texans attempted to run it on first down. It was a letdown throughout the stadium. You could see it in the formations. You knew exactly where the ball was going. This was a play calling fail from beginning to end. Furthermore, this felt like the Bill O’Brien era when they just asked C.J. Stroud to play hero ball at the end of each half. Take away those drives and this team did almost nothing offensively. Focus on Stroud The numbers will show that Stroud was 17 for 28 for 153 yards and two touchdowns. That feels lika a decent game, but as usual the numbers don’t tell the whole story. On the positive end, there were two or three horrible drops that would have changed the complexion of his numbers and the game. On the other hand, he threw a couple of balls that should have been easy picks and were dropped by the Giants. We will call that a wash. At the end of the day, this is just a data point. No one game should make any decision as even the Tom Bradys of the world had off days. Stroud was under constant pressure even though he was taken down only once. He was rushed and that caused some of his accuracy issues on the day. It is one of those days where his team did him no favors. His offensive line struggled for much of the day, his receivers dropped some balls, the running game sucked, and the defense couldn’t get off the field. So, one could credibly claim that no one was going to overcome the lack of support on this day. Except that is not exactly true. They were tied at the end of the first half and at the end of regulation. By sheer definition, this is a game where one play could have completely changed the outcome of the game. Stroud simply didn’t make that one more play. He still feels like a franchise quarterback even if he isn’t one of the tippy top guys like Mahomes, Allen, Jackson, and Burrows. That’s not a crime. There are only a handful of those guys. It would just be a mistake to give him his bag and then expect him to morph into one of those guys. It’s not likely to happen. We will have to settle for Dak Prescott, Jordon Love, or Jared Goff. At least that is the level of quarterback he is. Give him a top notch play caller and he could look like more. Unfortunately, that guy isn’t in town right now.

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Highlighting Colts’ individual performances from Week 7
summary: The Indianapolis Colts (2-5) fell to the Minnesota Vikings (6-0), 16-10, and now have a three game losing streak, with whatever slim playoff hopes they had quickly evaporating in what’s shaping up to be another lost season. There’s no need to relive another tough loss in great detail by any means, but I did want […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Dallas Turner #15 and Harrison Smith #22 of the Minnesota Vikings sack Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts in the second quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (2-5) fell to the Minnesota Vikings (6-0), 16-10, and now have a three game losing streak, with whatever slim playoff hopes they had quickly evaporating in what’s shaping up to be another lost season. There’s no need to relive another tough loss in great detail by any means, but I did want to highlight a few of the individual performances from Sunday—both the positive and negative: Horsepower Colts Running Game: Would’ve put Jonathan Taylor here individually, but after a few pass blocking gaffes that led to big plays by the Vikings defense, I’ll go with the Indianapolis ground game collectively instead and give kudos to their offensive linemen up front as well. Taylor rushed for 95 total rushing yards and a touchdown on 18 carries, averaging 5.3 yards per carry. He had the Colts lone big offensive play of the day, with his opening drive 38-yard touchdown run . DT Ade Adebawore: The Colts rotational defensive tackle continues to have a breakout 2026 campaign, and was incredibly disruptive in this one with 5 tackles, 2 tackles for loss, 2.0 sacks, 2 QB hits, 5 QB pressures and a pass defensed. It may hurt to lose DeForest Buckner in an imminent trade before deadline day, but Adebawore may help Colts fans sleep a little easier filling D-Fo’s rather large shoes for the remainder of this increasingly disappointing season. Indianapolis needs to lock Adebawore up long-term. S AJ Haulcy: There’s been a lot of growing pains for the Colts’ 3rd round safety, who’s been lost in coverage at times with blown assignments. He stood out in run defense (with a season high +78.1 run defense grade) and led the Colts with 9 tackles (5 solo) in this one. Hopefully, Haulcy is starting to find his groove in the backend of the secondary and get past that initial rookie learning curve. He’s playing better ball. Horseplay Daniel Jones: No one’s expecting Jones to be Superman here, but he at least has to provide the Colts consistently average to good starting quarterback play out there if they’re going to win another game this year. Head coach Brian Flores’ dominant Vikings defense blitzed the heck out of Jones , with great success the majority of the time. An issue that’s plagued Jones since around midseason of last year. Specifically, Jones completed 13 of his 22 pass attempts for a minuscule 4.9 yards per completion average, amassing just 108 total passing yards and the game-sealing interception with 1:15 left in regulation. Colts Edge Rush: Fill in cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt had more sacks than any Colts edge rusher in this one. This has been a season long issue, but can we please get consistent pressure from any edge? Buehler? Spencer Shrader: Look, Shrader’s been a great special teams story so far this year, reclaiming his Colts kicking job after a devastating season-ending 2025 knee injury and going a perfect 19-19 from field goal range up until Week 7’s dud. That being said, in a game where the Colts lost by just six points, his misses of 56 yards and 48 yards in the second half loomed large and proved to be the difference in tying this one up.

title: Ross Tucker said it best, “Colts need a better plan.”
summary: Tucker said this during the national broadcast and he was referring to our RBs inability to pick up an extra rusher, but it could be applied to most all-things Colts this year. I’m looking for a reason for optimism for the rest of the year, but coming up with that better plan is likely the […]
full_text: Feb 3, 2010; Fort Lauderdale, FL, USA; Ross Tucker at the Sirius XM Radio press conference at the Fort Lauderdale/Broward County Convention Center. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee/Image of Sport-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Tucker said this during the national broadcast and he was referring to our RBs inability to pick up an extra rusher, but it could be applied to most all-things Colts this year. I’m looking for a reason for optimism for the rest of the year, but coming up with that better plan is likely the only way I discover that reason. The problem is that a singular plan is not going to get it done. We need a new plan along all three phases of the game. Shane has his moments, but most of them are in the first 10 minutes of a game. He’s also good at calling a play that will get you a yard when needed. He hasn’t found a way to counter what teams have decided to do against us, for going on a year. I barf a little in my mouth when I quote Tom Brady, but he said the Patriots offense had a simple philosophy. When the defense is in the middle, go to the outside and vice-versa. It works the same vertically, so if they are near the line of scrimmage, go behind them and if they are deep, go in front of them. It seems pretty simple, but we can’t get behind them when they are close to the line and we don’t appear to be able to get to the outside, when they are bunched in the middle. I understand that Steichen watched his offense being ran exactly as he envisioned for eight games last year and loyalty is largely a good quality, but Jones is not that same guy right now. He can’t get behind or around defenses. So, while I have thought that AR would need an injury to see the field, there is a certain amount of sense made by putting him out there. We do know that AR has the arm to get it behind the D and legs to get outside. Jones isn’t going to ask out. Heck, he may know his limitations and understand that he is not healthy and even welcome the benching. That shouldn’t matter to Shane anyway, as he has one job and that is to try an win a game, with the hope of being able to build some momentum. I’m not sure that you would be doing AR a solid by starting him, because it could still go poorly. I can’t see it going well enough to use the franchise tag on him next year at 50+ million for a QB, but Jones needs a reset and you have tabbed AR as QB2, so call his number for as long as he can answer the bell. A quick sidebar on DJ. I don’t think we can win a game this year with him, as his current physical and confidence levels are nowhere near 100%. In short, he is broken. The league has seen him broken before and turn things around, so it is not a foregone conclusion that we never see a high level of play from him again. I know it will be up to someone that we don’t even know right now, but even if you wanted to throw a dart at a rookie, you’d want a vet as a placeholder. He won’t bring much in trade, so you either pay and play him, or pay and cut him. A quick look at the special teams saw us give up a long run and commit two return penalties that put us in a hole. Dulin being back might help, but dang, some of these players are only on the team because they are supposed to be good at special teams. Penalties were more of a problem than they had been, but along with turnovers, we do not have the ability to overcome any adversity. The defensive struggles mount as the injuries compound and it wasn’t a good unit before the bug hit. A secondary that I expected much more out of, is now a shell of itself. It wouldn’t matter, because unless Buck or Addy happen to get pressure, it doesn’t look like it will happen. “The best pass rusher in the draft” may have more pass breakups than sacks. Any thought of turning things over the kids, saw both LBs inactive this week, while Curry and Gumbs still got scraps. Not that any of the four have separated themselves, but the new GM will have to have a better idea of “weakest link” position groups, and honestly, all three levels could be the squeaky wheel by the end of the trade deadline. Obviously, my take is one of acceptance, of more bad play to come. So, I’ll weigh in on the fire-sale topic. Many have said that we should sell off parts, for whatever the return might be. I don’t think we have a player that brings back a #1, and if it does it will be from a team that picks later in that first round. I think you try dangling two guys for that #1, to a team that needs more help. It might not seem like much, but adding a Shrader to a deal, for a team that could use an upgrade, might be enough. Maybe taking back a bad expiring contract? Now, another way to go, might be to get a player back at a position that would essentially negate the need for taking one in the draft. My thoughts turn to a RT that could compete with Travis. I know that there are guys out there on other teams that are not starting and could outplay him. That sounded like I was making a statement of fact. I do not actually know, but it sounds right as I type it out loud. It would depend on if Dodd was allowed to make a move based on the current scouting department’s intel. I think one more thing to consider when mulling deals, is how big of a hole does it leave? How much cap space or draft capital will you have to use to replace the player? For this reason, I think JT is easiest piece to move. McGowen may not be what JT has put together as a career, but you have a decent chance that he can do as much or more in year two, than JT can do in year eight, while being under cheap control for three more years. While you might like Adebawore to replace Buck or Grove, he is an unrestricted free agent at the end of the year, so that bumps up the replacement price. I’d listen to my players and gauge just how bad they wanted out and how interested they are in returning. You may even find players who would be fine with a trade this year, but also be receptive to returning next year. Maybe they would want to wait and see who was brought in to run the show, before committing. That new person may not be interested in inviting them back. Here’s a question to leave you with. If Carlie is going to choose the next GM, will she ask candidates their thoughts on her being on the sidelines? Would it or should it matter to her what they thought?
author: Clydesdales

title: NFL trade deadline 2026: Colts should be sellers, but which stars should they move?
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are approaching a crossroads, and with the NFL trade deadline quickly approaching, the organization has some difficult decisions to make. Chris Ballard’s dismissal signaled that ownership is no longer satisfied with the direction of the franchise, and Sunday’s 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings only reinforced how far this team remains from […]
full_text: Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are approaching a crossroads, and with the NFL trade deadline quickly approaching, the organization has some difficult decisions to make. Chris Ballard’s dismissal signaled that ownership is no longer satisfied with the direction of the franchise, and Sunday’s 16-10 loss to the Minnesota Vikings only reinforced how far this team remains from competing with the NFL’s best. At 2-5, the Colts have lost three consecutive games, and their playoff hopes are looking increasingly bleak. Over the past week, I examined the hypothetical trade value of three of Indianapolis’ biggest stars: Jonathan Taylor , DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson . Those articles focused on what each player could realistically command on the trade market, without necessarily arguing that the Colts should move any of them. Given the team’s deteriorating situation, however, it is worth taking that discussion one step further. I believe Indianapolis should approach the deadline as a seller, although there is an important distinction between selling valuable assets and conducting a complete fire sale. The Colts still have talented players worth building around, and trading every established veteran for draft capital would risk creating even more problems for whoever takes over as general manager. The objective should be to identify players whose value to a contender is greater than their value to Indianapolis over the next couple of seasons, while retaining those who could play important roles in the next competitive window. That brings us to five players worth discussing, beginning with three veterans whose contracts expire after this season. DeForest Buckner — Trade Of the five players on this list, Buckner is the one I would be most comfortable moving before the deadline. This has very little to do with his performance. Buckner is still one of the best defensive players on the Colts, remains a productive interior pass rusher and has shown few signs of a significant decline at 32 years old. However, his contract expires after this season, and with Indianapolis potentially entering another transitional period, there is a legitimate question about whether keeping him for another few months accomplishes anything meaningful. Buckner has also appeared increasingly frustrated with the state of the franchise in his recent interviews, and it is difficult to blame him. He has spent the past six-plus seasons in Indianapolis, endured multiple quarterback changes and coaching uncertainties, and has yet to experience the sustained success the organization envisioned when it acquired him from San Francisco. At this stage of his career, an opportunity to join a legitimate contender might be mutually beneficial. #Colts DT DeForest Buckner, asked his level of frustration: “I don’t know. How about you guess. Yeah, I’m frustrated. Same thing, we lost.” Where do the Colts go from here and how does he stay sane? “Couldn’t tell you.” What’s missing? “I don’t know. … I couldn’t tell you.” pic.twitter.com/BDlUyXJLi3 — James Boyd (@RomeovilleKid) October 25, 2026 There is also an interesting development along the Colts’ defensive line that makes moving Buckner considerably easier to justify. Adetomiwa Adebawore is beginning to emerge as a legitimate interior pass-rushing threat. The former fourth-round pick has shown considerable improvement this season, including an impressive two-sack performance against Minnesota on Sunday. He has the athleticism and explosiveness to create problems from the interior and could potentially develop into Buckner’s long-term replacement. That does not mean Adebawore is already as good as Buckner, but giving him a larger role over the remainder of the season would provide Indianapolis with a much clearer understanding of what it has in the young defensive lineman. If the Colts are serious about transitioning toward a younger roster, creating opportunities for players like Adebawore should be part of the process. In my previous article, I projected Buckner’s trade value at a 2027 fourth-round pick. Given his age and expiring contract, that remains a reasonable expectation, and I believe Indianapolis should accept such an offer without much hesitation. The Colts could potentially receive compensatory draft capital if Buckner leaves in free agency, but that is far from guaranteed. He could sign a shorter, team-friendly contract with a contender, Indianapolis could offset his departure through its own free-agent signings, or he could even decide to retire. Any compensatory selection would also arrive in 2028. A guaranteed fourth-round pick in 2027, combined with an opportunity to evaluate Adebawore in a larger role, makes too much sense to ignore. Grover Stewart — Keep Stewart presents a much more complicated situation, even though his age and contract are similar to Buckner’s. At 33 years old, Stewart is playing out the final season of his three-year, $39 million contract and is unlikely to attract significant interest beyond teams looking for an established run-stuffing defensive tackle. His value comes primarily from his ability to occupy blockers, control the line of scrimmage and create opportunities for the linebackers playing behind him. That role is important, but it is also relatively specialized. Teams are generally less willing to surrender meaningful draft capital for a veteran defensive tackle whose primary responsibility is stopping the run rather than generating pressure on opposing quarterbacks. I would estimate Stewart’s trade value at approximately a fifth-round pick, with a fourth-round selection representing a particularly strong return. The problem is that losing Stewart would create a much bigger hole in the Colts’ defense than that compensation suggests. Jerry Tillery is currently the primary alternative at nose tackle, and he represents a substantial downgrade from Stewart, particularly against the run. Indianapolis also has a linebacker group that has struggled with consistency, making Stewart’s ability to occupy interior blockers even more important. Removing him would place additional pressure on a defensive front that has already experienced plenty of difficulties this season. There is also something to be said for retaining a veteran who continues to contribute in several areas. Stewart’s blocked field goal against Minnesota on Sunday was another reminder of the impact he can provide beyond traditional defensive statistics. Unlike Buckner, whose departure could open the door for an emerging player at the same position, trading Stewart would leave Indianapolis without an obvious replacement. The Colts would almost certainly have to address nose tackle during the offseason, potentially using some of the draft capital acquired in the trade just to find someone capable of filling the role. If another team offered a surprisingly strong package, I would certainly listen. However, moving Stewart for a fifth-round pick accomplishes relatively little, especially when Indianapolis could explore bringing him back on a more affordable contract next season. For now, I would keep him. Quenton Nelson — Keep, unless the offer is too good Nelson might be the most difficult decision of the entire group. At 30 years old, he remains one of the NFL’s best guards and has arguably been the Colts’ most consistently dominant player since arriving in Indianapolis in 2018. His contract expires after this season, but unlike some of the other veterans on this list, there is little indication that Nelson is particularly eager to leave the organization. title: Jaguars 2026 Rookie Analysis So Far
summary: Back in April, James Gladstone went against the consensus on all but one pick, and the consensus on Gladstone was that he’d pay for it. Some had him pegged as the worst GM in the game before any of his picks had taken a snap. Six games in, that verdict is already falling apart. Not […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 04: Josh Cameron #19 of the Jacksonville Jaguars runs runs with the ball against the Cincinnati Bengals during the game at Paycor Stadium on October 04, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images Back in April, James Gladstone went against the consensus on all but one pick, and the consensus on Gladstone was that he’d pay for it. Some had him pegged as the worst GM in the game before any of his picks had taken a snap. Six games in, that verdict is already falling apart. Not every selection has made an impact yet, but the early returns have been hard to argue with. Early hits Nate Boerkircher Nobody took more heat on draft night than Boerkircher, a largely unknown tight end Draft Twitter couldn’t wait to pile on. His box score is modest: six catches for 52 yards, and a one-handed touchdown grab last week that almost validated the pick on its own. But the numbers don’t capture what a key piece he’s been to the offensive success. Boerkircher has become the dirty-work blocker in heavier personnel packages the team desperately missed last season, and the Jaguars now lead the NFL in EPA per play (0.205) in multi-TE sets, with him playing a big role. Emmanuel Pregnon Pregnon was the one pick that lined up with the consensus board, and he’s delivered. He won the left guard job in camp and has started every game, with the ups and downs you’d expect, but he’s been about as good as you could hope for from a third-round rookie guard. The one thing to clean up is the penalties: six, tied for the league lead. That said, Pregnon looks like an absolute steal for the Jaguars and the needle is only pointing up for his potential. Josh Cameron Josh Cameron might be the best argument against the doubters. A polarizing wide receiver prospect in the draft community, he lasted until the sixth round and has delivered: eight catches for 117 yards, with sure hands and a willingness to block. He’s been impressive enough that he’s getting snaps over Brian Thomas Jr. He’s an even bigger weapon on special teams, averaging 27.2 yards on nine kick returns (245 yards, long of 46), and he’d have had a return touchdown if not for a questionable holding call. He’s added five special teams tackles on top of it. Opportunities coming Albert Regis Regis was drafted as a run stuffer out of Texas A&M, which fits this Jacksonville defense perfectly, but he also flashed as a pass rusher in the preseason. He has played in just three games and logged 22 defensive snaps so far after missing the earlier part of the season with an injury, but that added versatility makes it easy to see his role growing as the season goes on. Tanner Koziol Koziol was drafted as essentially a big slot, and he wasn’t considered much of a blocker coming out of Houston. That said, blocking is almost all he’s done so far, and he’s done a solid job of it. He has appeared in four games, logging 30 offensive snaps, mostly in the heavy tight end packages that have the Jaguars leading the league in EPA per play, plus 15 special teams snaps. He hasn’t caught a pass yet, but he was a real receiving weapon for the Cougars, and it will be fun to see him get a chance to make a play on offense. Gaps in the process Jalen Huskey Huskey was a third-round pick at No. 100, drafted as an experienced defender who knows how to play the game and brings versatility in the secondary. That kind of profile is supposed to translate quickly, which makes the lack of playing time tough to explain. He has been active for just one game, where he played two special teams snaps, and he hasn’t seen a defensive snap. A pick that high should be pushing for playing time by now, particularly with the injuries at safety, but that hasn’t happened. Wesley Williams Williams was picked just 19 picks later, and he came at edge rusher, one of the Jaguars’ biggest areas of need. He was drafted as an experienced pass rusher who consistently gets pressure, a high-floor, low-ceiling depth piece. That’s what makes it a tougher look: a player whose selling point is that he’s ready now has been a healthy scratch all season. It’s one of the few real knocks on Gladstone’s board so far. TBD CJ Williams Nobody expected much from a sixth-round receiver, so 10 offensive snaps and 6 on special teams aren’t a concern. He made countless plays in training camp, though, which gives him a case for a bigger role if injuries hit the receiver room. Zach Durfee The seventh-round edge rusher out of Washington has been on injured reserve all season, though the injury hasn’t been specified. He’s expected back this year, so he could still provide some pass-rush depth in the second half. Parker Hughes Hughes was drafted with special teams in mind, an athletic linebacker and a sure tackler. He’s been on injured reserve all season, with the injury also unspecified, so that role is still waiting for him. Early verdict Six games is a small sample, but the early evidence points one way: the people who wrote this class off before it played a snap were wrong about more than they were right. Boerkircher and Cameron are already making real contributions, Pregnon has held down the left side of the line, and Regis and Koziol look like they’re on their way to bigger roles. The one legitimate knock is Huskey and Wesley Williams, two high picks who haven’t earned playing time yet. The second half will tell us whether that’s a blip or a flaw in the process. Early grade: B What would you grade this draft class through six weeks, Jags fans?

title: Chiefs-Seahawks: 3 Winners and 6 Losers from the Sunday night loss
summary: Your Kansas City Chiefs are now 5-1 after getting thoroughly dominated by the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday night. This game reminded us of a Super Bowl — but not in a good way. It felt like one of the Super Bowls where the Chiefs lost: the offensive line was in over their depth, the receivers […]
full_text: (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Your Kansas City Chiefs are now 5-1 after getting thoroughly dominated by the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday night. This game reminded us of a Super Bowl — but not in a good way. It felt like one of the Super Bowls where the Chiefs lost: the offensive line was in over their depth, the receivers weren’t getting open or catching the football, the defense was almost good, but the pass rush couldn’t quite get to the quarterback— and the coverage often wasn’t good enough to protect against lightning-quick passes. Seattle had a superior game plan and overcame injuries to multiple running backs. They have one star player that teams need to game plan for, and he had a monster game. The Chiefs have an MVP at running back and at quarterback, but they couldn’t put them in position to succeed. Head coach Andy Reid and staff just didn’t have answers. The offense never reached the red zone, the defense didn’t record a sack, and the Chiefs were outgained 410-213. It’s a game we won’t want to remember, but a few Chiefs stood out against the Seahawks, more bad than good. 3 Winners Cornerback Nohl Williams: It’s often not a great sign when a cornerback has double-digit tackles, but on Sunday Nohl Williams was everywhere. In addition to his 10 tackles, he also had a pass defended and a tackle for loss. But the play of the day for the Chiefs was the endzone interception that Nohl returned 65 yards. Perhaps it was fitting that the offense squandered the opportunity, but that doesn’t take away from another great performance from the Chiefs’ outside corners. Cornerback Mansoor Delane: In what will undoubtedly be a learning experience, the Chiefs top pick went up against the league’s best wide receiver, Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Spagnuolo’s defense was unable to stop JSN, but Mansoor Delane proved that he was more than up for the challenge. The receiver still won with some incredible adjustments, but that’s not a knock on Delane. We’ve often seen that a perfect pass/catch can beat perfect coverage, thus is the life of a NFL corner. He ended with two passes broken up. Running back/kick returner Emmett Johnson : In a limited role, the rookie running back had a couple of catches and a downfield block for a big Mahomes scramble. He also looked promising on kick returns, including a 41-yarder. There weren’t a ton of positives for the Chiefs on Sunday night, so we’ll celebrate the glimpses of hope from the likes of Emmett Johnson. 6 Losers Cornerback L’Jarius Sneed: He was mercilessly targeted by the Seahawks offense until the Chiefs mercifully put Kristian Fulton in. It was a monster day for JSN, and another rough one for L’Jarius. The slot corner position is as important as any on the defense— especially against teams with a dominant receiver that they can move inside to take advantage of matchups. Kicker Harrison Butker: Against contenders, every point counts— and Harrison Butker left six on the field. There was another chance to make it a one-score game going into halftime, ending in another miss. Sure, it was from 58… but still. After hitting his next kick of 50 yards, Butker would miss a 45-yarder. At what point does Andy Reid stop sending him out there? Running back Kenneth Walker’s revenge game: The narrative around Walker’s return to Seattle didn’t age well. The Seahawks were the ones who got “revenge” with a swarming defense that would not let Walker find daylight, especially on the outside. The NFL’s (former) leading rusher averaged only 2.6 yards per carry and was held to 57 total yards on the night. It felt like he didn’t stand a chance—Ken’s old team was ready for him. Wide receiver Xavier Worthy: On a night where Seattle’s defense looked that fast– Worthy should have been part of the solution. Instead, he was blanketed downfield by a safety (albeit a great one) and had a ball go through his hands in a fourth-quarter crosser. The Chiefs were short on receivers, and they could have used a big game from #1– instead he turned six targets into 3 catches, 11 yards. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes: You could see the quarterback’s frustration and for good reason– there just wasn’t anything that worked well. Without much help from receivers or a run game, Mahomes threw a costly interception and missed on a number of passes that he’d typically complete. One of the most impressive things Mahomes did all evening was recovering his own fumble. Though it was a tremendous effort by the quarterback coming out from the bottom of the pile. Chiefs offensive line: Due to injuries and weirdness, Andy Reid had to roll out his backup (and backup backup) offensive tackles. The result was a predictably tough night against the league’s best defensive unit. Byron Murphy II, Derick Hall, and Leonard Williams looked dominant against the Chiefs front five. There were the typical problems including a low snap and a couple of holding penalties. What was both new and painfully familiar was how helpless the offense was—largely because the Chiefs couldn’t win up front. Note: Applying the labels “losers” is not intended to be a judgment on the talent or character of any of these individuals. It’s just a simple way to grade their job performance in a single game. No disrespect is intended.
