title: Saints vs. Steelers: The good, the bad, and the ugly in Week 7
summary: The Good: Chase Young and Carl Granderson The Saints pair of pass rushers was able to constantly put pressure on Steelers QB Aaron Rodgers on Sunday. Combining for 3 sacks, Granderson and Young are proving to be one of the better pass-rushing duos in the NFL. They rank 1st in the league for a duo […]
full_text: The Good: Chase Young and Carl Granderson The Saints pair of pass rushers was able to constantly put pressure on Steelers QB Aaron Rodgers on Sunday. Combining for 3 sacks, Granderson and Young are proving to be one of the better pass-rushing duos in the NFL. They rank 1st in the league for a duo with a combined 12.5 sacks, just ahead of the Texans Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter (11.5), and this is even with Granderson missing a game. Granderson has gotten 1.5 sacks in each of the last three games and is well on his way to his first career double digit sack season. The Saints took a risk investing long term in Chase Young given his injury history, but that risk has paid off in a big way, as the former second overall pick is looking every bit the player that warranted that pick with 17 sacks in his last 19 games. The Bad: Rushing Offense The Saints rushing offense hit a new low in Paris which is saying a lot given how poor it has been all year. The Saints ran 17 times for 18 yards, with the leading rusher being Tyler Shough with 3 carries for 7 yards. Alvin Kamara (3.0 ypc) and Kendre Miller (2.8 ypc) rank 37th and 39th respectively in terms of yards per carry among the 41 running backs in the NFL with 40+ carries. Prize free agent Travis Etienne Jr. has been out since Week 3 and was averaging 4.3 yards per carry before he went down. He is eligible to come off IR after the bye week, but even he won’t be enough to save the Saints ground game. The fact is they cannot block well up front as the offensive line is both banged up and also just not very good at run blocking. This was the fourth game this year where their leading rusher was held to 30 yards or fewer, and they have only eclipsed 100 yards as a team twice. Just adding a better running back will help a bit but will not fix the main cause of the Saints problems on the ground, and fixing the ground game should be arguably their highest priority in the offseason. The Ugly: Finishing long drives The Saints had four drives of 11+ plays on Sunday and only got points out of one of them. They opened with an 11-play drive that got to the Steelers 43-yard line before stalling due to penalties and being forced to punt but would go on to score on each of their next two drives which tied the game at 10. In the second half however, they had a 14-play drive that ended in a red zone interception, and an 11-play drive that ended in a missed 52-yard field goal. If they convert on each of those two drives, they are at least tied and have the ball with 7:04 left in the fourth quarter, and at best have a four-point lead and make the Steelers have to get in the end zone on their final drive. Before this game, the Saints had been good at finishing in the red zone, as this was Shough’s first red zone interception of his career, so let’s hope this is not a sign of things to come but just a one game anomaly.
author: Hayden Reel

title: Saints vs. Steelers Winners and Losers from Week 7
summary: The New Orleans Saints were defeated 16-10 by the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday to fall to 2-5. The Saints were hosts to the first game ever in Paris, and unfortunately couldn’t take advantage of the occasion. Not a lot looked good for the Saints in the loss, and there are a lot more questions than […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints were defeated 16-10 by the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday to fall to 2-5. The Saints were hosts to the first game ever in Paris, and unfortunately couldn’t take advantage of the occasion. Not a lot looked good for the Saints in the loss, and there are a lot more questions than answers. Up: WR Barion Brown After recording his first NFL reception last week, Barion Brown followed it up with a 3-reception, 57-yard game. Brown was also a factor as a returner, returning a punt for 20 yards and a kick for 42 yards. With Jordyn Tyson eyeing a potential return after the bye week, the Saints wide receiver depth is hoping to make an impact to earn playtime. With Brown continuing to be a factor and making plays, his snap count may continue to rise despite the return of the team’s eighth overall pick. Down: Run Game I mean, come on. Are we serious? The Saints’ run game on Sunday may be the worst I’ve seen in a long time, possibly ever. New Orleans rushed 17 times for 18 yards, with running backs averaging 0.8 yards per carry. This isn’t just a problem at this point; it is becoming an emergency. Even 42-year-old Aaron Rodgers rushed for more yards than any single Saints player. The Saints’ run game has been a problem since last season, and they’ve poured money into fixing it this offseason. David Edwards has been serviceable at best, and Travis Etienne hasn’t been healthy. But worst of all, the Saints’ run design is plain bad. Running backs are rushing for 0.0 yards before contact, and they have no chance. Worst of all for New Orleans, their run defense wasn’t able to slow down Pittsburgh at all. The Steelers rushed for 130 more yards than the Saints and dominated the trenches. New Orleans had a major problem last season, and it has failed to improve through seven weeks of the 2026 season. Down: Kellen Moore Kellen Moore bought himself some more time after the win over the New York Giants, but a slow and boring loss against the Steelers, where the Saints were totally dominated, keeps him on the hot seat. The Saints are undisciplined, and Moore can’t adjust. The locker room is close to breaking, and the Saints aren’t far off from looking for their next head coach. Moore may survive the bye week and into the home game against the Cleveland Browns, but another loss, especially in similar fashion in Paris, and the Saints will likely have an interim head coach for the rest of the season.

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know about the first place team in the NFC East. Is it time to … respect the Giants as favorites in the NFC East? | ESPN.com Does that feel sustainable? Not really. Narrowly winning (or tying) games over middling teams with late takeaways isn’t something you can count on every week, At the same time, somebody has to win this division. At 4-2-1, the Giants are two-plus games ahead of the Cowboys and Eagles, with the latter now starting Tanner McKee for the rest of the season and likely to be dealing players at the trade deadline. The Commanders, at 1-4-1, have spent the past few weeks embroiled in their own internal turmoil. ESPN’s Football Power Index gives the Giants a 39.0% chance of winning the NFC East, up from 10.5% before the season. Sometimes, teams claim divisions in triumphant fashion by dominating their competition. Others win by being the last team left standing. The Giants might be more likely to fall in the latter camp, but having not won a division title since 2011, I suspect their fans won’t care how they do it. While Sunday’s effort is merely a one-game sample size after a disappointing start to his career with the Minnesota Vikings, the 2024 first-round draft pick provided a spark for Big Blue. McCarthy set career-highs with 252 passing yards and a 71.4 completion percentage. He did so against the Houston Texans defense, which may not be playing quite as well this season but can still get after opposing quarterbacks. Less pressure is now on the third-year quarterback, because the Giants didn’t draft him in the first round or let Sam Darnold to walk in free agency before he won a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks. McCarthy is not even expected to be the long-term starter. This opportunity allows the young signal-caller to get comfortable and just play. That’s exactly what he did Sunday. Grade: B+ NFL Week 7 winners and losers: Cam Skattebo, J.J. McCarthy lift Giants | CBSSports.com Winners: Cam Skattebo, J.J. McCarthy and the Giants. Call it the Cam Skattebo redemption game. One week after John Harbaugh relegated him to the bench, the New York Giants running back amassed 124 yards and a touchdown in a bounce-back effort against the Houston Texans. He broke loose for a 42-yarder, which set the Giants up to win in overtime. Plus, it was the first 100-yard game of his career. Skattebo also held onto the ball, which should put him back in his coach’s good graces after he opened the year tied for the most fumbles by a non-quarterback through six weeks. This is McCarthy’s fifth win in as many starts dating back to his time as the Minnesota Vikings’ No. 1 quarterback. If he can keep it up, this is precisely the kind of upside the Giants bet on when they made the low-risk investment in McCarthy. McCarthy gives Giants chance to win rest of season| SNY.tv McCarthy, still just 23 years old and making only his 11th career start, looked very much like a player worthy of his first-round draft selection. He didn’t turn it over. He bought time with his legs. He layered throws and threw with anticipation. He worked through his reads playing within the structure of Matt Nagy’s offense. The Giants traded for McCarthy after Dart went down believing, once caught up to speed, he’d allow their offense to function with similar principles and concepts to that of Dart, where much of that needed to be thrown out with the statuesque Winston. McCarthy hasn’t stopped smiling since arriving in New York. He’s connected with teammates on both sides of the ball. There’s a working, back-and-forth relationship with Nagy to marry his offensive philosophies with what McCarthy is comfortable with. He’s as confident now as ever before, the game slowing down. title: Fantasy Football 2026: Waiver Wire, Week 8 edition
summary: Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 8. Week 7 saw a return to more normal scoring after the fantasy wasteland of Week 6. But for the third straight week, we’ve got four teams on Bye in Week 8. Between injuries and Byes, fantasy players are in the middle of a long and […]
full_text: This Jet is soaring | Getty Images Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 8. Week 7 saw a return to more normal scoring after the fantasy wasteland of Week 6. But for the third straight week, we’ve got four teams on Bye in Week 8. Between injuries and Byes, fantasy players are in the middle of a long and challenging stretch. The Waiver Wire figures to be busy again this week, as managers scour it for streamers, stashes, and even longer-term starting options. One trend to highlight is the emergence of the 2026 rookie receiving class. It’s good, and it’s deep, and we still haven’t seen the second receiver drafted. We’re up to a half dozen or so rookie receivers who are fantasy-relevant, and that number could jump to close to a dozen in the second half of the season. I say it every year – be patient with rookie receivers. Many of the rookies are rostered, but some are still available. The Process : Each week, I try to identify the top Waiver Wire targets and evaluate the short- and long-term prospects of those players. I also do my best to reveal which players who are coming off a big week are fool’s gold. Finally, I look at streamers who might help you in a pinch (this is usually more important during Bye weeks). Some players discussed won’t be available in your league. I try to list players who are available in more than 50% of leagues. But what does that even mean? A 10-team league with six bench spots will have a much larger Free Agent pool than a 14-team league with eight. Most leagues fall somewhere in between. This isn’t “one size fits all.” By way of example, I won’t list Baker Mayfield , Kirk Cousins , Rachaad White , K.C. Concepcion , Rome Odunze , DeVaughn Vele , Germie Bernard , Brenton Strange , or Michael Mayer , among others who probably aren’t available in any of your leagues. Note that I’m writing this column BEFORE the Week 7 Monday night game (DAL @ PHI). WEEK 8 BYES: Giants, Saints, Texans, 49ers Week 8 Waiver Wire Quarterback: Malik Willis was a popular sleeper in the preseason because of his dual-threat upside, on a rebuilding team expected to chase points all season. That upside didn’t show up in September, but he’s heating up. In each of his last two games, he ran one in and topped 20 fantasy points, albeit on low passing volume. Miami’s offense hasn’t been putting up points (their 28 against the Jets on Sunday was a season high), but their young receivers are getting better with more reps, and Willis could be a plug-and-play streamer as needed over the second half of the season. The Patriots pose a tough challenge this week, but the four opponents after that are tasty — Lions, Colts, Bills, and Jets again, this time at home. I’ve never been a J.J. McCarthy believer, but through five quarters he’s been surprisingly good – dare I say great — as the Giants’ main man. I’ll happily eat crow on this one, Big Blue View readers. The G-Men ran all over the Texans on Sunday, but McCarthy played mistake-free football on the road against a great pass rush and a talented secondary, and made a lot of terrific throws. He can also run, and his O-line and weapons are above average. He’s 100% worth stashing through New York’s Week 8 Bye if you need QB help in a Superflex league. I’ve been pushing Aaron Rodgers as a QB2/streaming option all season, and the old man continues to produce decent numbers. Another veteran who can put up some numbers in the right matchups is Geno Smith, who threw for three TDs against Miami and keeps getting more weapons back from injury. Need a Week 8 streamer? Last week I recommended Willis and Smith and both broke 20 fantasy points. Jacoby Brissett gets the Cowboys in Week 8, and Tanner McKee gets the Lions. Neither one is all that attractive, but if you’re stuck at QB, they’re worth considering. Finally, Michael Penix, Jr. and Sam Darnold can be decent streaming QB2 options in the right matchups. Running Back: Jonah Coleman is back and he played 50% of the snaps in his return. All three Denver backs should be rostered, but they’re hard to trust as starters week to week when all three are healthy, as they are now. The Giants are also deploying three backs without a clear bell-cow. Tyrone Tracy, Jr. and Cam Skattebo both suffered what appear to be minor hamstring injuries in the big upset win at Houston. Tracy and Devin Singletary , who scored the game-winner in OT, should be rostered. Samaje Perine saw a dip in touches this week, but Chase Brown is still struggling to produce. Perine should be on rosters. Tyjae Spears and Nick Singleton are stashes in deeper-bench leagues, even though both missed this week’s game. It’s a terrible offense, but Tony Pollard is a trade candidate (and that was some audition on Sunday). Seth McGowan , who saw a season-high 12 touches on Sunday, is also a stash, with Jonathan Taylor potentially on the move at the trade deadline (did the Vikings get an in-person audition?) A few other names to think about, if you’re in need and/or want some depth that could pop later: Tyler Allgeieir , Tyler Goodson , Emmett Johnson, Kaelon Black , Dylan Sampson , Jonathon Brooks (IR stash), and Mike Washington, Jr. Wide Receiver It seems less likely that we’ll see Tyreek Hill anytime soon, but he’s still worth stashing in deep leagues. Another stash I keep listing is Jordyn Tyson , who could return from IR right after the Saints’ Week 8 Bye. There are quite a few players who are worth considering at WR, and as I mentioned in the prelude and last week, rookies make up a good chunk of the options. Omar Cooper, Jr. tops the list, after back-to-back games with 100 yards and a score in his return from injury. The Jets will often have negative game scripts, which helps, and he looks really good. Dolphins’ third-round rookie Caleb Douglas was only targeted three times on Sunday, but he turned that into two TD catches, including a long one. In the two games he started and finished this season, Douglas has a 7-164-2 line. Malik Willis has a big arm, and while the passing volume hasn’t been high, favorable game scripts could help Douglas. I like him as a WR4-type add for rosters. Here are not two, not three, not four, but FIVE more rookie receivers who I think you can consider if you need bench help. I’ll list them in my preferred order: Antonio Williams, Ja’Kobi Lane, Makai Lemon, Malachi Fields , and Jordan Watkins . If you have an IR spot free you can also think about a sixth rookie — De’Zhaun Stribling , who could be back to the depleted 49ers in a few weeks. Need depth? I’ll repeat a bunch of names I’ve listed in recent weeks, together with some new ones: Keenan Allen , Malik Washington, Travis Hunter, Jakobi Meyers, Kendrick Bourne, Savion Williams , Brandin Cooks , Cyrus Allen , Tank Dell, and Tre Harris . Tight End: Four to target, if you need help at TE, and again this is my preferred order: Chig Okonkwo (gets a bump with Terry McLaurin gone for the season), A.J. Barner , Terrance Ferguson (IR stash), and Mason Taylor . I think both New England tight ends – Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon – are also in play if you need help. Finally, Darnell Washington has scored in three of the last four games. He’s purely TD or bust, but clearly Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers like those man vs. boy matchups of the gargantuan Washington against smaller DBs at the goal line. That’s all I’ve got. Good luck with your waiver claims! ***This column appears each Monday right here at Big Blue View. Each Thursday, my weekly fantasy preview with my rides, fades and sleepers (start/sit) appears here, and on Fridays you can find my weekly Giants Props of the week, also right here. ***
author: David Hartman

title: NY Giants won’t be changing placekickers
summary: Dominic Zvada’s job as New York Giants placekicker is safe, for the time being. After Zvada, an undrafted rookie, missed kicks of 56 and 44 yards in Sunday’s victory over the Houston Texans, making him just 4 of 9 on field-goal attempts in the last three games, many thought the Giants would at least hold […]
full_text: Dominic Zvada (34) after one of his two misses on Sunday. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Dominic Zvada’s job as New York Giants placekicker is safe, for the time being. After Zvada, an undrafted rookie, missed kicks of 56 and 44 yards in Sunday’s victory over the Houston Texans, making him just 4 of 9 on field-goal attempts in the last three games, many thought the Giants would at least hold a kicker workout during their bye week to assess their options. “We’re not going to be doing that right now, no,” head coach John Harbaugh said on Monday. Zvada won the job from Ben Sauls with an excellent spring and summer. He went 9 of 9 over the first three games of the season, but went just 2 of 5 in Week 5 against the Washington Commanders and missed both of his field-goal tries vs. the Texans. Harbaugh passed on a 55-yard kick in the third quarter on Sunday after those two misses, punting instead. Harbaugh expressed confidence in Zvada immediately after Sunday’s game. “I think he has to go ahead and pound that thing through straight,” Harbaugh said. “I think he’s doing what a lot of rookies do — just trying to get it through the uprights. I’m not really worried about Zvada. He just has to do it, but I’m totally confident he will because I know how good he is and know what a good head he has.” Zvada knows he has to be better. “I just pushed it,” Zvada said. “It’s unacceptable. Luckily … I’m surrounded by teammates who really support me and keep me ready for the next one. For us to win, that’s great. I’m going to do my thing during the bye to make sure I’m right for when we go to [play] Philly.” Zane Gonzalez (Miami Dolphins), and Jake Moody (Baltimore Ravens) are the only two veteran kickers currently on practice squads. Free agent kickers include 35-year-old Brandon McManus, and 42-year-old Matt Prater. Sauls has not had any reported tryouts since being waived by the Giants with an injury settlement. His injury, and the severity of it, is unknown.

title: How did the NY Giants spark their running game?
summary: Life comes at you fast in the NFL. Last week, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo was (effectively) benched following a game-changing overtime fumble against the Washington Commanders. He saw just six snaps and zero carries against the New Orleans Saints in what was the second-lowest point of his NFL career. (Last year’s season-ending […]
full_text: New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo celebrates a touchdown. | Getty Images Life comes at you fast in the NFL. Last week, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo was (effectively) benched following a game-changing overtime fumble against the Washington Commanders. He saw just six snaps and zero carries against the New Orleans Saints in what was the second-lowest point of his NFL career. ( Last year’s season-ending ankle injury being the lowest point of his career ) The Giants’ run game as a whole reached a new low after degrading over the three weeks from Week 4 to Week 6, and the Giants’ running backs were averaging just 2.4 yards per carry against the Saints. Fast forward seven days and Skattebo was once again the Giants’ starting running back. He responded to the lesson being conveyed by John Harbaugh by having the best day of his NFL career. The Giants’ running game got off to a bit of a slow start, but they eventually wore the Texans’ defense down and started breaking big runs. Skattebo had carries of 11 yards, 19 yards (4th down), 16 yards (touchdown), and 42 yards to set up Devin Singletary’s game-sealing 30-yard run. All told, Skattebo had 17 carries for 124 yards (7.3 yards per carry) and a touchdown. It was his first 100-yard game as a pro, and by far his most efficient day. Prior to this week, Skattebo hasn’t had a 100-yard performance as a pro and just two games of more than 80 yards. Singletary, meanwhile, had 41 yards and a touchdown on five carries (as well as 14 yards on three catches). The Giants’ running backs totaled 180 yards on the ground in just 28 carries (6.4 yards per carry), with three touchdowns. It would have been even more, except Skattebo also had a 7-yard run called back for unnecessary roughness. #Giants RB Cam Skattebo just absolutely obliterated #Texans S M.J. Stewart—but was called for unnecessary roughness for lowering his helmet. This is not the NFL you grew up watching. pic.twitter.com/6jt8xE4qXP — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 25, 2026 So what changed this week? How did the Giants’ running game go from non-existent to game-defining in the span of a week? We’ll start at the macro level and then zoom in. Schemed for success The decision to start J.J. McCarthy was a significant one for the success of the Giants’ running game. The threat of the zone-read or designed quarterback run added a critical element of indecision to the Texans’ defense that the Giants were able to exploit. That was demonstrated perfectly on Tyrone Tracy’s touchdown run. The Giants line up in 12-personnel on the 2-yard line. The condensed formation and short field leads to what is, effectively, a nine-man box while the Giants have just seven blockers on the play side. However, the play is also designed with an extended mesh between McCarthy and Tracy. That mesh creates the potential of a zone-read, which the Giants double down on by releasing Isaiah Likely into a shallow route to the right. ( Played at 1/2 speed ) The Giants run zone blocking to the offensive left, leaving the left defensive end (Jadeveon Clowney) and slot corner (Kamari Lassiter) unblocked on the offensive right. The extended mesh point and Likely’s route combine to freeze Clowney, Lassiter, and FS M.J. Stewart. The Giants’ offensive line does a great job of folding the Texans’ front to the offensive left, while the momentary indecision gives Tracy all the time he needs to get to the second level and across the goal line. Tracy himself shows solid vision to anticipate both his blockers and the defense at the first and second levels, as well as the agility to hug his blockers and find room where the frozen defenders simply can’t reach him. The Giants also made use of formations that, if they’ve used them before, they’ve used them extremely sparingly. Most notably, we saw the Giants align in the Pistol formation — as opposed to the Shotgun — in the second half of the game and use it to great effect. The Pistol is something of a hybrid formation that combines elements of the traditional I formation with the Shotgun formation. Like the I-formation, the running back is several yards behind the quarterback. The quarterback, meanwhile, is 3 to 5 yards behind the center as in the Shotgun. The Pistol combines the advantages of both formations, giving the quarterback the view of the defense he enjoys in the Shotgun, while also giving the running back the runway he typically gets in a traditional I-formation. The Pistol is also highly versatile and can be run as a spread formation with three to four wide receivers, or as a power formation with multiple backs or tight ends. The Giants used the Pistol on Skattebo’s flagged run up above, but perhaps the most notable example of that came on Cam Skattebo’s fantastic 16-yard touchdown run. And in this case, the Giants come out in a very heavy 22-personnel set with two tight ends, as well as fullback Patrick Ricard and Skattebo. The Pistol has a few distinct advantages for a back like Skattebo. While Skattebo doesn’t have much top-end speed, he has impressive acceleration, and the additional separation between him and the line of scrimmage allows him to take the hand-off in stride before continuing to accelerate. The extra two steps allow him to hit the hole that much harder than from the shotgun. Likewise, the extra second gives the Giants’ blockers time to lock in and their blocks develop, creating more defined holes for the back. Notably, there’s time for Chris Manhertz, Ricard, and Jermaine Eluemunor to seal off an alley for Skattebo on the right side, while Isaiah likely gets into position at the second level. The longer runway also gives Skattebo a bit more time and perspective to scan the defense, and better perspective to anticipate defenders at the second and third levels. The Giants probably shouldn’t eliminate the Shotgun formation completely, however using the Pistol at a much higher rate could be a positive development for the running game. The backs: Vision, patience, and physicality Before we talk about the running backs themselves, we need to give a tip of the cap to the Giants’ blockers. Perhaps another week of practice with Brian Hudson as the starting center helped the interior, and perhaps getting Eluemunor back (albeit playing through an injury) made a difference as well. But the Giants’ blocking was some of the best we’ve seen since Week 1. It wasn’t perfect, far from it in some cases, however the Giants maintained a physical edge throughout the game which eventually won out at the end. On top of that, the secondary and perimeter blockers like Malachi Fields, Manhertz, Isaiah Likely, and Ricard all played critical roles in turning merely “okay” runs into successful carries. But turning to the runners themselves, each of the Giants’ backs played with a level of patience that we haven’t seen from them previously. For example, one of the big topics of conversation has been how Skattebo would seek out contact and run full speed into defenders, not allowing blocks to develop or using his vision to find holes. The first play of the game showed Skattebo running with much better tempo and patience behind the line of scrimmage, as well as seeking out his running lane. Notice how Skattebo runs with a “slow to the hole, fast through” tempo, allowing the blocks in front of him to develop before hitting the line of scrimmage. He also does a very good job of using his pathing to pull second level defenders out of their alleys and allow for the blockers at that level to take them out of the intended running lane. Finally, he does a great job of waiting until Eluemunor makes his block to cut back to the right and access the running lane. Ricard isn’t quite able to win the initial leverage battle and is ultimately shed by edge Will Anderson Jr. to stop the run after just 3 yards. However, this run was set up to go much further had the block been sustained for just an instant or two longer. We can’t make the same types of…

title: Grades and advanced stats for the Giants’ victory over the Texans
summary: By almost any measure, Sunday’s overtime victory over the Houston Texans was the Giants’ most impressive performance of the team during the John Harbaugh era so far. Let’s look at Pro Football Focus grades and advanced stats to get a better feel for what underlies that statement. First, I don’t usually show this, but PFF […]
full_text: By almost any measure, Sunday’s overtime victory over the Houston Texans was the Giants’ most impressive performance of the team during the John Harbaugh era so far. Let’s look at Pro Football Focus grades and advanced stats to get a better feel for what underlies that statement. First, I don’t usually show this, but PFF gives overall team grades in different categories for each game, so let me back up my statement above with an independent opinion: You can see that overall, only the victory over the Cardinals beats yesterday’s win over the Texans overall…and Houston is a better team than Arizona. In PFF’s eyes it was by far the Giants’ best game of the season on offense, passing, and rushing. It was their second worst pass blocking game, but that’s because Houston has the best set of edge defenders in the NFL and both Giants tackles are battling injuries but still playing. On defense PFF sees the Giants as having had a number of better games, but the degree of difficulty playing against Houston was certainly higher than most of their previous opponents. What the Giants did give was their best overall pass rushing effort of the season. PFF grades: Offense Seven elite or very good grades on offense, 13 of 18 at least average, and none in the very poor or worse range is something we’re not used to seeing from PFF for the Giants. It’s of course a very small sample, but after 1+ games as a real NFL quarterback this season (i.e., ignoring the RPO cameos), J.J. McCarthy is PFF’s 10th ranked quarterback. (The highest ranked quarterback, as you no doubt will have guessed, is…Drew Lock, in an almost equally small sample.) McCarthy is just behind Drake Maye and…C.J. Stroud, whom the Giants beat on Sunday. Sunday, McCarthy was amazing in the first half and came back to Earth a bit in the second half, but for a guy just learning the offense, it’s quite a debut as starter. The thing about McCarthy is that among QBs with 50 or more dropbacks he’s leading the NFL with a 12.3 aDOT. I say it ad nauseum , but in today’s NFL, explosive plays win games, and McCarthy gave the Giants that dimension yesterday. It’s not just a fluke. Last year, among QBs with at least 275 dropbacks, McCarthy was tied for fourth in the NFL with a 9.5 aDOT, trailing only Matthew Stafford, Lamar Jackson, and Drake Maye. McCarthy had three “big-time throws” and no turnover-worthy plays, and five BTTs and only one TWP in his two “real” games. That’s quite an improvement from last year, when he had 19 BTTs and 15 TWPs as a Viking. Right now it’s a small sample; if J.J. keeps it up, we may conclude that Matt Nagy’s offense is just a better fit for him than KOC’s was…or that Nagy was better at adapting his offense to J.J.‘s skill set. Here is McCarthy’s spray chart from Sunday: That’s five throws more than 20 yards beyond the line of scrimmage. That loosens defenses up, even though only two were completed. Respect the deep ball, and the intermediate routes open up: He completed 5 of 7 passes in the 10-20 yard range. The other thing to say is that I thought it would be a better idea for the Giants to start Jameis Winston in Houston and then switch to McCarthy in the second half if Jameis played poorly or after the bye, which I thought would play better in the locker room. A few of you disagreed (lol). I’m not in the locker room and so I can’t say how the team reacted to the announcement that Jameis was being demoted to DTP (Designated Tush-Pusher). But regardless of that, winning cures everything, I suspect. At the other end of the passing game, Malik Nabers just keeps on truckin’, with an almost elite grade Sunday and his fourth consecutive 100+ yard receiving game. Here’s an amusing stat: 100+ yard games with JJ McCarthy at QB: Malik Nabers (2) Justin Jefferson (1) — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) October 25, 2026 Nabers’ 605 receiving yards for the season is fifth in the NFL, and he is within 30 yards of all the receivers ahead of him except the unreal Jaxon Smith-Njigba. The bigger story may be Malachi Fields, who had a career-high four receptions in 5five targets Sunday, and more importantly 40 YAC. With Nabers, Fields, and Isaiah Likely, who had a quiet two catches in three targets and may have played injured part of the time, the Giants may have a pretty effective receiver corps. H/T to Thomas Fidone, who had his first NFL catch for 29 yards and almost a TD. The running game was a big reason for this victory. The Giants don’t have an elite back, but Cam Skattebo was let out of the doghouse and ran for 124 yards, his season high and by far his best game of the season, and a TD, including the run that set up Devin Singletary’s game-winning OT run on the next play. Singletary likewise had by far his best game, capped by his winning TD run in which he eluded at least two tacklers. As you can see from the first chart in this post, it’s no coincidence that the Giants’ effective running coincided with the offensive line’s best run blocking effort since the opening game win over Dallas. First off, Patrick Ricard, whose run blocking had been at best average up to this point, had by far his best run blocking game of the season. The rest of the line was adequate at best in run blocking in PFF’s opinion, but that’s better than in recent weeks when PFF saw them as clearly below average. The pass blocking was a different story. PFF saw this as one of the Giants’ worst collective pass blocking efforts of the season. That’s no surprise given the Texans’ trio of Will Anderson Jr., Danielle Hunter, and Jadaveon Clowney on the edge. Unsurprisingly then, the Giants’ tackles, Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor, both playing at less that 100% health, had mediocre pass blocking grades. Thomas surrendered only his second sack of the season. That said, holding those two to one sack is a pretty good day at the office. It’s all relative (which PFF grades are not). The interior offensive line, though, did better, especially rookie Sisi Mauigoa, who got by far his best pass blocking grade of the season from PFF. Again, though, the strength of Houston’s defensive line is on the edge. PFF grades: Defense Overall PFF didn’t see this as the Giants’ best defensive effort of the season, but considering the quality of the opponent, perhaps it was. What they did have was three tremendous efforts by individual players. D.J. Reader is having an outstanding first season as a Giant, and by PFF’s reckoning, the best season of his career so far. He had three pressures of C.J. Stroud, a tackle and an assist, and no missed tackles. Someone to keep an eye on is draftee Bobby Jameson-Travis, the sixth-round pick out of Auburn, who saw action for the second week in a row and got a very good overall grade, primarily due to his run defense. Abdul Carter continues to excel, with four more pressures; that makes it 20 in the last four weeks. Kayvon Thibodeaux is starting to come alive: His three pressures were his third consecutive game with that many, and he almost intercepted a pass. Thibodeaux gets grief from fans because he never became the sack machine that Aidan Hutchinson, drafted three spots ahead of him, did, but Thibodeaux does a lot of the dirty work that allows Carter to find a path to the QB. Look at him being triple-teamed on this play as Carter forces a rushed throw: Abdul Carter teleportation 3rd down stop pic.twitter.com/XOvvsrlUYM — Dan Schneier (@DanSchneierNFL) October 26, 2026 Arvell Reese had another excellent game, getting two pressures and a sack. Elsewhere on the line, Shelby Harris had a rough game while Darius Alexander had an average overall score but got his first sack of the season. Elsewhere on the defense, it’s a bunch of mixed overall grades, but that hides some good performances in specific aspects of play. Deonte Banks is a good example (more on him below): OK overall defense grade, but very good coverage grade – he really shut down Nico Collins. Same thing for Paulson Adebo – he was invisible yesterday, right?…
author: Anthony Del Genio

title: Giants-Texans: 5 key plays in New York’s victory over Houston
summary: The New York Giants shocked the Houston Texans on Sunday in J.J. McCarthy’s first start with John Harbaugh. New York controlled the game on offense and defense, defeating the Texans, 27-21 in overtime.  Dennard Wilson’s defense held the high-powered passing attack 153 yards through the air, as Houston gained just 237 total yards. Tae Banks […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo (44) and Malik Nabers celebrate a touchdown. | Getty Images The New York Giants shocked the Houston Texans on Sunday in J.J. McCarthy’s first start with John Harbaugh. New York controlled the game on offense and defense, defeating the Texans, 27-21 in overtime. Dennard Wilson’s defense held the high-powered passing attack 153 yards through the air, as Houston gained just 237 total yards. Tae Banks shut down Nico Collins, Houston quarterback C.J. Stroud looked uncomfortable, and D.J. Reader continued to be a strong asset for the Giants both as a run defender and a pass rusher. The Giants’ offense incorporated a lot of PISTOL concepts and zone-read runs that helped to open up the rushing attack. McCarthy’s two 40+ yard passing plays in the first quarter helped to soften the box, as did the threat of his legs on read plays. New York gained 420 yards on offense. McCarthy threw for 252 yards, and, most notably, the rushing attack got going for 188 yards on the ground with an average of 5.5 yards per carry. Houston ranked third in the league in run defense prior to the game, and the Giants were 19th in rushing with three straight poor performances. The return of Jermaine Eleumunor certainly helped, but the Giants – in general – deserve a lot of credit for this complete effort, other than the poor kicking by Dominic Zvada. Here are five plays, or five sequences of plays, that were impactful in the game. Play(s) 1: Final two plays of the game The Giants have been bad at running the football over the last few games. The running backs were publicly called out by John Harbaugh, and Cam Skattebo played six snaps against the Saints. Skattebo responded, rushing for 124 yards on 17 carries with a touchdown. The vindication of the overall running game was best represented by the final two plays of overtime: Cam Skattebo with the longest run of his career right when the Giants need it most. That 42-yarder in OT puts them in perfect position to steal this one. pic.twitter.com/0AGcpWVepY — Nelson Idahosa (@ldsworld_nelson) October 25, 2026 Devin Singletary's game winning overtime touchdown. pic.twitter.com/rE5NDUNYQK — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 25, 2026 Skattebo rushed for 42 yards on the second play of overtime, which set up Devin Singletary’s 30-yard touchdown run to match the Giants’ win total from last season. New York now has confidence heading into a much-needed bye week. Play(s) 2: End of the first half The Giants were ahead by points with 3:32 left in the first half and Stroud marched down the field 90 yards to find Marvin Harrison Jr. for a touchdown, along with a two-point conversion on a shovel pass to Cade Stover: Marvin Harrison Jr. gets his first touchdown as a Texan! NYGvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/1zvTlVie4i — NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026 CADE STOVER IN FOR 2‼️ 📺: @nflonfox pic.twitter.com/11aoNjeqkL — Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) October 25, 2026 Arguably, the most significant play of the drive was a 43-yard catch and run to Tank Dell ( welcome back ). The ball didn’t even appear intended for Dell, but it was significant for Houston. Tank Dell gets his first catch back ❤️ NYGvsHOU on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/vgbBdB8eD5 — NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026 Dru Phillips and Ar’Darius Washington were flagged to help extend the drive; the flags totaled for 32 yards. I love that Harbaugh called his timeouts to give the Giants an opportunity to score points in the waning seconds of the half. It’s great to see the Giants have confidence in McCarthy in that situation. McCarthy connected with Malik Nabers for 27 yards, which put the Giants in field goal range. It was excellent coaching by the Giants, but, unfortunately, rookie kicker Dominic Zvada missed the 44-yard field goal and the half ended in a tie. New York dominated this game but it still ended in overtime – Zvada’s struggles were a big reason why. Play(s) 3: Excellent start J.J. McCarthy connected for 42 yards to Malik Nabers after the #Giants successfully converted on a 4th & 2. pic.twitter.com/2c4mVlWrxm — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 25, 2026 The J.J. McCarthy factor helps Tyrone Tracy Jr. score on the road against the Texans. The threat of McCarthy's legs held Clowney in place off the read. Touchdown New York. pic.twitter.com/rQWQ4418F9 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 25, 2026 The Giants had an excellent opening drive that resulted in a nine-play, 66-yard touchdown drive that included a few quality runs, a fourth-down conversion, and a 42-yard completion to Malik Nabers. McCarthy’s athletic ability kept the edge rusher honest and allowed Tyrone Tracy Jr. to hit the hole for a touchdown. New York needed a quick start on the road with a young new quarterback and they received exactly that. The defense responded with two early three-and-outs, a few pressures for Abdul Carter in the first three drives, and they dictated with a zone based defense, while also forcing several penalties on the Texans’ offense. Play(s) 4: Welcome back, Cam Skattebo! The Giants went on a 14-play, 80-yard drive that ended in a 16-yard touchdown run by Skattebo: Cam 👏🏽 Skattebo👏🏽 pic.twitter.com/AIaQgzSrpl — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 25, 2026 Skattebo received six snaps in last week’s loss and, by all accounts, he responded excellently in practice. McCarthy ran the Matt Nagy offense well. His third-and-9 conversion to Malachi Fields set up Skattebo’s touchdown. McCarthy delivered an impressively placed out route. The Giants also converted a third-and-1 earlier in the drive to Skattebo on a fake tush-push with Jameis Winston in the game: The Giants fake the tush-push and hand-off to Cam Skattebo for a 19 yard gain. I love this creativity after running successful tush-pushs to Winston earlier in the game. pic.twitter.com/OFndx0Kz06 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 25, 2026 Play(s) 5: The struggles of Dominic Zvada The Giants rookie kicker missed a 56-yard field goal that would have given the Giants a 10-point lead at the end of the first quarter. After that, John Harbaugh used his timeouts excellently to end the first half. McCarthy completed a 27-yard pass to Nabers with 29 seconds left in the half, putting the Giants in a position to go up three at halftime. Zvada lined up for a 44-yard field goal in a dome and sent it wide right. The Giants forgoed a field-goal attempt later in the game, resulting in 23 yards of difference after punting the football to the 14-yard line. Luckily, the defense was stellar in the game, and they forced one of their many three and outs. These struggles are noteworthy, of course, and they almost led the Giants to a devastating loss; Giant fans know too well how those situations can go. Still, Harbaugh gave Zvada a vote of confidence after the game, but it remains a situation worth monitoring.

title: Giants-Texans ‘things I think’: The Giants are in it to win it
summary: “We’re going to be in this thing until the end now.” That was New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh after Sunday’s stunning 27-21 overtime victory over the Houston Texans. The words got my attention. Because they, stunningly, feel like the truth. The Giants are 4-2-1 and leading the NFC East. They will still be […]
full_text: John Harbaugh shares a post-game hug with Tyrone Tracy on Sunday. | Getty Images “We’re going to be in this thing until the end now.” That was New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh after Sunday’s stunning 27-21 overtime victory over the Houston Texans. The words got my attention. Because they, stunningly, feel like the truth. The Giants are 4-2-1 and leading the NFC East. They will still be leading the division after the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys, both 2-4, play on Monday Night Football. The outside world can, and will, snicker at the NFC East. They can, and will, snicker at the Giants. It is hard to blame them. The Eagles have had a stunning fall. They are without Jalen Hurts for the remainder of the season, and the situation surrounding his blood clots could embarrass both the Eagles and the NFL. They have myriad injuries beyond Hurts, and an offensive line that does not resemble the dominant one they possessed not long ago. The Cowboys are, well, the Cowboys. In the current landscape, they probably have the most talent in the division. They keep, though, doing things Cowboys teams have done for three decades. Consequently, they keep falling short of expectations. The Washington Commanders are 1-4-1, winless in three tries in the division, and don’t seem to be able to tell time. They seem to be marking time at this point until owner Josh Harris fires head coach Dan Quinn. The Giants? It is pretty clear that nearly halfway through the season they are the only team in the division that feels good about itself. Why not? The Giants are already on their third starting quarterback, with their No. 1 — Jaxson Dart — out for the season. That’s usually a death knell for NFL teams. J.J. McCarthy, though, is clearly not an ordinary No. 3 quarterback, and he and the Giants appear to be a match. Maybe someone should tell Kevin O’Connell, whose team is somehow 6-0 without good quarterback play, that he might have traded the Giants his best QB. The Giants have lost defensive star Brian Burns for the season. They have also lost starters Tremaine Edmunds and Chauncey Golston, and never had 2025 starting defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris. A year ago, the Giants kept spitting the bit and turning victories into losses. This year, they keep finding heroes and winning games at the wire. The Giants now get to go into their bye week in first place. They will also come out of it in first place, as the best the Eagles and Cowboys could do is get to 4-4 before the Giants return to action. “It’s a massive energy shot in the arm. It’s a reward,” Harbaugh said after the game. “Now, you’ve got to make something of it. It doesn’t mean anything if you don’t build on it, right? But it means something, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to win a championship yet. It means we have an opportunity, though.” When the Giants return from their bye, they will face the Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field and then host the Commanders. “We have an opportunity to get ready for the next two games starting with Philadelphia, and then a quick turnaround, so we’ll be thinking about two games as a coaching staff over the bye week,” Harbaugh said. ”The two most important games of the season will be coming up after we come back from the bye, which will set the direction for the rest of the season, really. But we’re going to be in this thing until the end now. This was a pivotal game. This was a really high-pressure game for our team. We didn’t talk about that, but they all knew how important this game was, and they responded accordingly.” ‘Failure is not final’ Nothing really seems to shake the belief of this Giants team. That belief was built in the summer heat, when Harbaugh worked his team harder and longer than most NFL players are accustomed to being worked in an NFL that is much softer than it once was. Harbaugh’s team faced plenty of challenges leading up to Sunday’s game, not the least of which was going winless in its previous two games. Harbaugh changed quarterbacks despite Jameis Winston having lost just once in four starts. He said it was an “obvious choice” to go with McCarthy, but it could have backfired. To pare down the four-way timeshare Najee Harris complained about a week ago, Harbaugh cut Harris. Cam Skattebo was coming off a week in which he was taught a lesson the hard way, getting just six snaps and no touches. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson took the highly unusual public step of calling some of his players “traitors” for lack of effort against the New Orleans Saints. One of those traitors, Jihad Ward, was cut. The Giants lost Edmunds for the season during the week, and played Sunday without two starting defensive backs. Yet, the Giants went in to Houston as 10.5-point underdogs, made it clear from the start that they were playing to win, and came out with a critical, confidence-building victory. “I think that’s exactly the story. To me, that’s the point,” Harbaugh said. “It tells you who they are. You might have thought before the game, we’re going to find out about our guys. We’re going to find out about who they are, and we did, and you saw it. They did; they took the bull by the horns, and they got the job done.” Up until now, analysts and fans of other NFC East teams have looked at the Giants and said, basically, yeah, they’re in first place, but the Giants can’t really win the division. Can they? Maybe they will win it. Maybe they won’t. But it looks like everyone is going to have to get used to the idea that it actually is a possibility. That reality is starting to settle in for at least some analysts. Queue ESPN’s Dan Graziano on Sunday night: No one has wanted to take this seriously, but the first-place Giants are 4-2-1 and will carry at least a 1.5-game NFC East lead into Week 8 regardless of what happens between the Cowboys and Eagles on Monday night. Harbaugh has made a major difference in his first season as Giants head coach. They’re avoiding mistakes, overcoming injuries, and finding ways to win. Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy called an outstanding game for McCarthy. Skattebo bounced back after last week’s soft benching and said after the game that he agreed with and appreciated the way it was handled by the coaching staff. Edge rusher Abdul Carter basically dominated the second half on defense. Cornerback Deonte Banks shadowed Nico Collins effectively. The Giants are playing very good team football right now. Given what we saw in Minnesota, McCarthy is a tough guy to count on. But he’s also talented enough to have been picked 10th in the 2024 NFL draft, and it’s entirely possible that what he needed was a new situation. There is a world where he flops completely. There is a world where he’s inconsistent the rest of the way, and the Giants don’t have enough around him to cash in. But there’s also absolutely a world in which he and they play just well enough to win a bad NFC East. Right now, the math tells us that it’s absolutely possible, and the Giants are the betting favorite to win their division. Harbaugh was asked Sunday when he realized his team had the mental fortitude to handle getting knocked down. “I would say just a lot of moments stacked on top of each other because they just didn’t bat an eye and they continued to work hard and fight,” he said. “Every type of situation, they met the same way. Maybe it started with [QB] Jaxson Dart, then it went to the next, the next, the next, to [ILB] Tremaine Edmunds this week. “I don’t know, I just think it’s an ongoing type of a thing. That’s how you build — it’s shared experiences. It’s fighting through all these things together that draws people close together, and that’s how a team is built.” The new quarterback is also a survivor. A former first-round pick banished to third-string in Minnesota and traded away without hesitation. “Guys have scars. He [McCarthy] has scars. He’s been wounded. He’s been broken. He’s been battered. But you heal stronger, and you become better because of…

title: It feels like the end of the Aaron Glenn era after a horrific Jets loss to the Dolphins
summary: “You are what your record says you are.” That quote is popular in NFL circles. It has been widely attributed to Hall of Fame coach Bill Parcells. Parcells’ career contained many stops including a four year stint from 1997 through 2000 where he led the Jets. He was the head coach for the first three […]
full_text: Oct 25, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; New York Jets head coach Aaron Glenn looks on during warmups before a game against the Miami Dolphins at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect “You are what your record says you are.” That quote is popular in NFL circles. It has been widely attributed to Hall of Fame coach Bill Parcells. Parcells’ career contained many stops including a four year stint from 1997 through 2000 where he led the Jets. He was the head coach for the first three of those seasons and the general manager all four. Current Jets head coach Aaron Glenn played for Parcells. I personally am not a fan of the quote. It is most often used in the context of dismissing a team that has played better than its record. Here’s the thing. In the short run, a team’s record doesn’t always indicate its quality. A good team can have a rough stretch or an untimely injury. A bad team can run off a couple of wins against a soft portion of its schedule. Over the long run, however, there isn’t a better way to evaluate than by looking at win-loss record. After all, to cite another famous proclamation by a different Jets coach, “You play to win the game.” In a short stretch, you can find excuses around a poor record for a coach. Aaron Glenn started his first year 0-7. Glenn finished his first year losing five straight games by 23+ points, making the 2025 Jets the first team to ever record that dubious distinction. Glenn’s team lost a game it should have won against the Packers in Week 2, fumbling away a shot at a 2-0 start. Two weeks later the team was embarrassed by a Bears team playing its backup quarterback. Sunday at the Meadowlands the Glenn era hit perhaps a new low as the 0-5 Dolphins, widely believed to be the least talented team in the NFL, came into MetLife Stadium and beat the Jets. It wasn’t really a back and forth game. The Dolphins outplayed the Jets the whole way. Miami led for around three quarters of game time, and in the second half they were up by two scores approximately one-third of the time. Any of these individual failures are easy enough to explain away with excuses on their own. Glenn inherited a messy situation and a roster with no talent in year one. The roster deteriorated even further by the end of the year. Every team has bad games or lets contests slip away through the season. But at some point, the excuses run out. At some point, you actually are what your record says you are. I might be able to buy the excuses for Glenn’s failures individually, but over the last year and a half they have piled up. Combined, they tell the story of a 5-19 coach whose teams show no sign of playing above their talent level. In fact, they often play worse than their talent level. More than that, you can see tangible areas where the Jets coaching staff puts this team at a disadvantage. Glenn has been this team’s head coach now for 24 games. In those games the Jets have now been outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of the first half. That’s only 48 minutes of game action. It is a sign that Glenn does not prepare his teams to play situational football. It’s also a sign that coaching is putting this team at a disadvantage. The Jets did not call a timeout in the first half and allowed the Dolphins to run the clock down to 6 seconds left in the second quarter before scoring a touchdown. More aggressive use of timeouts would have left the Jets with a last drive in the first half. Can I guarantee the team would have scored? No, but losing a chance with the ball in a game you ultimately lost by 3 is a clear example of how the coaching staff is holding the team back. People who defend the coaching frequently put the bulk of team issues on the players. I’ll be honest. There definitely are moments when players get off too easy. But what is the point of a coach if not to give his team the most opportunities to win. Losing a possession in a tight game because of timeout mismanagement is the essence of a coach making a difference. On the offensive side of the ball, we see the same issues not get fixed over and over. The Jets can’t execute short yardage plays. They keep trying the same thing, and it isn’t working. They also seem to be fine phasing their number one receiver out of the passing game for long stretches. It’s difficult to comprehend how the Jets are so incapable of targeting Garrett Wilson when the offense is struggling. Contrary to what the CBS broadcast booth seemed to be suggesting during the game, double teaming the opponent’s best wide receiver is not a new and revolutionary defensive strategy in the NFL for which offenses have no solution. The Jets won’t even do basic things to free up Garrett Wilson like give him a steady diet of snaps from the slot where keying on a receiver defensively becomes much more difficult. I’m not trying to let the players off the hook because that performance was unacceptable in so many ways. A struggling Malik Willis looked like an unstoppable force. A Jets defense built to stop the run was incapable of doing so, and there were massive errors like Minkah Fitzpatrick’s missed tackle resulting in a key fourth quarter touchdown, Jason Sanders doinking a makeable field goal, and Geno Smith leaving plays on the field. Still, the number one big picture story for me is that Aaron Glenn and his coaching staff are out of excuses. This team faced a game that had the potential to break this season. And the Jets didn’t look prepared in any way. Aaron Glenn was a fantastic player. He might be a great assistant coach. But if you truly are what your record says you are, Aaron Glenn is in over his head running this Jets team.

title: New York Jets News: The Aaron Glenn Era Should be Over
summary: I take no pleasure in writing this column. I’m the eternal optimist. I’ve always looked at life with a glass-half-full perspective. We don’t control the cards we’re dealt, but we can control how we respond to them. However, the cards that we have been dealt prove, without a shadow of a doubt, that Aaron Glenn […]
full_text: New York Jets Head Coach, Aaron Glenn suffered another loss, this time to the previously winless, Miami Dolphins, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026, at East Rutherford. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co I take no pleasure in writing this column. I’m the eternal optimist. I’ve always looked at life with a glass-half-full perspective. We don’t control the cards we’re dealt, but we can control how we respond to them. However, the cards that we have been dealt prove, without a shadow of a doubt, that Aaron Glenn is not fit to be the head coach of the New York Jets. You can’t lose to a previously winless team at home. You can’t start your career in the AFC East as the head coach with a 0-8 record. You can’t be outscored 107-6 in the final two minutes of every first half. The evidence is simply mounting that Glenn is in over his head. It’s a sad thing to write considering Glenn is one of the true great players in franchise history. It’s a sad thing to write because, from Glenn’s opening press conference, he articulated how important this job was in turning around the Jets and how much he took it personally as someone who bled the green and white. However, wanting something just isn’t enough. If the Jets decided to fire Glenn after this putrid performance against the Miami Dolphins in Week 7, no one could blame Woody Johnson. Does he actually do it? Woody is the judge, jury, and executioner, so only he truly knows. title: Eagles vs. Cowboys: The good, the bad, and the ugly
summary: Let the tanking begin. With nine minutes left, large segments of open seats began to appear at Lincoln Financial Field Monday night. Not that it really mattered, because the Linc seemed lifeless all night anyway in a rare moment for an Eagles-Dallas Cowboys game. The Cowboys’ anemic running game, which averaged 76 yards rushing a […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Ceedee Lamb #88 of the Dallas Cowboys catches a pass for a touchdown against Cooper DeJean #33 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the first quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Let the tanking begin. With nine minutes left, large segments of open seats began to appear at Lincoln Financial Field Monday night. Not that it really mattered, because the Linc seemed lifeless all night anyway in a rare moment for an Eagles-Dallas Cowboys game. The Cowboys’ anemic running game, which averaged 76 yards rushing a game, certainly found a remedy in the Eagles’ tired, haggard defense in a 38-21 Dallas victory. The Eagles are in the throes of a five-game losing streak, the first of Nick Sirianni’s tenure and first for the Eagles since 2016, Doug Pederson’s first year as head coach. Dallas moved to 3-4 and the Eagles fell to 2-5, and even though the Cowboys are just a game better, the teams seem light years away from each other. The Eagles looked defeated in their eyes. They looked defeated in their play. They looked defeated in their body language. They looked defeated in trusting the game plan presented by the coaching staff. In his quest to tank, Howie Roseman may be calling every former high school star in the Delaware Valley over the next few months. The over-under apathy line was set last week at mid-November. Do not look now, but the shroud of apathy descended on the 2026 Eagles under a full moon on Monday night. Dallas won for the first time at the Linc since 2021. The Eagles have turned 2026 into an extended exhibition season. That’s the feel the empty Linc had in the fourth quarter Monday night. Prepare for the Linc to be primed for takeovers by contending teams like the New York Giants, Pittsburgh Steelers, and Seattle Seahawks—you know, teams that matter. The Cowboys ran 65 plays and the vaunted Eagles’ defense had zero tackles for a loss. Dallas pounded the Eagles for 416 total yards, averaging 6.4 yards a game, with 204 yards on the ground, averaging 5.4 yards a carry. Whatever the Cowboys wanted to do, they did. Dak Prescott completed 15 of 27 for 212 yards and three touchdowns. Javonte Williams sliced his way through the Eagles for 155 yards rushing, averaging 6.2 yards a carry. Tanner McKee was okay, completing 23 of 35 passes for 211 yards with one touchdown and one interception. But it was spotty defense that really took the blame for the Eagles’ most recent debacle. Dallas scored on seven of nine possessions. The Cowboys threw Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis around the field like ragdolls. Riq Woolen beat out everyone for best Halloween costume—he wore an Izel Jenkins mask. In two year’s time, the Eagles went from the pinnacle of the NFL, to one of the worst teams in the league with no solutions in sight. This is a new level of low. Let the tanking begin. There was little good, a mountain of bad and myriad piles of smoldering, steaming ugly in the Eagles’ 38-21 loss to the Dallas Cowboys. The Good The Eagles’ first drive of the second half. It’s the first time this season that the Eagles scored on the first drive of the second half, when Makai Lemon scored on a four-yard reception and a 21-20 Eagles’ lead. The Eagles’ 17-play, 9-minute, 16-second drive was their longest this season. They were 5-for-6 on third-down conversions and 1-for-1 on fourth-down conversions. Makai Lemon’s 15-yard reception on a fourth-and-one at the Dallas’ 24 on the Eagles’ first drive of the second half. At the time, it was Lemon’s team-high fourth catch for a team-high 50 yards. Lemon was one the best of a bad situation, with a game-high seven catches for a team-high 67 yards. Hollywood Brown’s 19-yard reception on the Eagles’ first drive of the second half. Saquon Barkley’s 12-yard run on the first play of the second marked the first time this season that the Eagles did not go three-and-out on their first drive of the second half. The Eagles’ first drive. It was the first time the Eagles scored on their first drive this season. The remarkable thing about the four-play, 75-yard drive that took just 2:05 off the clock is the Eagles never faced a second down. The huge play in the drive was Saquon Barkley’s 29-yard run that brought the ball to the Dallas’ 34. Barkley’s two carries amount to 37 of the 75 yards on the drive. Tanner McKee’s 21-yard completion to Makai Lemon brought the ball to the Dallas 13. The Eagles second drive. The Eagles went up 14-10 on a great drive that traveled 76 yards on 13 plays. The big play was a McKee-to-Darius Cooper 17-yard completion on a third-and-10 at the Cowboys’ 12, made on Cooper’s run-and-after catch zig-zagging his way through the Dallas secondary. Hollywood Brown did a nice job blocking cornerback DeRon Bland on Dameon Pierce’s 5-yard touchdown run with 13:25 left in the first half. The first punt of the game with 2:37 left in the first half. Punter Braden Mann nailing a 48-yard punt that Darius Cooper downed at the Dallas two-yard line. The Bad Running out of timeouts in the first half with 1:31 left in the half facing a third-and-10 at the Eagles’ 41. The Eagles had to settle for a 5-yard completion on third-and-five with 1:24 left at the Eagles’ 46. The Eagles gave the ball back to Dallas at the Cowboys’ 13 with 1:14 left and two timeouts. It led to a Brandon Aubrey 27-yard field goal and a 20-14 halftime lead. The Cowboys first drive. Dallascameout and drove 28 yards on seven plays, gaining 25 yards on the ground. The result of the series was a Brandon Aubrey 55-yard field goal. Cooper DeJean has not had a good season this year. Another case in point came on the 17-yard pass interference call with 14:11 left in the game. DeJean earlier in the game gave up a first-quarter touchdown covering CeeDee Lamb in the slot, who DeJean attempted to cover—and failed. The Ugly Riq “Reek” Woolen had himself a game. He completely lost CeeDee Lamb with 12 seconds left in the first half for a 30-yard completion to the Eagles’ nine-yard line. Woolen was fortunate Lamb lost his balance and had to crawl out of bounds. The Cowboys had to settle for an Aubrey 27-yard field goal (3 points thanks to Woolen) . The Cowboys scored on four of five drives in the first half. Woolen ran away from adversity, he declined to speak after the game. Woolen did not have a good game. On a third-and-nine on the Cowboys’ first drive of the second half, he was flagged for holding, giving the Cowboys a new set of downs. He was later burned on the same drive by Ryan Flournoy for a 16-yard completion on a first-and-10 to the Eagles’ 27. On the same drive, Woolen was smoked by Lamb in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard touchdown and a 28-21 Cowboys’ lead with 1:30 left in the third quarter (11 points thanks to Woolen after Prescott’s two-point conversion). Earlier in the game, Woolen gave the Cowboys’ Flournoy took much space on a third-and-eight on Dallas’ second drive. Prescott found Flourney open on the sideline, and Woolen proceeded to miss him, turning a good gain into a large gain, from the Cowboys’ 31 to the Eagles’ 34. It was the crushing play on the Dallas touchdown drive. Five plays later, Prescott hit CeeDee Lamb for a nine-yard touchdown pass in the corner of the end zone for a 10-7 Cowboys’ lead. Lamb caught the TD pass over DeJean, who has not had a good season. In two drives, the Cowboys scored twice. Did anyone see Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis? While Woolen was very ubiquitous in his blunders, Carter and Davis were invisible in theirs. They got no push up front. They created no roadblocks to stop the Dallas running game. They were nowhere to be found. They had quarterback pressures and were knocked off the ball the whole night. Carter, the highest paid defensive tackle in the NFL, ran from the adversity and declined to talk to the media after the game and wished everyone a good night. McKee’s fourth-quarter…

title: Eagles-Cowboys final score: Philadelphia’s defense gives Dallas offense a get-right game
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles are 2-5 after losing to the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on Monday night. Final score: 38 to 21. Well, this game wasn’t on total offensive ineptitude for once! The Eagles started the game strong with two touchdown drives and then had another to begin the third quarter. They sputtered at […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Ceedee Lamb #88 of the Dallas Cowboys catches a touchdown pass against Riq Woolen #2 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the third quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles are 2-5 after losing to the Dallas Cowboys at Lincoln Financial Field on Monday night. Final score: 38 to 21. Well, this game wasn’t on total offensive ineptitude for once! The Eagles started the game strong with two touchdown drives and then had another to begin the third quarter. They sputtered at times but that was to be expected with Tanner McKee and a bunch of backups playing on offense. But Philadelphia’s defense was a problem throughout the night with the Cowboys scoring 38 points and producing 416 yards with 212 coming on the ground. The Eagles’ highly paid defensive line produced zero TFLs, zero sacks, and zero quarterback hits, allowing Dak Prescott to be entirely too comfortable. This was a get-right game for a Cowboys offense that only managed to muster 29 points combined over the past two weeks. The Eagles have now lost five games in a row for the first time since the 2016 season. Next up for the Eagles: a road game against the Washington Commanders, who are coming off their bye week. Read on for a recap and stay tuned for BGN’s postgame coverage. Also, check me out talking about this game on the PHLY Eagles postgame show. FIRST QUARTER The Eagles won the coin toss and elected to defer, per usual. The Cowboys began at their own 35-yard line. Dallas picked up two first downs on their first three plays to move into Eagles territory (a flag was thrown for what seemed like offensive holding but it was picked up). Facing 3rd-and-8, Dak Prescott overthrew CeeDee Lamb while throwing quick against Vic Fangio’s blitz. Brandon Aubrey made a 55-yard field goal attempt … but there was an illegal formation penalty. Instead of taking the points off the board and attempting a 4th-and-3 conversion, Brian Schottenheimer settled for three (coward). Could’ve been worse! EAGLES 0, COWBOYS 3. The Eagles took over at their own 35-yard line. The Eagles opened in under center and Tanner McKee completed a pass to Saquon Barkley for a first down! Then Barkley ripped off a 29-yard run where he looked gimpy after running out of bounds. Then McKee hit Makai Lemon for 21 yards! The Cowboys got called for a neutral zone infraction and then Barkley took a run for eight yards to the end zone! Wow! What is this?! Success on offense?! I guess the Dallas defense truly is terrible. But credit to the Eagles for actually taking advantage! EAGLES 7, COWBOYS 3. WELCOME BACK, 26 pic.twitter.com/hrkFoZNlNT — Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) October 27, 2026 The Cowboys took over at their own 18-yard line and immediately ran for a first down. Riq Woolen broke up a Dak Prescott pass to George Pickens to force third down. Facing 3rd-and-8, Woolen didn’t pick up Ryan Flournoy in coverage quick enough and then missed a tackle on him to allow 35 yards. Volatile player. The Cowboys drove into the red zone with success on the ground. Facing 3rd-and-2, Prescott hit CeeDee Lamb in the end zone with Cooper DeJean trailing. 9-play, 82-yard drive by Dallas. Not a good drive by the defensive line, which got pushed around too often. EAGLES 7, COWBOYS 10. Just so hard to defend CeeDee 💿 DALvsPHI on ESPN⁰Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/A5Uv7gzDL0 — NFL (@NFL) October 27, 2026 The Eagles took over at their own 24-yard line. Facing 3rd-and-6 after picking up one first down and McKee overthrew Hollywood Brown downfield, McKee hit Dallas Goedert just short of the sticks. Facing 4th-and-short, the Eagles lined up for a tush push and McKee fumbled the snap for a Cowboys recovery but Dallas was clearly offside to extend the drive. Good job by Nick Sirianni to be aggressive and keep the offense on the field in that situation, regardless of result, which was good! Two straight Dameon Pierce runs picked up another first down. McKee hit Hollywood Brown (!) for another first down just beyond the marker along the right sideline. Brown had a nice little celebration for his first catch of the season. Facing 3rd-and-10 after Darius Cooper dropped a sure completion (ouch!), Cooper redeemed himself with a screen reception (a successful screen?!) that he took for 17 yards and a first down! Bold decision by him to cut it back inside against the defense instead of taking the safer first down route but it worked out to end the first quarter with a first down in the red zone. Darius Cooper flipping his way to a first down 🦅 DALvsPHI on ESPN⁰Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/w8v8cFmXqQ — NFL (@NFL) October 27, 2026 For the Eagles, 10 points and 124 yards are both their most in a 1st quarter this season (averaged 0.5 PPG and 56.7 Yds PG in the 1st quarter in the 1st 6 weeks). Per ESPN Research. — Tim McManus (@Tim_McManus) October 27, 2026 SECOND QUARTER Facing 3rd-and-8 after two Barkley runs didn’t pick up much, McKee missed his throw but the Cowboys were flagged for roughing the passer due to Cowboys defender LT Overton getting called for roughing the passer. One play later, Dameon Pierce took a carry to the end zone! 13 plays, 76 yards, TD! Kudos to the Birds for taking advantage of a bad Dallas defense. EAGLES 14, COWBOYS 10. Dameon Pierce coming through 😤 pic.twitter.com/rP7opSam3M — Philadelphia Eagles (@Eagles) October 27, 2026 Two Eagles drives, two Eagles touchdowns 4 plays, 75 yard, TD 13 plays, 76 yards, TD This Cowboys defense isn't beating the allegations. Good on the Eagles for taking advantage! — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) October 27, 2026 This #Eagles offense is looking varied, creative, and competent…all for the first time in over a month. — Deniz Selman (@denizselman33) October 27, 2026 The Cowboys had a kick return touchdown (while missing All-Pro returner KaVontae Turpin in this game) nullified by a hold on Ty Robinson. The Cowboys took over at their own 19-yard line instead. Dallas picked up multiple first downs with the Cowboys’ offensive line having their way against Philly’s defensive front. Facing 3rd-and-10 after Jalen Carter knifed into the backfield for a tackle for no gain, Prescott hit Pickens just short of the sticks. Facing 4th-and-1, the Cowboys hurried to the line and the Eagles called a timeout while looking a bit out of sorts. Facing 4th-and-1 for real, the Cowboys were able to easily run for a first down. Dallas picked up another first down with his legs. Facing 3rd-and-3, Prescott stepped up against pressure and delivered a dime to Pickens with Andrew Mukuba trailing along the right sideline of the end zone. Pickens’ second foot was nearly out of bounds. Nearly. But not enough. Gotta tip your hat to the Cowboys on that one. 14-play, 81-yard TD drive. EAGLES 14, COWBOYS 17. DAK TO PICKENS WHAT A PLAY DALvsPHI on ESPN⁰Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/nlz2rotipP — NFL (@NFL) October 27, 2026 The Eagles took over at their own 35-yard line. Facing 3rd-and-5 after a screen play didn’t work (Landon Dickerson did not look very good moving in space), Lemon drew a flag for getting hooked to give the Eagles a first down. Then Pierce ran for another first down into Dallas territory. Facing 3rd-and-10, Joey Porter Jr. broke up a McKee back shoulder throw to Brown. Good play by the Cowboys corner. Facing 4th-and-10, Nick Sirianni kept the offense on the field but clearly only to try to draw an offside penalty, which Dallas was never going to fall for. Braden Mann’s punt bounced down to the 2-yard line, where the ball was fielded by Darius Cooper. Nice special teams play. The Cowboys took over at their own 2-yard line with 2:28 on the clock and three timeouts to work with. Facing 3rd-and-8 after Quinyon Mitchell broke up a pass that nearly could’ve been a pick six, the Cowboys went with a coward’s draw. That was a gift for this Eagles defense. Big forced…
