title: 49ers fans have a real officiating gripe vs. the Falcons—and it’s not the catch rule
summary: The San Francisco 49ers lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons. Regardless of injuries, they played poorly. And that’s an understatement. In the game threads, there were a lot of comments about the officiating (me included). The officiating didn’t cost the 49ers the game—defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa jumping on fourth down cost them the game (or […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - JANUARY 17: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers reacts after an interception during the third quarter against the Seattle Seahawks in the NFC Divisional Playoff game at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons. Regardless of injuries, they played poorly. And that’s an understatement. In the game threads, there were a lot of comments about the officiating (me included). The officiating didn’t cost the 49ers the game—defensive tackle Osa Odighizuwa jumping on fourth down cost them the game (or at least three points); Kaelon Black’s fumble cost them the game. But the two aren’t mutually exclusive. Many of those comments compared Falcons safety Jessie Bates III’s interception of quarterback Brock Purdy to wide receiver Jordan Watkins phantom touchdown. The question comes from the consistency of the catches. Watkins’ touchdown was wiped off because he didn’t maintain control to the ground out of bounds and bobbled the ball, while in Purdy’s interception, Bates did just that and it was ruled a catch. Ehhhhh, that’s a bit of a stretch. Here’s the interception from Purdy. The ball moves, but it looks like he has firm control of it. Purdy was trying to throw it out of bounds, and Bates made a good play. “I thought maybe Christian Kirk on the scramble was going to be there,” Purdy said after the game. “But then towards the end, as I was getting ready to throw. I was, ‘like no it’s not’ and so I just went to throw it away by the sideline and then Bates all of a sudden came across and made a good play.” Was it a bad throw? Sure, but I think nine times out of ten, Bates probably isn’t going to make that play. Especially when you consider a minor detail we’ll go over. Still thinking about this @jlbiii3 interception 🤯 pic.twitter.com/8SLLJAXUJl — Atlanta Falcons (@AtlantaFalcons) October 26, 2026 The ball moves, but I didn’t see much bobbling. You do see some bobbling on the Watkins catch below: After review, this play was ruled an incomplete catch. Agree with the call? 📺️: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/0DWmWDMwUw — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) October 25, 2026 That’s the rule, unfortunately. Watkins made a hell of a catch, and Purdy threw a nice ball; Watkins just couldn’t stay inbounds. Thus, yet another Brock Purdy magic touchdown is only an ‘almost’ and sits with that run against the Arizona Cardinals this year and that Brandon Aiyuk pass that was dropped in the NFC Wild Card. The officiating crew was very inconsistent, but these two plays don’t really add to that. Both are pretty clear in my view. If you disagree, feel free to jump in. But we’ll get to that in a moment. Back to the pick: there’s another question that needs answering. When Brock threw the ball, why did Jacob Cowing quit? Credit to Matt Nahigian for calling this out on .X. I blamed Purdy for throwing this interception, but after further review, why did Cowing stop running? pic.twitter.com/OhI7FFdQfC — Matt Nahigian (@mattnahigian) October 26, 2026 That’s a good question. Why wasn’t Cowing jumping ahead of Bates to get it? I didn’t even notice this in real time, but he just slows down when Purdy throws the ball away. Cowing’s a fast guy; had he taken off, maybe he could have plucked that thing before it went out of bounds—or at least helped his quarterback by swatting the ball away. If you do want to argue that the calls are inconsistent, I see where you’re coming from. My follow-up would be: if Cowing didn’t stop here, would any of this have happened? Even if it was a bad call, the interception may not have happened if Cowing plays to the whistle. Perhaps we’ll get an answer to this when Shanahan next talks to the media. You know what was a bad penalty? Offsides because the officials wouldn’t let the 49ers substitute. the 49ers pull off the rare double-penalty by having 12 men on the field at the snap, then having that 12th man run onto the field from behind the line of scrimmage for an offsides pic.twitter.com/B31axuCy8N — Christian D'Andrea (@TrainIsland) October 25, 2026 Now that is something irritating. The Falcons offense substituted their players; by rule, the 49ers defense needs a chance to match. That is why teams run a hurry-up offense and don’t substitute players—so the defense stays on their heels. The moment a substitution goes in, the officiating crew must allow time for the 49ers to do the same. The Falcons got to sub, and the 49ers didn’t, basically. This was the beginning of what was a poor and often one-sided game by Clay Martin’s crew. And let’s not get to all the stoppages for two-minute discussions between the officials. This is also called the ref show, and it’s the absolute worst show to watch. Some calls were easy to make; others were just long conversations to restate the obvious. Despite how bad Martin’s crew was, the 49ers had opportunities to get off the field and regain the lead. Unfortunately, they couldn’t play disciplined enough or take care of the football to do so.
author: Patrick Holloway

title: NFL insider would be ‘shocked’ if the 49ers don’t make a trade after linking them to 3 pass rushers
summary: NFL insider Jordan Schultz appeared on a podcast and discussed two potential teams that could be aggressive at the trade deadline. Schultz went as far as saying he’d be “shocked” if the San Francisco 49ers didn’t make a trade: “I think we’re headed for a very active deadline,” Schultz said. “I think we can see […]
full_text: Photo by Olivia Vanni/Getty Images) | Getty Images NFL insider Jordan Schultz appeared on a podcast and discussed two potential teams that could be aggressive at the trade deadline. Schultz went as far as saying he’d be “shocked” if the San Francisco 49ers didn’t make a trade: “I think we’re headed for a very active deadline,” Schultz said. “I think we can see anywhere from 12 to 20 trades—and two teams I’m watching very closely: The 49ers and the Bears. I’ve heard both teams connected to several defensive players, including rushers Josh Sweat, Khalil Mack, and DeForest Buckner, along with some names who aren’t necessarily on the trade block. I think both Chicago and San Francisco wanna be aggressive. I’d be shocked if they don’t make a move before the deadline.” The 49ers and Bears, with Caleb Williams under center, are two of the NFC’s top offenses. It makes sense why they’d want to add a pass rusher. In the Niners’ case, they’re 24th in the NFL in pressure rate. One thing the Falcons did well against Kyle Shanahan’s offense was to get pressure with four rushers. It’s something every team strives to do. There’s little reason to think Arizona would help a divisional foe by trading them an asset like Sweat. Mack is in the final year of his contract. The 35-year-old has three sacks, six tackles for loss, and 14 pressures on the season. In Week 4 against the Seahawks, Mack had two tackles for loss, three pressures, and a sack. John Lynch probably made the call to the Chargers after he watched Mack in Week 4. Would it surprise you if the 49ers made multiple trades? Is there a world where they make a move for Mack and Buckner?
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers turnovers drastically swung their win probability against the Falcons
summary: We haven’t had a chance to talk about how win probability shifts in a game because the San Francisco 49ers have largely played clean games during their six-game winning streak to start the season. That changed against the Atlanta Falcons, who forced four turnovers. According to Next Gen Stats, the Falcons gained +41.8% win probability […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images We haven’t had a chance to talk about how win probability shifts in a game because the San Francisco 49ers have largely played clean games during their six-game winning streak to start the season. That changed against the Atlanta Falcons, who forced four turnovers. According to Next Gen Stats, the Falcons gained +41.8% win probability on the Niners’ four turnovers. If sports have taught us anything, it’s that no lead is safe. San Francisco’s win probability peaked at 80% when they took a 14-3 lead after Kaelon Black’s 30-yard touchdown run to begin the game. Even after Atlanta trimmed the lead to 14-9 in the second quarter, San Francisco still had a 73% win probability. That climbed back to the high 70s after Luke Farrell recovered Jordan James’ fumble. Kaelon Black’s fumble dropped its win probability to 68%. One turnover shouldn’t kill you in a game where you’re bound to get double-digit possessions. The Falcons still needed to march over 70 yards to score. For a brief moment, the Niners’ chances of winning rose to 70% on 4th and 4. The Falcons tacked on a field goal before the half. At 14-12 heading into halftime, San Francisco had a 57% chance to win. Michael Penix completed an 11-yard pass to Austin Hooper on 2nd and 7. At 13:08 in the third quarter, the win probability split 50/50 for the first time. That was the first time it had been that way in the game. When Penix found Drake London on 3rd & 7 for 10 yards against Jack Jones, the Niners dipped to 46%, dropping below 50% for the first time all game. After the Falcons took the lead, the probability changed to 38%. It was 19-14 with nine minutes left in the third quarter. That’s an eternity. After their third double-digit gain of the drive, the Niners were at Atlanta’s 35-yard line, with a 52% win probability. They lost 12 percentage points, dropping from 44% to 32% after Purdy’s interception on a target along the sideline. The defense looked like they were going to get off the field and give the ball right back to the offense, but a penalty on 2nd and 20 and a 19-yard gain on 3rd and 3 swung the win probability 14% in two and a half minutes. When the Falcons scored to make it 26-14 to begin the fourth quarter, their win probability was as high as 87%. The Niners’ hopes looked bleak, but they still had a chance. After a touchdown and a forced punt, the Niners got the ball back with 4:08 left, and a 22% chance to win. But an interception with 2:42 left dropped the Niners’ win probability from 20% to 1%. The swings were drastic in this game. Both sides had outlier performances. We haven’t seen multiple interceptions from Brock Purdy or fumbles from the running backs. It was the first time Atlanta has forced multiple turnovers all season. It’s a loss that’ll be dissected all week since the 49ers have their bye, but they win if they hold onto the ball. It’s as simple as that. 49ers in the red zone The 49ers score a TD on 86% of their red zone trips. The Cowboys are second at 77%. Shanahan and Purdy have been excellent in the red zone this season. Once they get inside the 20, you’re as close to a guaranteed touchdown as you can get. Purdy’s first interception was at Atlanta’s 25 on 2nd and 14. On the drive where James and Black fumbled, the 49ers had picked up 7, 10, and 11 yards leading up to those two plays. The offense had the ball at Atlanta’s 28. Even if you remove the two fourth-quarter turnovers, you’re leaving 10-14 points off the board. That’s the difference in the game. Add in the probability of scoring on the two fourth-quarter drives, and it’s hard to poke holes in anything other than the turnover luck.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers grades: The defensive line laid an egg; Secondary struggles continue
summary: The San Francisco 49ers dropped their first game of the season as penalties and turnovers cost them on both sides of the ball, and a missed extra point made the final drive moot. Let’s look at the Week 7 grades against the Atlanta Falcons to help tell the story of the game. Quarterback: B Brock […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers dropped their first game of the season as penalties and turnovers cost them on both sides of the ball, and a missed extra point made the final drive moot. Let’s look at the Week 7 grades against the Atlanta Falcons to help tell the story of the game. Quarterback: B Brock Purdy finished 21st in EPA per play in Week 7, but sixth in passing success rate. Interceptions heavily influence that EPA number, so that’s not a surprise. Purdy still completed 67% of his passes, with a respectable 7.2 yards per attempt. On the first interception, Purdy had the running back open, but he was hesitant to pull the trigger. Not sure how this is on Cowing. Purdy has Black up the sideline for a first down. He looks at him. Black's open. Purdy doesn't pull. When he goes to release the ball, Bates is closer to the sideline than Cowing. It looks like he's throwing to Kirk and doesn't see Bates https://t.co/UDrBc3hLP4 pic.twitter.com/dlNCdmqrnF — Kyle Posey (@KP_Show) October 26, 2026 Purdy only had two deep attempts. His EPA is probably much higher if he completes the second deep attempt. One area where Purdy stood out was his ability to create. He ran out of a pair of sacks and turned those into first downs, keeping the offense on the field. Atlanta did a good job of keeping Purdy at bay from a scrambling perspective. He had zero scramble yards. Scanning advanced stats, Purdy had the 8th-highest on-target percentage, but did throw short of the sticks more than usual. A fourth-down sack and the first interception hurt Purdy’s grade. He’s a playmaker, and the Niners are always in the game with Purdy under center. A team that can win when its quarterback throws a pair of interceptions is a contender. Running backs: B+ Christian McCaffrey only had seven carries after leaving with a thigh injury. He returned, probably by necessity. You can’t ignore the fumbles, which is why the grade is B+, but the runners ran well. McCaffrey had a 71.4% success rate. James spun off a tackle for six yards. Black had a great jump cut on his touchdown run and averaged 5.25 yards per carry. Black also picked up 61 of his 63 yards after contact while forcing two missed tackles. Jordan James and Kaelon Black had fumbles on back-to-back plays. Kyle Juszczyk had a terrific block to spring Black on his touchdown run. Juszczyk played a big part in the 49ers’ rushing success, no surprise there. McCaffrey caught six of his seven receptions for 61 yards. James took his one pass for 11 yards. Juszczyk caught a touchdown on all three of his targets. It was the best Black looked all season. But the fumble and a couple of stuffed runs Pass catchers: B Luke Farrell caught a first down and blocked well. George Kittle was all over the place, catching eight of his 19 targets for 88 yards, including 40 yards after the catch. Kittle fumbled to end the game. I was more disappointed that he didn’t catch either of his contested catches. Purdy targeted four wide receivers who either weren’t on the roster, weren’t active, or weren’t running routes in Week 1. Technically, the first interception was a target to Jacob Cowing, who caught a first down as the team was driving. Cowing caught his other two targets, totaling 38 yards. He was 1-for-2 in contested situations and did well adjusting to lower throws. Cowing wasn’t an issue in this game. He was open. The same cannot be said for Brandin Cooks, who caught one of three targets. He turned a 3rd and 4 into a 3rd and 9. Cooks did not catch the third-down target. He had another play where he got too deep and nearly ran into Kittle for the second straight week. The margin for error when targeting Cooks is non-existent. I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s released by the time the Niners take the field. Cautiously optimistic describes Jordan Watkins in this game. Watkins made a great fingertip grab in the third quarter where he dove for a throw. At the beginning of the fourth quarter, Watkins was wide open down the seam on a play that was underthrown. If he’s hit in stride, it’s arguably a touchdown. On the first pass where Watkins didn’t complete the catch through the ground, it was a great release to get open, but you have to secure the catch. The same is true for his end zone target. Both were A+ throws that you have to reward your quarterback. If you simulate the final two targets to Watkins 100 times, he probably catches it 97 times. Unfortunately, the Niners were on the wrong end of variance in Atlanta. Christian Kirk wasn’t targeted, but he ran away from A.J. Terrell on multiple crossing routes. On some plays, he was open while Cooks struggled. He didn’t get the ball, but it was a promising debut for Kirk. He ran only 14 routes but reached 20.42 miles per hour. The 49ers will lean on that speed moving forward. Offensive line: B+ Jake Brendel got beaten, and Connor Colby watched the defender run right by him on the first sack of the game. Black didn’t do a good job chipping, either. The only other sack came on 4th and 10, when the Falcons brought six, Trent Williams helped off his defender, and Purdy couldn’t get the ball out. Connor Colby gave up 5 pressures. Nobody else had more than two. Purdy was pressured 6% below league average on 42 dropbacks. McCaffrey and James each had 2.0 yards before contact. The rushing lanes were huge, especially early in the game. Colby’s holding call set the offense back. Trent had a false start on the first play. But the offensive line never seemed to prevent the offense from moving the ball. They were quite good once again, as they’ve been all season. Defensive line: D+ The group that has punched above its weight class all season finally came back down to earth. We’ve been spoiled by defensive tackles who controlled the game. That was not the case in Atlanta. Gracen Halton was invisible for the first time. Sebastian Valdez’s only stat was a missed tackle. Osa Odighizuwa has the same pass-rush win rate as Kyle Shanahan, who tore Odighizuwa a new one on the sideline after the veteran jumped offside on 4th and 4. Rookie James Thompson was the most active, with a pressure and two run stops. But, and this wasn’t on him, a penalty gifted Atlanta a fresh set of downs on 3rd and 2. Three edge rushers played over 30 snaps: Romello Height (38), Keion White (35), and Mykel Williams (31). The edge group had zero tackles for loss. Mykel missed a pair of tackles. He had one pressure. Keion had two. Romello had zero, but he and Williams both had run stops. They bottled up Bijan Robinson, who had only one 10+ yard run, but they still moved off the ball more than usual. Robinson had 19 yards before contact, and Khalil Herbert had four on two carries. It was the defensive line’s first true stinker of the season. That’s acceptable, but it still doesn’t change the fact that it happened. Linebackers: B- Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw combined for 25 tackles and only missed two. They also had 6 run stops. The problem was in coverage. Warner did his job. Jaden Dugger limited the damage, allowing 12 yards on four targets. Pre-snap motion messed with Greenlaw. He was consistently out of position and never gave himself a chance to compete. Greenlaw allowed seven receptions on eight targets for 64 yards, including three first downs. It’s a shame, because they played well on the run, and Dugger looks more confident with every snap. Neither of the trio generated a pass rush on nine attempts, either. Cornerbacks: C- The more we see from the cornerbacks, the less confidence there is. Upton Stout was active but served more as an emergency player while nursing a shoulder injury. When rookie Ephesians Prysock has to play, you know something did not go your way. After the game, Shanahan said it wasn’t part of the plan to play Prysock, but the team wanted to try something new. The initial plan was Ashytn Davis in the slot. He lasted seven snaps before giving up a six-yard catch.…
author: Kyle Posey

title: 3 stars from Week 7 for the 49ers: Slim pickings after an off game
summary: It was ugly, it was sloppy, and it was bad. But somehow the San Francisco 49ers found themselves with a chance to take the lead with three minutes left in the fourth quarter. Brock Purdy’s second interception of the game killed that hope, and the 49ers suffered their first loss of 2026, falling 29-20 to […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images It was ugly, it was sloppy, and it was bad. But somehow the San Francisco 49ers found themselves with a chance to take the lead with three minutes left in the fourth quarter. Brock Purdy’s second interception of the game killed that hope, and the 49ers suffered their first loss of 2026, falling 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons. Since the Arizona game, it’s felt like the 49ers’ first loss was coming, but San Francisco staved off defeat with back-to-back one-possession wins before finally succumbing to Atlanta. With the 49ers taking a 6-1 record into the bye week, these are the three stars from the Week 7 loss: 3rd Star: RB Kaelon Black Let’s get it out of the way now: the fumble sucked, and it was the first sign that Sunday might not be the 49ers’ day. But on a day where the defense had no standouts, Black’s first NFL touchdown and his performance in relief of McCaffrey were good enough to earn the third star, despite the fumble. With McCaffrey missing most of the first half, it was on Black to step up. And it was a rough start for the rookie. His day opened with a run that lost four yards, a play blown up by Kendal Daniels. He’d get back to zero yards with his next touch, but it wouldn’t be until his fifth carry to get his rushing yard total greater than zero. But then Black would explode from there. The 49ers’ third drive would start with an 11-yard catch from George Kittle, but it would be all Black from there. He would move the 49ers into plus territory with a 15-yard run followed by a gain of seven. Black would close the drive with a mostly untouched 30-yard touchdown run to put the 49ers up 14-3. His next and last impact on the game would be his fumble, but it was an encouraging overall performance with 12 carries for 63 yards and the touchdown in the spell of McCaffrey. 2nd Star: TE George Kittle Sunday’s loss was such a stinker that half the reason Kittle earned the No. 2 star is that it was a good game on National Tight End Day. Kittle celebrated the occasion with a game-high eight receptions for 88 yards, responsible for 30 percent of the 49ers’ passing offense. The tight end’s day started with a 17-yard reception with the 49ers facing a third-and-4 on the team’s second drive of the game. He’d then open the 49ers’ next drive with an 11-yard catch to start what would end up being a touchdown-scoring drive. He’d have a few more short receptions before closing his day with his longest reception, a 21-yard catch, but Kittle fumbled for the 49ers fourth turnover, ending the 49ers slim hopes of a comeback. Not the best game from the People’s Tight End with the turnover, but a good enough performance on a holiday he created (although Kyle Juszczyk being called an “honorary tight end” should be enough to end the gimmick) to earn a star. 1st Star: RB Christian McCaffrey Just like with Mike Evans last week against Washington, McCaffrey’s knock on Sunday completely hampered the 49ers offense. It was painfully obvious Sunday was a scheduled McCaffrey game, with the 49ers running back getting six touches of the 49ers’ 10-play opening drive. He would take those touches and give the 49ers 69 total yards, ending the drive with a one-yard touchdown run to put San Francisco up 7-0 early. The 49ers’ second drive would start with Purdy connecting with McCaffrey for a five-yard pass with a little under seven minutes left in the first quarter. That would end up being McCaffrey’s last touch until the 8:15 mark in the third quarter, with the running back dealing with a thigh injury for most of Sunday. In the time McCaffrey was off the field, the 49ers offense had three drives that lasted a combined 18 plays for 122 yards, ending in a punt, touchdown, and a fumble lost (on a drive. San Francisco had six drives with McCaffrey on the field, running 47 plays for 281 yards with two touchdowns, but the four others ended in some type of turnover, none at the fault of McCaffrey. Three drives without McCaffrey averaged six plays for 41 yards, while the six with the running back averaged nearly eight plays for 47 yards. McCaffrey finished Sunday with 13 touches for 100 yards (his second 100-yard game in a row) with the touchdown. Curious just how different Sunday’s game could have gone had McCaffrey not missed those two drives. Nonetheless, his performance was easily the best by a 49er in Atlanta. Throughout the season, we will track the three stars of the season by tallying points for each star award using a complex scoring system: three points for being the first star, two for the second, and one for the third. Through Week 7, the standings are: WR Mike Evans – 8 points QB Brock Purdy – 7 points RB Christian McCaffrey – 5 points
author: Andrew Pasquini

title: NFC West Recap: 49ers’ lead shrinks to two; Seahawks, Rams both win
summary: 6-1. The unbeaten run is over. The San Francisco 49ers lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons, and they did it in the most 49ers way possible: three turnovers, a missed extra point, and a parade of defensive penalties on the drive that decided it. Yes, they were injured and a loss was expected, but it […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 07: Head coach Kyle Shanahan of the San Francisco 49ers shakes hands with Head coach Mike Macdonald of the Seattle Seahawks after the game at Lumen Field on September 07, 2025 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images 6-1. The unbeaten run is over. The San Francisco 49ers lost 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons, and they did it in the most 49ers way possible: three turnovers, a missed extra point, and a parade of defensive penalties on the drive that decided it. Yes, they were injured and a loss was expected, but it was a brutal display of errors they simply couldn’t afford to make. Taking it one step further, even with backups, they were very uncharacteristic errors on top of it. To make matters worse, the 49ers special teams picked a bad time to remember they were 49ers special teams, with some atrocious kickoff coverage letting the Falcons start with good field position. It started fine. Running back Christian McCaffrey ripped off chunks on a 10-play opening touchdown drive, and when a thigh injury sent him to the sideline, rookie running back Kaelon Black ran in a 30-yard touchdown for a 14-3 lead. His first touchdown, mind you. Then the giveaways started, the 49ers’ lead was blown, and anything bad that could happen, pretty much did. After all the gifts, 29-20. The 49ers go into the bye up two games over the Seattle Seahawks, and desperately need to get healthy. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) The Seattle Seahawks beat embarrassed the Kansas City Chiefs 20-3 on Sunday Night Football. That leaves the Minnesota Vikings as the lone undefeated team. After two straight losses (which we, as 49ers fans, enjoyed), the Seahawks smothered Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who threw for 165 yards and an interception. Kansas City never reached the red zone. Sam Darnold forgot he was Sam Darnold and went 20-of-28 for 257 yards passing with a touchdown and an interception, and not a single sack. Running back Emanuel Wilson also notched his first 100-yard game as a Seahawk against the Kansas City defense. However, a bill is coming in injuries. Wide receiver Rashid Shaheed (knee) and running back Velus Jones Jr. (hamstring) were ruled out, and left tackle Charles Cross was rolled up on in the fourth quarter. To add insult to the Chiefs, running back Kenneth Walker, who left the Seahawks in the offseason for the Chiefs and was a sleeper MVP pick this year, got only 36 yards on 14 carries. Basically, Walker was doing what the Seahawks had been struggling to do up until this game: run the ball. And thus, the Seahawks begin digging themselves out of the hole. Arizona Cardinals (2-5) The Arizona Cardinals put Larry Fitzgerald in their Ring of Honor and retired his No. 11 at halftime. Nice of the Denver Broncos to bring enough fans to make it feel like a road game. It was more Denver than it was Arizona, which is probably what you get as Arizona when you go into the game 2-4. Then there was the actual game. A game Denver won 30-16. Arizona gave up a 62-yard touchdown run to quarterback Bo Nix and a 52-yard screen touchdown to running back R.J. Harvey, and the Broncos tied their season high in points. Tight end Trey McBride caught 10 passes for 111 yards receiving and the Cardinals’ first touchdown in over 100 game minutes. Yes, you read that right: 100 game minutes. Congrats to McBride. Running back Bam Knight averaged nearly seven yards per carry. Those highlights aren’t going to matter because the Cardinals who marched for a walk-off win in Los Angeles last week couldn’t finish anything here. The Cardinals went 1-for-5 in the red zone, and they’re 12-of-28 on the season. If you really want a single drive that can recap this game, just look to the final drive: five snaps inside the 1-yard line thanks to Denver penalties, a sack back to the 5, and nothing on fourth down. I don’t think 49ers fans need to worry about the Cardinals this year… Los Angeles Rams (3-4) The Los Angeles Rams are no longer in last place. It’s not quite “Ram-ing” it, but going to third place is certainly progress. They beat the Las Vegas Raiders 35-21, and it was closer than that sounds—at least in the fourth quarter when the Raiders managed 15 points and their first two touchdowns. Quarterback Matthew Stafford threw three first-half touchdowns, and running back Kyren Williams added one on the ground for a 28-6 halftime lead. Then the Rams did Rams things. Las Vegas converted a fake punt. Williams fumbled. Running back Blake Corum’s touchdown run came back on a facemask. Stafford threw an interception when tight end Colby Parkinson popped the ball into the air. Corum finally put it away late with a rushing score. Special teams, turnovers, penalties: the same problems that have followed this team all season. They just won anyway. The Raiders, meanwhile, are starting to remember they are the Raiders. This was not the game we wanted them to remember that detail. Onto Week 8 The 49ers are on bye. This means Christian McCaffrey’s thigh also gets a bye. It also means that we can do something else on Sunday. So, bye. The Seahawks host the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football. The Bears had quite a Thursday Night Football game, beating the New England Patriots 30-24. Playing on Thursday night gives them extra rest before they travel to Seattle. If anyone can get the 49ers’ three-game lead back, it’s da Bears. Do it for Ditka. The Cardinals travel to face the Dallas Cowboys. The Cowboys are doing NFC East things on Monday Night Football, but sit at 2-4 as of this writing. The NFC East hasn’t been anything special lately, and that shouldn’t change after Monday. It wouldn’t be surprising to see a Cardinals win here. The Rams host the Los Angeles Chargers in the battle for Levi’s South housesitters SoFi Stadium. The Chargers have failed to win a game yet this season, so maybe Jim Harbaugh and company can get their first victory over the Rams. The last thing 49ers fans want is to have the Rams crawling back into this, so there’s a three-way battle for the division. Please Chargers? 1st: San Francisco 49ers ; Next: BYE 2nd: Seattle Seahawks ; Next: vs. Chicago Bears (Monday Night Football) 3rd: Los Angeles Rams ; Next: vs. Los Angeles Chargers 4th: Arizona Cardinals ; Next: at Dallas Cowboys
author: Patrick Holloway

title: 49ers News: Pain
summary: 49ers ‘took a step back’ in first loss of season against Falcons“Losing is never great, but when you do lose, I think especially in this organization, it makes everybody really just look at yourself in the mirror,” Kittle said. “It’s definitely going to sour our entire bye week, and I think that’s good because I […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 25: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers scrambles with the ball against the Atlanta Falcons during the fourth quarter at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images) | Getty Images 49ers ‘took a step back’ in first loss of season against Falcons “Losing is never great, but when you do lose, I think especially in this organization, it makes everybody really just look at yourself in the mirror,” Kittle said. “It’s definitely going to sour our entire bye week, and I think that’s good because I think when we get back next week, I think our guys are going to be incredibly focused. “Would I rather win? Absolutely. Way more fun. But hey, like I said, it could be worse. We didn’t have a bunch of guys get injured today. I think we made it out pretty healthy. And we got guys coming back, so I’m excited about that.” 49ers go a-stumbling into the bye (paywall) “The secondary was terrible, especially Ji’Ayir Brown and Jack Jones. Brown was late to everything. Jones didn’t know his job, held on almost every play, and got benched for Ephesians Prysock. The 49ers played a bunch of Cover 3, and Atlanta was more than happy to eat up the underneath yardage. But it was no Mike Evans eventually broke down the structure of the offense. So much was decided by every single choice route being wrong. Brock Purdy could not seem to get on the page with anyone, even Christian McCaffrey. Everyone broke in too early, or out too late, or kept going when he expected them to sit. In an offense predicated on timing and expectations, that can mean doom.” Kawakami: What needs fixing and what definitely doesn’t as the 49ers hit the bye (paywall) “The 49ers cannily played the long-game this weekend by not pushing Mike Evans and Nick Bosa out there when they weren’t 100% healthy; and they had Upton Stout in uniform only on an emergency basis — then suffered for it when Jack Jones got torched again and again. But can you imagine if the 49ers played any of those guys, perhaps aggravated their nagging injuries, and still lost? This game was on a short week on artificial turf after a long flight on a 10 a.m. body-clock start. They’ll never say this, but the 49ers knew they could afford a loss on Sunday. And if the 49ers (who outgained the Falcons 400-295) didn’t commit four turnovers, they still easily could’ve won this game, anyway.” Despite 49ers’ hot start, changes loom at kicker, CB, WR and perhaps D-line (paywall) “ Some of the names being bandied about — Josh Sweat, Khalil Mack, Daron Payne and DeForest Buckner — would be strong additions, and Buckner certainly would fit the homecoming theme the 49ers have struck all year with one-time players like Samuel and Dre Greenlaw. Heading into the weekend, multiple reports said the Indianapolis Colts would hold off on a fire sale to see whether they could reverse their freefall in coming weeks. On Sunday, they lost to the Minnesota Vikings 16-10, dropping their record to 2-5. Buckner, a 2016 first-round pick of the 49ers, is in the final year of his contract and is still beloved by the San Francisco fan base, the front office and those who played alongside him. He currently has four sacks, which would lead the 49ers.” 49ers’ depleted WR corps contributes to Brock Purdy’s forgettable day: ‘That’s a real thing’ (paywall) “ The beat-up wideout corps meant Purdy was operating with a stripped-down game plan devised by Shanahan and offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak.” 3 Winners and 11 Losers from the 49ers’ loss to the Falcons “ I didn’t watch Week 7 thinking, “Purdy cost the 49ers the game.” There was an objectively bad decision on an interception that should’ve ended up in the 10th row. If you’ve ever played quarterback, it’s one you’ve probably thrown because you thought you had more space along the sideline than you actually did — and probably because you waited too long to decide who to throw the ball to. Purdy had dropback on the drive before where he scrambled, and it felt like he was in the pocket for 10 seconds. He bought enough time for his tight end and picked up a first down on what would’ve been third and long. On another play, Colton McKivitz was beaten cleanly off the line of scrimmage, which would result in a sack for 90% of quarterbacks. Purdy danced around the pocket just long enough before shoveling the ball to Jordan James, who ran for a first down—another second-and-long turned into a first down. The second interception is one you tip your cap to the Atlanta Falcons on a design that has gotten the best of Purdy throughout the years. Purdy finished in the top five this week among quarterbacks in success rate. His throws to Jordan Watkins, especially the one in the end zone, were on the money—the end-zone one is about as good a throw as you can make. He made a few different throws that were contested that his pass catchers did not haul in. They are the same throws we’ve taken for granted because Evans has caught them all year.”
author: Yinon Raviv

title: Commanders WR Antonio Williams snaps to increase with Terry McLaurin out
summary: The question of who steps up with Terry McLaurin out for the season has been answered. Commanders head coach addressed that topic during his Monday afternoon press conference coming out of the bye.   Quinn has had a bye week to ponder how to proceed after McLaurin suffered a season-ending knee injury during a Week […]
full_text: The question of who steps up with Terry McLaurin out for the season has been answered. Commanders head coach addressed that topic during his Monday afternoon press conference coming out of the bye. Quinn has had a bye week to ponder how to proceed after McLaurin suffered a season-ending knee injury during a Week 6 loss to the San Francisco 49ers . He was asked if it raises Stefon Diggs’ activity. Not necessarily. That was his answer, in sum. The veteran receiver will keep doing his thing. We should see a whole lot more of third-round rookie Antonio Williams . “(Diggs’) workload shouldn’t change as much,” Quinn said. “I think it will be others who climb up more. Antonio is one that you would see getting more targets. We’ll look through the week, but I like Stef especially on the options and third downs with the things that he can do, so the natural progression is probably Antonio more. Not necessarily at the same spot, but at a higher volume.” Let’s decode that for a second. The Commanders like Diggs doing his thing, with his current responsibilities and his role within the offense. Williams will see an uptick in snaps and likely targets, but not while playing McLaurin’s X position (though he moved around a lot more under David Blough than he did under Kliff Kingsbury). While this wasn’t mentioned directly by Quinn, it’s fair to assume that Treylon Burks and, at times, Dyami Brown, will man McLaurin’s position and route responsibilities. You’d figure Williams will remain a heavily used option operating from the slot. He has been effective there in college and the pros, so the Commanders won’t mess with a good thing. Williams has 18 receptions for 205 yards and one touchdown on 26 targets. He has played 55% of Washington’s offensive snaps to this point and that should increase. So should his target share, which ranks third on the team to this point. While Williams has made some rookie mistakes in the early going, there’s optimism he’ll continue to develop and turn into a quality NFL receiver with a bright future ahead. We’ll get the rest of the season to see how he functions as a primary target and without McLaurin pulling coverage away. It will be an important data point in deciding where Washington goes at the receiver position. What are your thoughts on Williams stepping into a bigger role as a rookie, maybe over some others, with McLaurin out? Let us know in the comments below:

Commanders links Articles Last Man Standig (paywall) The Jayden Daniels conversation is worth having; everyone will be okay The third-year QB has played well since rejoining the lineup, but two baffling mistakes, a prolonged winless stretch and questions about his decision-making deserve scrutiny Something feels off with Jayden Daniels — and it’s okay to discuss why. This isn’t about questioning whether the third-year player is Washington’s franchise quarterback. He is! Daniels’ potential is what keeps hope alive during tough stretches. The question is why a player whose poise, command and decision-making defined his extraordinary rookie season is suddenly making mistakes and choices that seem so out of character. I’m talking about game awareness — the clock-management debacle against the Giants in Week 5 and throwing the ball away on fourth down against the 49ers. Two of the season’s most inexplicable plays, in consecutive games, involving a quarterback who previously seemed well beyond such moments. Questions also linger about Daniels’ aggressiveness in the passing game. Pro Football Hall of Fame quarterback Kurt Warner discussed that concern as a recent guest on “Last Man Standig” (video below). The NFL Network analyst was impressed with Daniels’ performance against the 49ers in real time. A closer look at the tape left him wanting more. But this is about more than two plays or passing up opportunities. The Commanders don’t win anymore. For more from Ben Standig, click here On video talking about a few things from added help for Daronte Jones to Jayden daniels (not perfect; none are. but playing well) and more. @ESPNRichmond @ESPNRichmond https://t.co/YZ3UJpEoNT — John Keim (@john_keim) October 23, 2026 Sports Illustrated Jayden Daniels — “I failed to the standard I hold myself to” Week 6 — Following the Giants tie Question: Looking back at the final play against the Giants, did the players realize how much time remained? “I mean, just going back and reflecting on it and, you know, sitting back and ultimately, I know it’s a lot of he say or whatever you’re trying to make, but ultimately, like, it’s on me at the end. I know DQ is getting a lot of slack for it or whatever, you know, but regardless of what happens, I’m the person on the field that’s supposed to calm everything, control everything, and I failed to the standard I hold myself to and the standard in this organization. So it’s just something for me to move on. Not saying I’m proud of it or anything. Obviously looking back, like, it could have resulted in a loss, we tied, but it was a fail in my eyes and, you know, I know I’m better than that. I hold myself to a higher standard than that.” At the bye : There has been plenty of criticism directed at Quinn and the coaching staff, but Daniels wasn’t interested in letting them take all the blame . He understood what happened and recognized that he had a responsibility to manage the situation on the field. That’s part of becoming the leader Washington needs him to be. The talent has never been the question with Daniels. How he handles moments like this will help determine what kind of quarterback he becomes. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Jayden Daniels: A new scheme and growing pains Under relentless pressure, Daniels has occasionally looked rushed and confused. The constant threat of immediate pressure has accelerated his internal clock, causing him to abandon clean pockets prematurely or scramble before deeper route concepts can develop downfield. Hall of Fame quarterback and analyst Kurt Warner highlighted this dynamic in his film breakdown, noting that Daniels is occasionally passing up open opportunities downfield. Warner claims that although Daniels has played “good” this season, his lack of aggression is preventing him from being great. This leads to a larger question: is Daniels becoming too risk-averse? The analytics back up Warner’s evaluation: PFF logs Daniels’ Big-Time Throw rate (BTT%) at just 2.9%, well below the league average for starters. While his extreme care with the football (0 INTs) protects possession, the low BTT% reveals a tendency to take safe check-downs or pull the ball down to run rather than attacking tight coverage windows. What I’d like to see after the bye week is a renewed commitment from the coaching staff to protect Daniels in the pocket, alongside Daniels showing the poise to pull the trigger on downfield shots. The designs are producing open receivers on film, even if Blough’s overall sequencing and game feel have drawn criticism. Once Daniels regains comfort in his protection, he can overcome the gun-shy tendencies that have crept into his process. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Kurt Warner on JAYDEN DANIELS WEEK 6 | Kurt Warner Studyball 2026 Sports Illustrated Daronte Jones — The defense should know what it is within four games Week 2 — Before the Dallas Cowboys game Question: “When you’re implementing a new scheme, at what point in the season does it usually click from your experience and kind of come to life in the way that you envision it?” “In the past, it varies. You would like, as a goal, to be the first quarter of the season, you know, in those first four games. Sometimes it happens faster, like that Game 3, because you’re still working out some of the kinks. Sometimes you’re trying to get the continuity together, especially if you have a lot of new guys. Some things that goes into that. But definitely by the first quarter of the season, you have a good beat on, ‘Okay, this is who we are. This is how our guys respond and how they play.’ And then you can kind of build even from a staff perspective in terms of, you know, we’re still — I know I am — in terms of, you know, you watch these guys in practice and so forth like that, but also, you know, we say practice execution becomes game reality. So how they respond in games, you kind of understand, ‘Okay, this player is better at that than I thought he was, so let’s utilize him more in that way,’ or, ‘He’s not quite where we want to be in that particular space, so let’s keep him out of those spaces.’ And so I think by the first four games, you kind of have a better idea of the team and the defense as a whole.” At the bye: We’ve passed that four-game mark, and the defense still doesn’t look like a finished product . There have been encouraging performances, particularly when it comes to creating turnovers, but the consistency Jones discussed remains a problem. Washington has had stretches where the defense looks capable of taking over games, followed by others where it struggles to get off the field. title: The effects of eight offensive tactics on offensive effectiveness and QB injuries
summary: There has been considerable discussion on Hogs Haven about the desirability of using offensive tactics such as motion, play-action passing and the shotgun formation.  However, the commentary is based mostly on the poster’s preferences and biases. There is surprisingly little hard evidence about how well those tactics work. This article is based on a unique dataset with […]
full_text: There has been considerable discussion on Hogs Haven about the desirability of using offensive tactics such as motion, play-action passing and the shotgun formation. However, the commentary is based mostly on the poster’s preferences and biases. There is surprisingly little hard evidence about how well those tactics work. This article is based on a unique dataset with measures of eight common offensive tactics and two types of outcomes: offensive effectiveness (three measures) and quarterback injuries (two measures). I created the database using six different data sources. You are seeing it all here at Hogs Haven , folks, and not from behind a paywall. If there is sufficient interest, I will write another article that takes a deeper dive into how teams package tactics into offensive schemes. That is a complex topic that requires a full separate article. (Teaser: the common wisdom about what NFL teams use which offensive schemes is wrong.) Since most readers want to know what difference the tactics make for scoring, wins and QB injuries, we focus on those relationships in this article. I assume that the offensive tactics and outcomes considered in the paper are familiar and that readers can dive straight into the results of my analyses, which is what most readers will care about. Therefore, I have organized this article back-asswards from an academic article. I will put the sections that cover the rationale for each tactic, hypotheses (without using that term), measures, sources and methods at the end of the article in separate sections. Those who are interested in the analytical detail can read the appendices. Summary of Measures I used data from the full 2025 regular season . I did not include preseason or postseason games in the analysis. The formal definition for each measure, the rationale for using it and its data source are provided in the first appendix. Anyone who has the time and interest could recreate my database and conduct their own analyses using that information. The list of measures used in this article is shown in the following table. Variables Analyzed Offensive Tactics Outcomes Motion Rate Scoring Play Action Rate EPA Air Yards / Attempt (AYA) Wins Shotgun Rate QB Injuries No Huddle Rate QB Weeks Out QB Run Yards % Rushing Yards Pass Rate over Expected (PROE) Use of Eight Offensive Tactics by NFL Teams The next table provides the descriptive statistics (means, standard deviations, medians and range) for the eight offensive tactics. Note that the mean (average) and median (50 th percentile) are quite similar for almost all these measures. That indicates that the distribution of the data for those metrics is relatively normal (and that makes your author happy because the analysis is more straightforward). The biggest gap between mean and median is for no huddle rate and that distribution is very skewed. The Commanders were a huge outlier in 2025 and under then-offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury, using no huddle 60% of the time (more than 6 times the mean), and the Giants and Saints used no huddle more than 20% of the time (more than twice the mean). The table suggests several conclusions about the use of these tactics. All NFL teams use almost all these tactics to some degree. It is not a matter of using some and not others. For example, one of the more controversial tactics for Hogs Haven posters is use of the shotgun rather than starting the play from under center. The average NFL team used the shotgun almost two-thirds of the time; the team that used the shotgun the least (the Rams) still used it 40% of the time. (Washington made the heaviest use of it in 2025 at a whopping 87% of the time.) Similarly, all teams made relatively heavy use of motion (range of 39% to 68%). The Kingsbury-led Commanders used it 49% of the time. Descriptive Statistics for Offensive Tactics Mean Standard Deviation Median Range Low/High Teams Motion Rate 53.7 7.57 52.2 39-68 NYG-MIA Play Action Rate 15.5 2.37 14.8 11-21 CIN-LAR Air Yards / Attempt 7.8 0.85 7.8 6.0-9.2 SEA-NWE Shotgun Rate 65.3 11.36 65.8 40-87 LAR-WAS No Huddle Rate 9.8 10.41 7.2 2-60 NWE-WAS QB Run Yards 302.8 184.90 305.0 -9-630 LAR-WAS % Rushing Plays 43.9 4.1 44.0 34.1-52.1 ARI-SEA Pass over Expected -0.02 0.04 -0.02 -10.3-4.7 NYJ-ARI However, some tactics are used much less commonly than expected. There has been extensive discussion of play-action passing on Hogs Haven , but it’s used rarely. The league average is 15.5%, and the heaviest user (the Rams) only used it 21% of the time. There are two possible explanations. The first is that play-action doesn’t work well unless it has been set up by the running game and is relatively rare and thus surprising. The second explanation might be that the heavy league-wide use of the shotgun limits play-action usage. However, Washington used the shotgun 87% of the time and still ran play action 17% of the time, above the league average, so that doesn’t appear to be true. Some tactics are used within a narrow range. Nearly all teams ran the ball between 40% and 49% of the time. Only four teams ran less than 40% of plays (the Cardinals were the lowest at 34%, followed by the Bengals, Titans, and Raiders) and only two teams ran at least 50% of the time (the Seahawks at 50.0% and the Bills at 50.6%). One question outstanding is whether the bad teams that ran less performed poorly because they didn’t run the ball enough or whether they passed more because they were consistently behind in games; and whether the two teams at the high end succeeded because they ran so much or whether they ran so much because they were consistently leading late in games and running out the clock. Pass Rate over Expected addresses this last question to some degree. Considering the total situation (down, distance, field position, etc.), teams were still inclined to run slightly more than expected (average was -.02, meaning more runs than expected). PROE varied quite a bit. Teams with the highest PROE (more likely to pass than expected) were the Rams, Chiefs, Cardinals, and Patriots. Teams with the lowest PROE (more likely to run than expected) where the Jets, Ravens, Seahawks and Falcons. Obviously, there were playoff teams (including a Super Bowl team) and bad teams on both lists. Note that the list of teams high and low in rushing % and PROE did not overlap strongly. Air Yards / Attempt (AYA) was in a fairly narrow range. Teams threw beyond the line of scrimmage but not too far beyond – enough for a first down if the team had some yards after catch or positive yardage on other plays. But on average, teams weren’t throwing deep enough for a big gain unless the receiver broke free. The average AYA was 7.8 yards. All teams threw between 6.0 AYA (Seahawks, followed by the Lions at 6.4) and 9.2 AYA (Patriots, followed by the Rams at 9.1 and Eagles at 9.0). It’s interesting that both the high and low lists were heavily populated by playoff teams (with a Super Bowl team both highest and lowest). Given the narrow range, NFL passing clearly is now oriented toward ball control. One metric where there was a large difference across teams was QB run yards . The average was 303 yards rushing from quarterbacks, but the standard deviation was over half that total (185 yards). Washington (630 yards), the Giants (616), Bills (585), and Chargers (583) led the pack, while the Rams had minus-9 yards, the Lions had 42, and the Steelers had 67. Both scheme and having a skilled running quarterback (or multiple running QBs) predict the number of yards. Outcomes Offensive Effectiveness Outcomes: Scoring shows a nice, normal distribution. So does EPA (Expected Points Added) per play. Note that the mean for EPA is 0; the average play neither adds nor subtracts points from expected. Wins averaged 8.5 for the season, or exactly half the games played, realizing the NFL dream of perfect parity, again with a nice distribution. Good distributions for most of the tactics and for all three outcomes…

title: Tyler’s Take – Is Commanders GM Adam Peters using Dan Quinn as his fall guy?
summary: It’s rare you see an NFL general manager say, “Yeah, that was on me. I messed up.” However rare, it’s very refreshing. Former Broncos general manager John Elway once admitted in an interview that his biggest mistake was passing on Josh Allen in the 2018 NFL Draft. Just this year Eagles general manager Howie Roseman […]
full_text: It’s rare you see an NFL general manager say, “Yeah, that was on me. I messed up.” However rare, it’s very refreshing. Former Broncos general manager John Elway once admitted in an interview that his biggest mistake was passing on Josh Allen in the 2018 NFL Draft. Just this year Eagles general manager Howie Roseman admitted to Sports Illustrated that trading a late-round pick for Andy Dalton was a mistake . These are small blips on the radar compared to the Vikings… General Manager Kwesi Adolfo-Mensah was fired by ownership less than 24 hours after he publicly admitted that letting Sam Darnold walk because they had drafted J.J. McCarthy was a mistake. Maybe the above is why Adam Peters has kept relatively quiet on his mistakes. Is Peters forcing “his guys” on the coaching staff? On Oct. 9, Commanders beat reporter Candi Waller tweeted this: #Commanders GM Adam Peters is the final decision maker on the roster, per HC Dan Quinn. Question asked by @BenStandig — Candi "CWall" Waller (@cwallse) October 9, 2026 From the outside, this tweet looks pretty innocuous. But a bit later, Candi followed up her original tweet with this: I promise I would not have even tweeted this if it didn’t matter folks. USE YOUR CLUES. https://t.co/FKCgfyC18k — Candi "CWall" Waller (@cwallse) October 9, 2026 So, the “USE YOUR CLUES” in all CAPS definitely raises some eyebrows. She then used this same phrase as a reply to many people who had quote-tweeted her original tweet. So, what does Candi know that the average fan may not? I think this is pretty obvious! Peters wants his draft picks to be successful. To be successful, they have to play. Coaches are the ones who decide who plays – PERIOD! No general manager should have a say in who plays and when and where they do. However, Candi may be suggesting that there are internal struggles between Peters and the coaching staff about who plays. My guess is a lot of this stemmed from the release of Kaytron “Fatman” Allen from the active roster but grew in lore with the benefit of some hindsight. Mike Sainristil , who had a good rookie year followed by a poor second season, began the year as a starter on the outside opposite Amik Robertson. After struggling mightily to begin the season, his reps slowly began decreasing week after week. Now he’s a reserve playing special teams. Tight end Ben Sinnott has seen a more prominent role as evidenced by his increase in snaps, however, he’s still not being targeted in the passing game. There COULD BE and SHOULD BE a time where the struggling left tackle Brandon Coleman is benched, but could Peters be behind his former 2024 third-round pick staying in the lineup? Another question begs to be asked: Did Adam Peters force Nick Allegretti on the coaching staff? Did he force HIS draft pick Matt Gulbin on Quinn at right guard when starting right guard Sam Cosmi first went out with a concussion, even though it was evident to even the most novice fan that Gulbin had NO BUSINESS being on the field? If Candi is correct with her tweet, I think you may have the answer to this question… Roster Mistakes Every general manager makes mistakes. Hell, if you have above a 60% hit rate on draft picks and top free agent acquisitions, you are considered a genius. The difference between a good general manager and a poor one is the ability to see your mistake and move on with a better plan. At this point, I don’t think Adam Peters has the ability to do so. He is still relying on the “aging vet” model that we saw him go to in 2025: Stefon Diggs (albeit a good signing) Austin Ekeler Craig Reynolds Van Jefferson Lucas Patrick (a necessary signing after the “Allegretti experiment”) Rasul Douglas Fabian Moreau Isaac Yiadom We’ve seen him lose two valuable running backs — one who was signed off the practice squad (Robert Henry Jr.), and Fatman, who was cut with hopes he’d revert to the practice squad but was claimed by the Dolphins. The “wonder boy” experiment at center this offseason is a move that should be investigated by ownership… Going into the season with limited depth along the offensive line has CRUSHED the team this far. The “staff” appears to finally be moving on from Sainristil as a starter, but you have to wonder how much Peters pushed back on this before realizing he’s not playable. Are Newton, Sinnott, Coleman and McCaffrey next? There is ZERO doubt in my mind that Adam Peters wants this to be his team and he probably views head coach Dan Quinn as a dead man walking, which is why he may be, as Candi subtly hints, meddling. Is Adam Peters using Dan Quinn as his “fall guy”? Does he TRULY believe his players are not the problem and it’s more on the coaches? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Jay-Z's road to the Super Bowl: Were the clues there all along?
summary: With Hov headed to SoFi Stadium's halftime stage in Los Angeles, we revisit the breadcrumbs that might have pointed us there.
full_text:
"I said no to the Super Bowl: You need me, I don't need you. Every night we in the end zone, tell the NFL we in stadiums too." -- Jay-Z, "Apes---" 

 The man who famously rapped about turning down the Super Bowl in 2018 has changed his tune.

 Jay-Z is headed to SoFi Stadium to headline the Super Bowl LXI halftime show, putting one of hip-hop's deepest catalogs on football's biggest stage. Apparently, "I don't need you" left a little room for "see you in Inglewood."

 Hov is already well acquainted with the operation. Roc Nation, the entertainment company he founded in 2008, has partnered with the NFL since August 2019 as the league's "live music entertainment strategist." He has helped shape the halftime spectacle from behind the scenes, beginning with Shakira and Jennifer Lopez's performance at Super Bowl LIV in 2020.

 
 Now, after a run of headliners including Kendrick Lamar and Bad Bunny, the businessman (read as: business, man) helping put the show together is putting himself on the bill. From the boardroom to the halftime stage, consider it a promotion.

 Jay taking his talents to midfield might surprise anyone still holding him to those "Apes---" bars. But saying no isn't the same as saying never, and a closer look suggests this moment didn't come entirely out of nowhere.

 Has Hov been telling us all along? Here are the hints that hit a little differently now.

 

 A little stadium practice: On to the next stage 
 

 Jay-Z got a few stadium reps alongside his wife, Beyoncé, with his three surprise appearances on her Cowboy Carter Tour in 2025, popping up in Paris, Atlanta and Las Vegas.

 His June 22 appearance at the Atlanta Falcons ' Mercedes-Benz Stadium marked the couple's first live performance together in seven years, with the 2003 hit "Crazy in Love" among the songs on the set list. He also made a surprise appearance for the July 26 tour finale at the Las Vegas Raiders ' Allegiant Stadium.

 A few guest verses don't necessarily signal a halftime audition, but in hindsight, those stadium cameos could be read as an intriguing warmup.

 

 'Politics as usual' in Philly 
 

 Before plotting a showing on football's biggest stage, Hov got back to headlining in Philadelphia. Announced March 17 , his Roots Picnic appearance came with a warmup: an invite-only preshow the night before at The Foundry .

 His May 30 Roots Picnic set marked his first solo headlining show since at least 2019, and the city was familiar territory. Jay-Z launched the Made in America there in 2012, turning Labor Day weekend on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway into a recurring destination for music's biggest names. In hindsight, that experience bringing stars together feels like a fitting prelude to Roc Nation's halftime work.

 His return to the City of Brotherly Love came with a reunion, bringing out longtime Philly-based collaborators including Beanie Sigel, Freeway, Peedi Crakk, Memphis Bleek and the Young Gunz. He sported a new look, too: an afro (in place of his freeform locs) that honored his father, who often wore the same style. A fresh set and a fresh silhouette? With Hov, even a hairstyle can have a backstory deeper than just a trip to the barber.

 

 Allow him to reintroduce himself 
 

 Big anniversaries call for big stages, changes -- and apparently, a fresh cut. With 2026 marking 30 years of "Reasonable Doubt" and 25 years of "The Blueprint," Jay-Z and Roc Nation announced a three-night celebration at Yankee Stadium on March 18. By July 10, the self-proclaimed "Mariano of the Marriott" was onstage for the first of three sold-out hometown shows, sporting his signature low-cut Caesar.

 For fans who keep tabs on Hov, a haircut is enough to get the group chat going. "Usually I don't cut my hair when I'm recording," he told GQ in 2006 , making a fresh Caesar a potential clue that he's ready for his next chapter. He even acknowledged the speculation during a 2023 "CBS Mornings" interview with Gayle King : "I'm working through whether to cut it or not. I'm just letting the world know." Earlier this year, Beyoncé shared, in a video aptly named "The Blueprint," that Jay-Z initially grew his hair to support their then-5-year-old daughter Blue Ivy as she struggled with confidence in her own hair.

 The Yankee Stadium cut didn't come with a new album -- at least not yet -- but Pharrell Williams made sure the switch didn't go unnoticed during their July 11 performance.

 "They poked the bear and now the bear cut his hair," Williams said.

 In June and July, he announced that the anniversary celebrations were going international  with September stops in London and Paris, respectively. The next stop back in the U.S.? An Oct. 23 show at SoFi Stadium , the home of Super Bowl LXI.

 Consider that breadcrumb stadium-sized.

title: Steelers Aaron Rodgers, QB room lead NFL Week 7's best arrivals
summary: NFL stars continue to turn game-day arrivals into their own weekly fashion showcase.
full_text:
Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback room set the fashion standard high Sunday in Paris, simulating European-style looks from their favorite show "Peaky Blinders" with three-piece suits and flat caps. 
 
 

 The idea spawned from backup quarterback Mason Rudolph , who reached out to clothing designer Mitch Purgason to have the suits custom-made for this game.

 Rudolph explained that the Steelers quarterback room bonds over "Peaky Blinders." The show is extremely British, not French. But Rudolph's idea was to lean into United Kingdom experience and display with energy that they connect with personally.

 Purgason said he flew up to Pittsburgh to custom-fit the Steelers quarterback room 13 days ago, then he and his associate stylist, Rachel Leskowsky, went to work making the suits in about nine days. Purgason then flew up to hand-deliver the fits last minute before their flight to Paris.

 The work is worth it for looks as clean as the Steelers quarterback room. They posed for pregame pictures in Paris, and it exuded boss energy. Will this lead to more NFL positional groups leaning into translating their personal connection niche into fashion?

 Here are Week 7's most fashionable NFL player gameday fits that caught our eye:

 

 Monday night drip 
 Ahead of "Monday Night Football" against the Philadelphia Eagles , Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott rocked a mint green suede bomber jack for a clean look. The starting quarterback on the other side, Tanner McKee , wore a suit that included a special message -- images of his family are sewn inside his jacket.

 

 Sunday's best 
 A return game for Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III on "Sunday Night Football" prompted a simple, yet sleek outfit. He wore all-white ahead of his first game against the Seattle Seahawks since signing with Kansas City in the offseason. His fellow teammates, Patrick Mahomes , Travis Kelce , Chris Jones and L'Jarius Sneed , all rocked suits.

 

 It was tracksuits galore in the afternoon slate, with Rams defensive tackle Aaron Donald styling a black look with a pair of shades. Meanwhile, Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby broke out a white jumpsuit, showing off his ink with an unzipped jacket. 
 
 
 
Though Sunday marked a holiday in National Tight Ends Day, that didn't stop Rodgers and the Steelers quarterback room from channeling their inner "Peaky Blinders" in Paris with coordinated suits, boots, flat cap and all. 
 
 

 

 
Thursday's looks 
 Caleb Williams kept it sharp ahead of "Thursday Night Football," pairing a navy suit with a black crewneck shirt. The Chicago Bears quarterback skipped the tie but not the wired earbuds. Naturally, he had his matcha drink in one hand and a structured brown leather bag in the other.
