title: Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 8: WR trade for Chiefs? Goff for MVP?
summary: Get ready for Week 8 with takes on the Chiefs' trade deadline plan, Jared Goff's sneaky season, Kevin Stefanski's Coach of the Year case and the Ravens' struggling defense.
full_text:
Are you excited for NFL Week 8 ? This is our first loaded slate of the season. Ravens at Bills. Vikings at Lions. Browns at Steelers. Chiefs at Broncos. Bears at Seahawks. Even the not-so-great games (Falcons at Buccaneers and Colts at Jaguars) mean a lot for divisional standings.

 Every Tuesday of the NFL season , I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

 
 Subscribe: 'ESPN's Leaguewide' 

 
 This week, I'll start with a prediction/plea for the Chiefs to make a trade for a receiver. Then I'll put all my hope and joy on the back of a fourth-round rookie. And finally, I'll admit I can't do my job.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Chiefs will make a WR trade 
 Stefanski will be Coach of the Year 
 Goff is a sleeper MVP candidate 
 Coleman could save Broncos' offense 
 Ravens' D disqualifies them from contention 
 QB3 Leonard starts for Colts by Week 10 
 Young is a complicated study 
 Some extra inklings 

 
 

 

 I think ... the Chiefs' loss to Seattle will bully them into making the trade they need to make 
 Have you ever gotten embarrassed on national television? Me neither.

 The 2026 Chiefs sure have. Kansas City scored three points against the Seahawks on Sunday night, marking only the second time in Patrick Mahomes ' career that his team has been held to three or fewer points. The 11 first downs the Chiefs accumulated were their fewest in 153 Mahomes starts, and this was only his fourth start without a single explosive pass. The offense averaged 4.3 yards per play (148th out of 153), produced minus-0.13 EPA per play (148th) and had a success rate of 34% (152nd).

 It's easy to explain this one. The Seahawks, off a two-game losing streak, were hosting an unbeaten Chiefs team at home -- that defense was amped-up for four quarters. The Chiefs were down both starting tackles ( Josh Simmons and Jaylon Moore ) along with two of three starting receivers ( Tyquan Thornton and Rashee Rice ), and the passing offense played like it. Even the Chiefs' ace in the hole -- their interior offensive line's dominance in the running game -- was beaten in this game, as they ran into the league-best defensive tackle duo of Leonard Williams and Byron Murphy II . I didn't think it would look as bad as it did, but it's not too surprising it fell to such dramatic pieces.

 

 Let's also consider the larger context. Simmons didn't just miss this game -- he has been out all season, and ESPN reported Sunday that Reid and Mahomes had to kick Simmons out of a meeting last Wednesday after frustrations boiled over. He has missed the entire season because of back issues, has recently been placed on injured reserve and missed time last season for personal reasons and a wrist injury. Rice has now missed 27 of the 43 games he could have played since the start of the 2024 season for injury or suspension. It's not just that the Chiefs' star receiver and early-drafted left tackle missed this past week -- it's that they've proven to be consistently unavailable. Meanwhile, Chiefs' first-round receiver Xavier Worthy dropped another pass in Week 7 as he continues to be unusable on most downfield routes.

 This was a one-off in that the Chiefs were dramatically outmanned and should get some of these players back from the medical tent soon. But this was not a one-off in the sense that Rice, Simmons and Worthy are just unreliable players.

 The Chiefs should clearly consider drastic measures. Undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson has played well enough in Simmons' absence that there's no need to make a big trade for a left tackle. But the need for a three-down receiver who can endure a large target volume and succeed at all three levels of the field is glaring. Worthy isn't even the best speed receiver on the team when Thornton is healthy, so I think Worthy should be dangled in trade packages as well -- he has more value in theory right now than he does in practice.

 Whether the Chiefs actually will consider a big deadline trade is less clear. General manager Brett Veach has typically been active around the deadline, executing at least one in-season trade in five consecutive seasons from 2020 to 2024 before going quiet in 2025. The biggest such deal was the future third-round pick traded for Kadarius Toney in 2022. The Chiefs had just traded Tyreek Hill in the 2022 offseason and were looking for speed on offense. Toney didn't hit as a receiver, but he provided a big punt return in the Chiefs' Super Bowl victory that season.

 This Chiefs team (5-1) is as well suited for a postseason run as that Chiefs team (5-2 at the time of the trade). Through seven weeks of the 2026 season, the Chiefs are fifth in offensive EPA per play and fourth in defensive EPA per play. They are ninth in offensive points per drive and third in defensive points per drive. With an actual running game well in hand and a reinvigorated defense, this is as balanced of a Chiefs team as I can remember. They just need some more juice on offense.

 

 ESPN's Adam Schefter has reported as such. From "The Pat McAfee Show" on Monday: "They have been calling around, and I don't think it would be a surprise to see them continue to attempt to add a wide receiver before the trade deadline."

 I have five deadline deals for a receiver in mind. These are not sourced and were first written down on the back of a napkin. It's very likely the other teams in these hypotheticals would not even listen to deals for their wideouts. Do not yell at me on the internet about these trade proposals.

 1. Send Worthy and a 2027 third-round pick to the Jaguars for Brian Thomas Jr . 

 Jacksonville benched Thomas in the second half of its Week 6 game. The only value the Jaguars were getting from him was theoretical field stretching -- Worthy can do much the same, and Mahomes and the Chiefs can give Thomas a chance to rediscover his 2024 form in a new zip code.

 2. Send a 2027 third-round pick and 2028 conditional fifth-round pick to the Cowboys for George Pickens . 

 The Cowboys have 2025 trade acquisition Pickens and 2026 trade acquisition Joey Porter Jr . playing on contract years, and it's hard to imagine they extend both ex-Steelers at market rates. If Pickens would recoup a third-round compensatory pick in free agency, the Chiefs can sweeten the pot with a future pick conditional on production levels and give the Cowboys their third-round comp pick without having to manipulate the formula this offseason. How the Cowboys play in Weeks 8 and 9 (vs. Cardinals, at Colts) will have a big impact here.

 3. Send a 2027 fourth-round pick to the Eagles for Dontayvion Wicks . 

 If I were the Chiefs, I'd be putting a first and then some on the table for DeVonta Smith . It absolutely would not work -- Eagles GM Howie Roseman isn't going to trade both A.J. Brown and Smith in the same season -- but you have to try as the Eagles stare down the barrel of a rebuild in 2027. In lieu of Smith, Wicks has all the traits of a three-level receiver -- ball tracking, ability to catch away from his frame, burst, size -- without any of the route or hands consistency. Grab him for a Day 3 pick and hope to run hot!

 

 4. Send Worthy and a 2027 seventh-round pick to the Saints for Devaughn Vele and a 2027 sixth-round pick. 

 Before you laugh, that's tied-for-22nd-in-total-receptions Devaughn Vele to you! Vele is an entirely unexciting target, but he is also basically what the Chiefs need. He's a big-bodied receiver who can take a ton of contact and endure 10-plus-target games. He also makes good catches away from his frame and provides red zone value --…

title: NFL Power Rankings: How all 32 teams stack up for Week 8, plus offseason adds
summary: How does every NFL team stack up heading into Week 8? We made our 1-32 list and picked the best offseason additions -- coach or players -- for every team.
full_text:
As is the case in every  NFL season , a handful of offseason additions are making splashes with their new teams. In Week 7 , rookie second-round pick Jacob Rodriguez helped the Dolphins to their first win and maintained his NFL lead for most tackles per game (11.4). Meanwhile,  Kenneth Walker III , who signed with the Chiefs in free agency, leads all running backs in yards per carry (5.8). Also, coaches Todd Monken and John Harbaugh have the Browns and Giants at the top of their respective divisions.

 So which additions have had the most impact so far? Along with the weekly 1-32 rankings, our NFL Nation reporters picked the best offseason addition from each roster. They chose from 2026 draft picks , free agent signings , trade acquisitions or coach hirings .

 To form the list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another. Here are a few highlights from this week's rankings:

 
 The Bengals-Ravens matchup caused a big stir in our rankings, sending the Ravens down five spots and the Bengals up four. Baltimore led at the halftime despite being without quarterback Lamar Jackson  ( ankle ) but blew a double-digit advantage. It is just the sixth team in NFL history to do that three times in the first seven weeks of a season, per ESPN Research -- and the first since the 2022 Ravens. Cincinnati quarterback  Joe Burrow  was nearly perfect in the second half, completing 16 of 18 passes for 249 yards and four touchdowns. 
 All four AFC North and all four NFC North teams are over .500 through seven weeks. It's the fifth and sixth times under the current division format (since 2002) that all teams in a division are .500 or better at this point of the season, per Elias Sports Bureau. In our rankings, the lowest-ranked NFC North team is the Packers (No. 15) and the lowest-ranked AFC North team is the Browns (No. 16). 
 The Buccaneers are getting back on track after a  dominant win over the Panthers brought them to 2-1 over the past three weeks. Sunday's victory also marked the return of quarterback  Baker Mayfield , who missed the past three games because of a dislocated right thumb . Tampa Bay was as low as No. 30 in our rankings this season, but the Bucs are now in the top 25 ahead of a divisional matchup against the Falcons . 
 
 Let's get into the full list, starting with the same No. 1 team from last week .

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1) 
 Week 7 result: Lost to the Falcons 29-20 
 Week 7 ranking: 1 

 Best offseason addition: WR Mike Evans 

 

 The 49ers signed Evans  in free agency to be their primary X receiver and produce against man coverage. Through the first six weeks, that's exactly what he did. In a Week 5 win over Seattle , quarterback Brock Purdy had a QBR of 90 when Evans was on the field versus 56 when he wasn't. Achilles tendinitis kept Evans out of San Francisco's only loss, driving home his value to the team. -- Nick Wagoner 

 
 

 2. Buffalo Bills (5-1) 
 Week 7 result: Bye 
 Week 7 ranking: 3 

 Best offseason addition: WR D.J. Moore 

 

 The Bills' offense has survived while Moore rehabs a shoulder injury , but it's clear how much smoother the team's passing attack works when he's involved. Moore's field-stretching talents lead to explosive plays and lighten boxes to create bigger alleys for rushing attempts by running back  James Cook III and QB Josh Allen . No player this season is averaging more yards per route run (2.47) with as deep of an average depth of target (15.9 yards) as Moore. He was acquired from the Bears for a 2026 second-round pick this offseason.  -- Nick Suss 

 
 

 

 3. Minnesota Vikings (6-0) 
 Week 7 result: Beat the Colts 16-10 
 Week 7 ranking: 4 

 Best offseason addition: QB Kyler Murray 

 

 In reality, the Vikings' offseason was more about subtractions than additions. But Murray remains the most significant acquisition they made despite his individual performance being uneven in five games. The Vikings have won all of his starts, and there are some signs that he is settling in. His QBR since Week 5 (75.1) ranks sixth in the NFL, powered in part by nine scrambles that gained 94 yards and converted four third downs. -- Kevin Seifert 

 
 

 4. Kansas City Chiefs (5-1) 
 Week 7 result: Lost to the Seahawks 20-3 
 Week 7 ranking: 2 

 Best offseason addition: RB Kenneth Walker III 

 

 Despite his disappointing return to Seattle on Sunday, Walker has perhaps been the biggest reason the Chiefs are atop the AFC standings. He is second in the league with 701 rushing yards; his production has made life easier for quarterback Patrick Mahomes , who has excelled at play-action passes. At this point last season, the Chiefs realized they didn't have any explosion in their running attack. Now the Chiefs' biggest strength on offense has been when Mahomes hands the ball off to his new teammate.  -- Nate Taylor 

 
 

 5. Seattle Seahawks (4-3) 
 Week 7 result: Beat the Chiefs 20-3 
 Week 7 ranking: 6 

 Best offseason addition: RB Emanuel Wilson 

 

 With the Seahawks reserving all their big offseason deals for in-house extensions, they made a few bargain signings in free agency, including Wilson on a one-year, $1.6 million deal . Their run game has not been a strength, with rookie first-round pick Jadarian Price missing the past four games and Zach Charbonnet having yet to make his 2026 debut , but Wilson has helped keep it afloat. He has rushed for 403 yards (3.6-yard average) and three touchdowns, with another touchdown through the air. Much of that has come in a leading role since Price, who is now eligible to return, went on IR ( chest ).  -- Brady Henderson 

 
 

 6. Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) 
 Week 7 result: Bye 
 Week 7 ranking: 5 

 Best offseason addition: LG Emmanuel Pregnon 

 

 A back injury to right guard Patrick Mekari forced the Jaguars to shuffle the offensive line in training camp. Left guard Ezra Cleveland moved over to right guard, which gave Pregnon the opportunity to earn first-team reps. The third-round rookie has a 71.6% run block win rate (fourth highest among Jaguars starting linemen), but he has helped them be much better in short-yardage runs -- a priority for coach Liam Coen in 2026. The Jaguars averaged 1.3 yards per carry on runs in third-and-short (2 yards or fewer) in 2025, which ranked last in the NFL. They're averaging 3.1 yards in that situation in 2026 (eighth-best mark). -- Michael DiRocco 

 
 

 7. Chicago Bears (5-2) 
 Week 7 result: Beat the Patriots 30-24 
 Week 7 ranking: 9 

 Best offseason addition: S Dillon Thieneman 

 

 Thieneman and fellow rookie DB  Malik Muhammad II  have nearly identical stat lines this season, but the No. 25 pick gets the nod here for how he has handled the highest snap percentage of any Bears defender (97.58%). Thieneman is No. 1 or tied for the team lead in total tackles (47), passes defensed (five) and interceptions (one). He also has 1.5 sacks and three QB hits. Thieneman has had his share of learning moments, but the stability he has provided can't be overstated for a secondary that has dealt with moving parts since the start of training camp. -- Courtney Cronin 

 

 
 

 8. Denver Broncos (5-2) 
 Week 7 result: Beat the Cardinals 30-16 
 Week 7 ranking: 10 

 Best offseason addition: WR Jaylen Waddle 

 

 Rookie running back Jonah Coleman has played in only three games because of an ankle injury , and he might win the impact-per-snap-played quotient, but Waddle leads the Broncos in receptions (26) and receiving yards (276). His numbers would likely look better if he had not been caught up in the swirl of Denver's passing struggles. Waddle left Sunday's game because of an apparent shoulder injury, but if it's not serious and the Broncos can simply get him the ball…

title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald ,  who unretired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sits two behind 30th.  
 
 As for Garrett, he entered his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach career top-five territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  in August, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks heading into the season was 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research. The pass rusher recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the career list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White's.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 7 update 

 Hunter and Watt were the only ones to record sacks this week, with Hunter jumping back over Campbell in the rankings. 

 Week 6 update 

 With Garrett still out, it was another quiet week on the sack front. Of the active leaders, it was the oldest that recorded the lone sack of the week in Campbell. He moved back in front of Hunter. 

 Week 5 update 

 Hunter was the only player among the active leaders to record a sack this week, moving him ahead of Campbell to No. 26 all-time. Hunter now has three sacks through five games. 

 Week 4 update 

 Watt kicked off things in Week 4 on "Thursday Night Football" in an impactful way. He had one sack, one forced fumble and a fumble recovery to move his total to 4.5 sacks on the season. Other than that, there wasn't much activity with Garrett continuing to be on IR. 

 Week 3 update 

 There wasn't much movement on the list this week with only Mack (1) and Hunter (.5) recording sacks. Watt, Campbell, Hunter and Mack (in that order) now make up 25 to 28 on the all-time list. Along with Campbell, the three top active leaders -- Miller, Jordan and Garrett -- have yet to record a sack this season.  

 Week 2 update 

 The second week of the season saw little movement near the top of the career list, but Watt's hot start continues, with the defensive end recording 1.5 sacks to now put him at 3.5 through two weeks (No. 2 in the NFL this season) and break a tie with Campbell to move to 25th. 

 Hunter (27th) and Mack (29th) also recorded one sack apiece over the weekend to break ties and move up one spot on the list. 

 Donald (33rd) made his  season debut on "Monday Night Football" against the Giants after taking two years off. He finished with three tackles, one for a loss, but did not record a sack. 

 

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: Is Bills' Josh Allen the best goal line rusher ever?
summary: Out of the 153 players who've carried from the 1- or 2-yard line at least 30 times since 1977, Allen has done it best.
full_text:
ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. -- Josh Allen is quantifiably the best goal line rusher in NFL history -- well, at least since 1977.

 There's no hyperbole here. No recency bias. No twisting the numbers to make them say something they don't. It's just a fact, one as plain as Allen wearing No. 17 for the Buffalo Bills .

 Dating back to 1977 (sorry, Jim Brown fans) when play-by-play data for NFL games became available, 153 players have carried from the 1- or 2-yard line at least 30 times. Allen, who's carried 53 times, has converted those carries into 43 touchdowns, a scoring rate of 81.1% to top the list.

 No one is within five percentage points of Allen's scoring rate, and only three players (Hall of Fame running back Earl Campbell, MVP quarterback Cam Newton and mid-aughts battering ram T.J. Duckett) land within 15 percentage points of Allen.

 

 Allen has seven goal line rushing touchdowns this season -- one of the reasons the Bills are 5-1 -- in just six games. The only quarterbacks who've ever reached seven goal line TDs over a full season are Newton, Jalen Hurts and Allen himself. Heck, Allen's already halfway toward besting the single-season mark for short-yardage TDs set by any player, which stands at 13 -- set by Jamaal Williams in 2022.

 Ask Allen, his teammates and his coaches and they'll tell you there are nights of intricate, bespoke game-planning required to make these sneak plays work. But there's also an awareness in the locker room that's a tad unnecessary. As one teammate told ESPN, the plays work because Allen's bigger and stronger than just about any other goal line threat.

 For all the tendency evaluations and pre-snap motions and dummy counts the Bills can throw at opponents, so much of the success can be simplified to Allen being a one-of-one siege weapon.

 "I wish I could tell you that it's just 'Hey, we just put it up' and then move on to the next play," coach Joe Brady says. "But there's a lot that goes into it. Maybe sometimes too much. We just are fortunate that we have a 6-foot-4, 230 or 6-foot-5, whatever he is, guy that usually does a good job going and getting it."

 

 Tush push effect 

 With 87 career rushing touchdowns, Allen's already crossed the goal line more times than any QB in NFL history, and his eight rushing touchdowns this season is tied for the league lead and is on pace to break he and Hurts' single-season rushing touchdowns record for a quarterback (15).

 He was in rarified air to start the season, becoming only the fourth player to rush for multiple touchdowns in the first three games -- matching Priest Holmes (2003), Stephen Davis (1999) and Hall of Famer Jim Brown (1958).

 With 39 rushing yards on Sunday against the  Baltimore Ravens  (1 p.m. ET, CBS), Allen would become the fifth QB in league history to surpass 5,000 for a career, joining Lamar Jackson , Michael Vick, Russell Wilson and Newton. With two more rushing touchdowns, Allen will become the eighth player this century, regardless of position, to run for double-digit touchdowns in four consecutive seasons.

 

 Before getting too much further, let's be honest and address the tush-push-shaped elephant in the room. Campbell didn't have a tight end giving him a boost.

 When Newton sprung up for a Superman celebration, there was never a fullback standing next to him pretending to be his greatest supporter -- a la Jimmy Olsen. Meanwhile, 22 of Allen's 43 short-yardage TDs (51%) have come on traditional push plays.

 Two things, though: First off, changes to rules, strategies and circumstances unseat record holders in all sports. Babe Ruth's short porch home runs still count, as do Michael Phelps' gold medals from before the full-body swimsuit was banned.

 And second, there's the Hurts comparison. If the "Brotherly Shove" was the whole reason for Allen's success, then its poster boy wouldn't be nearly 20% less successful in converting goal line carries into touchdowns.

 That said, 21 of Allen's 22 tush push scores have come since Brady took over as the Bills' playcaller midway through the 2023 season. Since that point, just six of Allen's 27 short-yardage touchdowns have come on non-push plays. And that list of six still includes two from early this season where the Bills didn't line up in push formation but a back still came to Allen's aid late in the play.

 

 

 Pushing through the pain 
 End of the day, it's all circular logic anyway. Push plays are a big reason for Allen's success, and Allen's size and power are a big reason why the Bills are comfortable running so many push plays. Whether the tush push is the chicken or the egg, Allen's still scoring.

 And crucially, those plays don't gain their reputation for being automatic without a whole lot of gritting, grinding effort.

 "It's torture," offensive tackle Dion Dawkins says. "It's torture under there."

 "Those sneaks aren't as glamorous as everyone thinks they are," Allen adds. "You're putting yourself up to getting some nice little hits on you there."

 Therein lies the central conflict of Allen's scoring pace. Brady and Allen are adamant that the plan is to build an offense that allows the quarterback to absorb fewer hits.

 Yet the offense is unambiguously gearing up for more short-yardage scores than ever. From 2019 to 2024, just 14% of the Bills' drives reached the opponent's 5-yard line. In 2025, that number jumped to 19%. This season, it's hovering around 21%.

 So now it's time to play the odds against the protective instincts. As established, Allen scores on 81% of his carries from the 2-yard line and in. Bills running back James Cook III scores at a 50% clip (11-for-22 career).

 The Bills are making their choice clear. This year Cook has three carries in these situations and has scored once. Allen has seven carries in these situations and has scored every time.

 It all but makes sense to go with what's automatic.

title: Browns balance relishing close wins, lamenting slow starts
summary: Despite a "complete game" by Deshaun Watson, offensive struggles are still lingering for the AFC North-leading Browns.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Smiling in another victorious  Cleveland Browns  postgame locker room, cornerback Denzel Ward made light of the team's latest close victory before getting serious.

 "I got to give the fans something to watch and enjoy, you know," he said. "It boosts the NFL ratings, so I know they are loving that. But no, we definitely just got to continue to fight early on, to eliminate the mistakes and just put us in better position towards the end of the game to where it don't have to be a last-second drop."

 Before the Browns finished their latest game-winning drive, an NFL-high fifth this season, they had to overcome a first-quarter, 14-point deficit to the Tennessee Titans . Kicker Andre Szmyt 's hit a game-winning 32-yard field goal as time expired in a 27-24 win .

 

 The victory moved the AFC North-leading Browns to 5-2 for the first time since 2020 and just the second time since the franchise returned to Cleveland in 1999. Their growth, though, and legitimacy in the AFC hierarchy will be tested in Sunday's divisional matchup against the host  Pittsburgh Steelers  ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ). The Browns defeated the Steelers in Cleveland in their first matchup, a 27-24 win in Week 4, but haven't won a regular-season game in Pittsburgh since October 2003, which spans 22 straight losses.

 Despite the Browns' strong start to the season, Cleveland's minus-13 point differential is the second lowest by a team to start 5-2 or better over the past decade (behind only the 2020 Browns, who had a minus-21 point margin). Almost every victory has followed a similar script: a slow start, typically on offense, followed by clutch plays late to eke out a close win.

 Struggles particularly on offense (19 points per game, fifth fewest in the NFL) are a big reason why the Browns still have the lowest odds to win the AFC North , despite having a 2-0 record in the division with wins against the Steelers and Baltimore Ravens . According to ESPN Analytics, Cleveland has a 5.5% chance to win the division. The Browns also have a 26.8% chance to reach the playoffs, the lowest odds in the division.

 Cleveland, though, witnessed signs of growth against the Titans, specifically on the side of the ball that has seen the most issues. The unit totaled a season-high 491 yards as quarterback Deshaun Watson threw for 308 yards, his first 300-yard passing game with the Browns.

 "That was the most complete game," Browns coach Todd Monken said. "That was close to Pittsburgh in terms of where to go with the ball, being in control with his composure. The way we operated was better, not perfect, but better on the road. But a real credit to [Watson], and that's all we're trying to do. He has something in him to be able to make plays when it counts and we're trying to flatline our play earlier in the game to be more consistent."

 The return of running backs Quinshon Judkins and Dylan Sampson from injury also helped spearhead a running game that registered a season-high 183 rushing yards.

 "We ran the ball better. To me that's the biggest thing," Monken said. "It is so hard if you can't run the football, and we've been making it hard."

 

 The composure and ability of the Browns to execute late is maybe even more impressive given the team's youth. Cleveland has the second-youngest team in the NFL but hasn't wavered in late-game situations, whether it be at home or on the road.

 "Coach Monk has put us in these situations in practice time after time after time after time again," said rookie wide receiver KC Concepcion , who recorded a career-high 152 scrimmage yards. "So whenever we get into the game and whenever we get into these situations, we already have the confidence to go down there and set up a game-winning drive."

 There's a delicate balance, though, between appreciating the resiliency that has allowed the Browns to string game-winning drives in each victory and not becoming complacent about the mistakes that have placed them in those close-game predicaments. Watson put a positive spin on Cleveland's string of close wins.

 "We wish we had some blowout games. But again, it's hard to do in this league, man," Watson said. "So right now, I think we finished these games and we build this hope and this chemistry, and this feel where we know we can finish these games, and hopefully soon we can get some of those games where we can put them away.

 "With a young team and a young staff and everyone new, it's actually good and can be beneficial for us in the long run that we have these type of games."

title: Cowboys handle Eagles on Javonte Williams' career night
summary: Williams rushed for a career-high 155 yards and added a touchdown for Dallas.
full_text:
PHILADELPHIA -- The Cowboys were able to go on the road and handle business against the Eagles , winning 38-21 on "Monday Night Football" after an impressive showing by Dallas running back  Javonte Williams  and the offense.

 Williams finished with a career-high 155 rushing yards and punched in his eighth rushing touchdown of the season, tied for the NFL's lead.

 If the Cowboys were going to be considered an actual threat in the NFC East, they had to start winning games.

 An offense that scored a combined 29 points over the previous two contests was able to light up the scoreboard to beat the Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field for the first time since 2021. The Cowboys ran the ball as well as they had all season, finishing with 204 yards.

 Dallas quarterback  Dak Prescott registered three touchdown passes -- two to CeeDee Lamb  and one to George Pickens  -- and the offense had a turnover-free outing. 

 The Cowboys' defense was still up and down, but it made plays against a backup quarterback, Tanner McKee , that it did not make against another backup quarterback, the  Tampa Bay Buccaneers '  Jalon Daniels , two games ago.

 The win moved the Cowboys (3-4) into second place in the NFC East -- behind the New York Giants (4-2-1) -- with ESPN Analytics giving Dallas a 57% chance of winning the division.

 Here are the most important things to know from Monday night for both teams:

 

 

 

 Dallas Cowboys (3-4) 

 What to make of the QB performance:  Prescott struggled in the two games coming into this one -- throwing four interceptions while under a ton of pressure from the Tampa Bay and  Green Bay  defenses. The Eagles did not put up the same pressure -- on just 15% of Prescott's dropbacks through three quarters -- and he made them pay. It was the sixth time Prescott tallied at least three touchdown passes versus the Eagles. And it was the ninth multiple-touchdown passing game Prescott has had against them; only Eli Manning (15) and Sonny Jurgensen (10) logged more while facing Philadelphia. Prescott, now 39-11 versus NFC East foes,   finished the night 15-of-27 for 212 yards.

 Trend to watch: One way the Cowboys discussed getting Pickens more involved in the offense was moving him around the formation. His first two catches came with him in the slot. His first went for nine yards, aligned on Cooper DeJean . His second came with him being defended by safety Andrew Mukuba  while running a wheel route down the sideline for a 21-yard score. In the first half, Pickens lined up in the slot seven times, which was as many times as he had lined up in the slot in an entire game over the first six weeks. He ended up doing so nine times in Monday's game. 

 Stat to know: The Cowboys' defense must not know when games begin. For the fifth time this season -- and the fourth straight game -- Dallas allowed a touchdown on the opposing team's opening possession. This time, it was with a less-than-100% Saquon Barkley on an 8-yard run out to cap a four-play, 75-yard drive. The 35 points allowed on the opening drive is the second most in the league, and the Cowboys' five opening-drive TDs allowed is tied for the most with the  Cleveland Browns and the Miami Dolphins .  -- Todd Archer 

 Next game:  vs. Arizona Cardinals (1 p.m. ET, Sunday)

 

 

 

 Philadelphia Eagles (2-5) 
 The problem with a bad season is it's never just one thing.

 The Eagles' offense finally got going Monday, but the defense was diced up all night in allowing 416 yards, resulting in a fifth consecutive defeat.

 Barkley's gutty effort on a bad hamstring and rookie wide receiver  Makai Lemon 's first-career touchdown weren't enough as Philadelphia inched closer and closer to a lost season. 

 Barkley clearly was playing through pain -- he spent time in the medical tent, got stretched out of the team bench and often looked hobbled -- yet was still extremely effective. He had seven carries for 62 yards and a touchdown while adding two receptions for nine yards. But it appears Barkley sustained another injury Monday, as it was announced in the fourth quarter that he was questionable with a back injury. He did not return.

 McKee, making his second start in place of Jalen Hurts , went 23-of-35 for 211 passing yards and a touchdown with one interception.

 Most surprising performance: The pattern through the first six weeks was that the defense would put up a good fight for most of the game before succumbing in the fourth quarter, in part because it wore down while playing opposite an offense that was unable to sustain drives. Monday night's contest was a different story. Prescott faced little pressure in the pocket, the Cowboys' run game met little resistance and Dallas amassed 330 yards of offense before even getting the ball in the fourth quarter. This will go down as one of the worst defensive performances in coordinator Vic Fangio's two-plus years with Philadelphia.

 Trend to watch: Facing Dallas' defense helped the Eagles shake their slow-start blues. They scored 10 points and racked up 124 yards in the first quarter, both season highs. Philadelphia came in averaging 0.5 points and 56.7 yards in the opening frame. This was the third time since the start of last season that the Eagles scored a TD on each of their first two drives; all three have come against the Cowboys. 

 Stat to know: Barkley became the first starter in the past 20 seasons to play at least nine offensive snaps in a game and get a touch on all of them. The last non-starter to do it was Jaylen Wright for the Dolphins against the  Atlanta Falcons  in Week 8 of last season (10 touches on 10 snaps).   -- Tim McManus 

 Next game:  at Washington Commanders (8:20 p.m. ET, Sunday)

title: Sizing up NFL Week 7: Time to trust the Giants? Start Mendoza? Worry about Henry?
summary: Let's make sense of six takeaways from Sunday and spin them forward. Just how good is the Vikings' defense? What's wrong with the Ravens' run game? Are the Giants legit?
full_text:
Seven weeks isn't a long time, but it might as well be an eternity in football. Seven weeks ago, we were wondering whether the Chargers might have the most explosive offense of the 2026 NFL season , if anybody would be able to stop the Rams from marching to the Super Bowl and whether the Browns were actively tanking to land  Arch Manning  with the first overall pick in next year's draft. A lot has changed.

 Of course, in a league where each week can feel monumental and significant, actually separating the passing trends from what's really meaningful is both difficult and important. This time a year ago, the Chiefs' offensive struggles might have felt like a mirage, but they turned out to be real. And while Sam Darnold 's hot start didn't stick around into the second half, the Seahawks quarterback established that he had a higher ceiling than most of us would have expected before later showing that off with a brilliant performance in the critical NFC title game victory over the Rams.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Today, I want to take a closer look at some of the key players and storylines from Sunday's action and try to get a sense of whether what we saw was a notably good (or bad) day or a more substantial trend. And with two of the three unbeaten teams heading into Week 7 losing for the first time, it only seems reasonable to start with the last remaining undefeated.

 

 
 Jump to whether it's time to: 
 ... call the Vikings defense historically great 
 ... give up on the Texans' defense as elite 
 ... treat the Giants as NFC East favorites 
 ... move on from Glenn as Jets HC 
 ... start Mendoza in Las Vegas 
 ... start worrying about Henry in Baltimore 

 
 

 

 Is it time to ... start treating the Vikings as a historically great defense? 
 I don't think anybody is very surprised that the Vikings are fielding one of the best defenses in football. Brian Flores' unit was fourth in the NFL in points allowed per drive in 2024 and then again in 2025. There were changes during the offseason, notably the departure of edge rusher Jonathan Greenard , but the Vikings brought back Flores and many of the pieces that fueled the team's success over the past couple of seasons. Projecting the Vikings to be a top-five defense heading into 2026 wouldn't have been controversial.

 The Vikings are not just a top-five defense, though. They're No. 1, and it isn't particularly close. Through six games, Minnesota is allowing 1.1 points per possession. To put that in context, there's only one other team in the NFL allowing fewer than 1.7 points per drive, and that's the defending champion Seahawks at 1.4. After allowing the Packers to score two touchdowns in the first half of Week 1 , Flores' defense has allowed a total of four offensive touchdowns over the ensuing five and a half games.

 

 Is that historically great? It depends on where you set your cutoffs. Elite defenses from the turn of the century, such as the 2000 Ravens and 2002 Buccaneers, were playing in a different era of football with more liberal defensive rules against offenses that played more conservative styles and at slower paces. There were a handful of defenses from that era that allowed fewer points per drive than these Vikings, but it's more appropriate to start that look back in 2007, when the Patriots kicked off a more modern offensive era.

 Across that timeframe -- and looking at teams only through six games each season -- the Vikings are the 10th-best defense of the past 20 seasons. The No. 1 defense by a considerable margin through the first six games of those respective seasons was the 2019 Patriots, who were allowing a miniscule 0.4 points per possession.

 That Patriots team played a remarkably easy slate of opponents early in the season, and it's fair to wonder whether the Vikings might have also enjoyed a generous slate of opposing quarterbacks, given that they've faced Baker Mayfield , Malik Willis  and Tyler Shough in recent weeks. Of course, they also held a Bears offense that has been explosive and dynamic with Caleb Williams at the helm to three points through three-and-a-half quarters before Williams left the game with a hamstring injury .

 On Sunday against Indianapolis ,  Jonathan Taylor opened the scoring with a 38-yard touchdown run. But the Colts did precious little on offense afterward. Former Vikings backup Daniel Jones was limited to 64 net passing yards on 26 plays while being blitzed on more than 85% of his dropbacks. It was the highest blitz rate for any defense in a single game since 2013, and the Vikings unsurprisingly have the five highest on the list.

 The Colts made it into the red zone only once more, at which point they were forced back out by a holding penalty and a Jones sack. While Spencer Shrader missed two field goals on a frustrating day for Shane Steichen's team, the Colts barely mustered anything on offense after the early score.

 And what makes the Vikings such a particularly devastating unit is how the blitz and the threat of the blitz force offenses to react. While the Vikings are a dominant defense when they send extra pressure, they're an even more impressive pass defense when they don't send extra players after the quarterback. They allow just 3.6 yards per attempt and 2.8 yards per dropback when they rush four or fewer, both of which are the best marks for any defense through six games in the QBR era, which dates back to 2007. That's a direct product of shell-shocked offenses overloading their pass protection to account for Flores' blitzes, only to then see a limited number of eligible receivers flooded by seven or eight defenders dropping into coverage.

 

 The blitzes also keep teams out of play-action passing, which is the league's favorite way to create explosive plays on offense. The Vikings have faced play-action attempts on only 18% of opposing dropbacks this season, the second-lowest rate in the league. Teams try to run them out of the blitz and avoid third-and-long, but while they allowed a long touchdown to Taylor on Sunday, the Vikings have also been the league's best run defense in terms of success rate, preventing opponents from staying on schedule 66.7% of the time. Flores' defense turns everyone into dropback passers and then runs their pass protection through a shredder.

 And of course, while so many great defenses feature Hall of Fame talents, it's even more remarkable to see Flores' unit elevating players who weren't stars elsewhere. Harrison Smith was a Pro Bowl-caliber safety for a long time, and Dallas Turner is a first-round pick in the middle of a breakout season, but Minnesota has gotten so much out of players who weren't previously perceived to be standouts. That includes players such as  Andrew Van Ginkel , Byron Murphy Jr ., Isaiah Rodgers  and Eric Wilson .

 On Sunday, that spotlight shined on linebacker Blake Cashman . A backup with the Jets before emerging as a starter with the Texans, Cashman has taken his game to a new level during his three years in Minnesota. He wrecked shop against the Colts, with two sacks, four quick pressures and five total pressures on 12 rush attempts. The veteran looped around the line for one sack to knock the Colts out of field goal range, then ran through Taylor to overpower the star back and take down Jones. Having linebackers such as Cashman and Wilson who can hold up in coverage and absolutely terrify running backs in pass protection makes Flores' defensive vision come to life.

 Many of the defenses ahead of the Vikings in the top 10 for points per possession since 2007 weren't able to sustain their dominance over a full season. The 2009 Jets, 2019 Patriots and 2008 Ravens are the only teams to finish the season allowing fewer points per drive than the Vikings have so far this year. And there are elements of Minnesota's game that might not stick. The Vikings are second in turnover rate (15.9% of drives) and have allowed touchdowns on a league-low 23% of drives…

title: Jay-Z's greatest sports lyrics, ranked ahead of his Super Bowl show
summary: The Super Bowl headliner's catalog is packed with sports references -- here are the ones that top our list.
full_text:
One of the greatest rappers of all time -- or the greatest in many eyes -- Jay-Z is still out here adding to his legacy. We finally have an answer to a question that has hovered over 2026 ever since Jay-Z dubbed this year all about offense in his March 2026 cover story with GQ.

 

 Would Jigga actually select himself to perform on the Super Bowl stage he helped revitalize? 

 The answer is: you damn right, he will. So while we don't yet know the teams who'll be taking the field, we do know the man born Shawn Carter will be there at the 50-yard line waiting on them.

 History and Hov are well acquainted.

 The show is going to be full of trademark Jay hits. It'll also be full of sports lyrics, because if there's one thing Hov knows, it's sports. From deep dives into Michael Jordan history to NASCAR, scrambling quarterbacks and everything in between, a Jay-Z album might have more sports references than "SportsCenter" does.

 With such a robust history of sports references, we decided to rank his 10 best, most unexpected and clever. As they say, "the list is fluid."

 

 10. "And I sport fly s--- I should win an ESPY" - "Party Life" (2007) 
 This is a little bit of bias, so pardon us. Jay-Z shouting out the ESPYS is just pretty cool. Now he just needs to pull up and host or perform one of these years. When he does, he has our full permission to rap this exact lyric. Heck, he could even win an ESPY for the reference alone. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 

 9. "It's Hov tradition, Jeff Gordon of rap/ I'm back to claim pole position, holla at ya boy" -- "Never Let Me Down" (2004) 
 If there's one NASCAR driver who's going to get referenced in rap songs, it's going to be Jeff Gordon. His rap credentials are certified. It doesn't get more certified than a nod from Hov. As always, there's a double meaning here. In 2004, Jay had taken his short-lived retirement, and this was his claim that he's back to lead the way like he never left. Well, he kind of never did. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 

 8. "You cats is home screaming the fight's on/ I'm in the 1500 seats, watching Tyson/ Same night, same fight/ But one of us cats ain't playing right/ I let you tell it" -- "I Love The Dough" (1997) 

 

 One of rap history's great what-ifs is how much more music Jay-Z and his close friend the Notorious B.I.G. could've made if the latter hadn't been slain in 1997. The Mike Tyson reference here calls to mind Jay and Roc-A-Fella Records' 1995 trip to Sin City to watch Tyson's first post-prison fight against Peter McNeely. This same fight would also live in another Jay-Z classic, "Can I Live." -- Justin Tinsley 

 
 7. "I don't even know y'all name/ I'm too big for ya, the rap LeBron James " -- "Blow The Whistle" (2008) 

 

 Let this next sentence marinate. LeBron James has been playing in the NBA so long that Jay-Z once defended him against ... DeShawn Stevenson and Soulja Boy. Too $hort's "Blow The Whistle" was already a cultural classic and party anthem well outside The Bay by spring 2008. With Jigga jumping on the track, and the subject matter being LeBron during the NBA playoffs, the reach went nuclear. We never did get a response track from Soulja and DeShawn, though. In case you're wondering, too, The King averaged 30 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists in a six-game, first-round defeat of Washington . -- Justin Tinsley 

 
 6. "I told you '96 that I came to take this s--- and I did/ Handle my biz, I scramble like Randall with his/ Cunningham, but the only thing runnin' is numbers, fam" -- "Heart of the City" (2001) 

 

 Jigga held you down six summers, damn.

 Sorry, just had to finish that line. Among the quarterbacks of the past 50 years, one of the most underrated is still Randall Cunningham. He's one of the most beloved forces in Philadelphia Eagles  history. He put together a historic season in 1998 with the Minnesota Vikings alongside Cris Carter and a young rookie named Randy Moss. And, yes, the dude could scramble and make all kinds of plays with his legs. On Hov's timeless classic from a quarter century ago, Cunningham's mention lives on in musical bliss. -- Justin Tinsley 

 

 5. "I'ma stay winnin', rock the custom drop Bentleys/ Never eat at Denny's and party like Lil' Penny" -- "Who You Wit II" (1997) 

 

 Two of the best things Chris Rock ever did were "Everybody Hates Chris" and voicing Lil' Penny -- the charming, boisterous figurine that helped make Penny Hardaway a marketing darling. It's a reference you had to live to really appreciate. But, Hov, what's your beef with Denny's? You ever been there at 3 a.m. after a night of partying? Don't knock it until you try it! -- Justin Tinsley 

 

 4. "More than a street legend, homie, it's Hova/ More than a relief pitcher, I'm the closer/ The Mariano of The Marriott/ If money talks, the whole world's about to hear me out" -- "Go Crazy" (2005) 

 

 Being a legend in New York City is unlike being one anywhere else on the planet. Young Jeezy was the hottest rapper on the planet, and with his seminal 2005 classic "Thug Motivation 101," Jay couldn't resist temporarily pausing his "retirement" to get on the remix of one of the project's standouts. And, buddy, he delivered an absolute masterclass, equipped with a nod to the legendary New York Yankees closer Mariano Rivera. -- Justin Tinsley 

 

 3. "Worry I'm not the Mike Jordan of the mic recordin'/ It's Hovi Baby, you Kobe, maybe, Tracy McGrady/ Matter fact you a Harold Miner/ JR Rider, washed up on marijuana/ Even worse you a Pervis Ellis" -- "Pump It Up (Freestyle)" (2003) 

 

 If there's one thing Jay-Z is going to do, it's belittle his rap competition by making sports comparisons. This one is particularly nasty, as he tossed out these insults to Joe Budden -- over the beat of Joe Budden's song. Here's some lore, as the kids say: Joe Budden was supposed to be one of rap's next big stars, and his big single was "Pump It Up." Jay had heard the rumblings and wanted to remind everyone that he was still king of the mountain. So while dropping this freestyle over the "Pump It Up" beat, he made it known he was one of the GOATs and Joe was, well...all respect to Pervis Ellis. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 

 2. "Jiggaman is Diesel when I lift the 8 up" -- "Lyrical Exercise" (2001) 

 

 This one gets a healthy nod simply for the fact it took us so long to even understand what was going on here. The song, "Lyrical Exercise," is full of double entendres as he relates gym workouts to, well, any number of violent or illegal activities. For instance, "I spot ya, I lift the weight of ya watch of ya arm" is pretty straightforward. This lyric, though? Is not. At first blush, it's about holding up a weapon. However, it's actually a reference to this picture of Shaq (Diesel) lifting up teammate Kobe Bryant (No. 8). Whoa. It took the internet more than a decade to put this together, too. -- David Dennis Jr. 

 
 1. "I ball for real/ Y'all n---as is Sam Bowie/ And with the third pick, I made the Earth sick/ MJ, Him Jay, fadeaway perfect" -- "Hola Hovito" (2001) 
 

 Leave it up to Jay-Z to offer some real draft analysis in the middle of a verse. Of course, this is a reference to one of the biggest NBA draft blunders of all time when the  Portland Trail Blazers  picked Sam Bowie over Michael Jordan in 1984. And the rest, as they say, is history. Jay is making the comparison here that all these other rappers are busts and he's the real MJ. -- David Dennis Jr.
